abstract: The Adaptive Solutions CN APS architecture chip is a general purpose neurocomputer chip. It has 64 processors, each with 4 K bytes of local memory, running at 25 megahertz. It is capable of implementing most current neural network algorithms with on chip learning. This paper dis(cid:173) cusses the implementation of the Back Propagation algorithm on an array of these chips and shows performance figures from a clock accurate hard(cid:173) ware simulator. An eight chip configuration on one board can update 2.3 billion connections per second in learning mode and process 9.6 billion connections per second in feed forward mode.

This paper dis(cid:173) cusses the implementation of the Back Propagation algorithm on an array of these chips and shows performance figures from a clock accurate hard(cid:173) ware simulator. paragraphs: This paper describes implementing backpropagation on an array of CNAPS neurocomputer chips. Each chip contains 64 processors, each with 4 kilobytes of local memory, operating at 25 megahertz. The architecture is intended as a general-purpose platform for neural computation and supports learning on the chips themselves.

The focus is how a familiar neural training algorithm can run on this parallel hardware. The paper reports performance from a clock-accurate hardware simulator, which models the timing of the architecture. The configuration described combines eight chips on a single board, allowing the implementation to use the processing resources of multiple chips together.

For that configuration, the reported learning throughput is 2.3 billion connection updates per second, while feedforward processing reaches 9.6 billion connections per second. These figures distinguish the work involved in changing a network's weights from the work involved in evaluating it. The contribution is an implementation and simulated performance account showing how a programmable neural computing architecture can support both training and feedforward operation at substantial connection-processing rates.
summary.tldr: A clock-accurate simulation of eight CNAPS chips reports 2.3 billion connection updates per second for backpropagation.

title: Back Propagation Implementation on the Adaptive Solutions CNAPS Neurocomputer Chip

paragraphs: The paper introduces a fast software simulator for large networks of spiking neurons and synapses. It uses an event-driven representation to make simulation efficient while retaining several biologically relevant behaviors. The purpose is to support large-network studies without incurring the time required by a full compartmental-model simulation.

The simulated elements include spikes, refractory behavior, adaptation, and axonal delays. They also support the summation of postsynaptic current pulses and tonic current inputs. These features let the simulator represent both discrete firing events and important influences on when neurons fire. The authors report that the event-driven approach simulates large networks in a fraction of the time needed for the more detailed comparison model.

The work also connects software simulation to physical implementation. Corresponding analog CMOS VLSI circuit primitives were designed and characterized, allowing large circuits to be simulated before fabrication. The contribution therefore serves two related purposes: efficient exploration of spiking-network behavior and advance evaluation of circuits built from matching neural components.
summary.tldr: An event-driven simulator accelerates large spiking-network simulations and supports evaluation of corresponding analog circuits before fabrication.

title: Event-Driven Simulation of Networks of Spiking Neurons

abstract: We introduce a new approach for on-line recognition of handwrit(cid:173) ten words written in unconstrained mixed style. The preprocessor performs a word-level normalization by fitting a model of the word structure using the EM algorithm. Words are then coded into low resolution "annotated images" where each pixel contains informa(cid:173) tion about trajectory direction and curvature. The recognizer is a convolution network which can be spatially replicated. From the network output, a hidden Markov model produces word scores. The entire system is globally trained to minimize word-level errors.

Words are then coded into low resolution "annotated images" where each pixel contains informa(cid:173) tion about trajectory direction and curvature. The recognizer is a convolution network which can be spatially replicated. From the network output, a hidden Markov model produces word scores. The entire system is globally trained to minimize word-level errors.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a system for recognizing handwritten words recorded as writing trajectories, including words written in unconstrained mixed styles. Its design combines preprocessing, a spatial representation, a convolutional network, and a hidden Markov model. The components are trained together with the goal of reducing errors on complete words.

Preprocessing normalizes each word by fitting a model of its structure with the EM algorithm. The word is then represented as a low-resolution annotated image. Pixels carry information about the writing trajectory's direction and curvature, so the representation preserves aspects of pen movement within an image-like arrangement that the recognizer can process spatially.

A convolutional network analyzes this representation and can be replicated across space. A hidden Markov model uses the network's outputs to produce scores for candidate words. Global training ties these stages to the final recognition objective. The contribution is an integrated route from trajectory information to word decisions, with training organized around the errors that matter at the system's output.
summary.tldr: A globally trained handwriting recognizer combines trajectory-annotated images, a convolutional network, and a hidden Markov model to minimize word errors.

title: Globally Trained Handwritten Word Recognizer using Spatial Representation, Convolutional Neural Networks, and Hidden Markov Models

abstract: We formulate a model for probability distributions on image spaces. We show that any distribution of images can be factored exactly into condi(cid:173) tional distributions of feature vectors at one resolution (pyramid level) conditioned on the image information at lower resolutions. We would like to factor this over positions in the pyramid levels to make it tractable, but such factoring may miss long-range dependencies. To fix this, we in(cid:173) troduce hidden class labels at each pixel in the pyramid. The result is a hierarchical mixture of conditional probabilities, similar to a hidden Markov model on a tree. The model parameters can be found with max(cid:173) imum likelihood estimation using the EM algorithm. We have obtained encouraging preliminary results on the problems of detecting various ob(cid:173) jects in SAR images and target recognition in optical aerial images.

To fix this, we in(cid:173) troduce hidden class labels at each pixel in the pyramid. The result is a hierarchical mixture of conditional probabilities, similar to a hidden Markov model on a tree. paragraphs: This paper builds a probability model for images by organizing information across a resolution pyramid. It first shows that any image distribution can be decomposed exactly into conditional distributions of features at one resolution given image information at lower resolutions. This gives a precise way to relate finer image structure to coarser context.

Making the model manageable also calls for factoring computations across spatial positions. The authors identify a problem with that step: it can lose dependencies between distant parts of an image. They introduce hidden class labels at every pyramid pixel to address this issue, producing a hierarchy of mixtures of conditional probabilities with a structure resembling a hidden Markov model on a tree.

The model's parameters can be estimated by maximum likelihood using expectation-maximization. Preliminary applications include detecting objects in synthetic aperture radar images and recognizing targets in optical aerial images. The authors describe these results as encouraging. The contribution combines an exact multiresolution starting point with a structured probabilistic model intended to make image modeling tractable while retaining broader dependencies.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical image model uses hidden labels across resolution levels to address dependencies lost by simple spatial factorization.

title: Hierarchical Image Probability (H1P) Models

abstract: We extend recent work on the connection between loopy belief propagation and the Bethe free energy. Constrained minimization of the Bethe free energy can be turned into an unconstrained saddle-point problem. Both converging double-loop algorithms and standard loopy belief propagation can be inter- preted as attempts to solve this saddle-point problem. Stability analysis then leads us to conclude that stable (cid:12)xed points of loopy belief propagation must be (local) minima of the Bethe free energy. Perhaps surprisingly, the converse need not be the case: minima can be unstable (cid:12)xed points. We illustrate this with an example and discuss implications.
originalAbstract: We extend recent work on the connection between loopy belief propagation and the Bethe free energy. Constrained minimization of the Bethe free energy can be turned into an unconstrained saddle-point problem. Both converging double-loop algorithms and standard loopy belief propagation can be inter- preted as attempts to solve this saddle-point problem. Stability analysis then leads us to conclude that stable (cid:12)xed points of loopy belief propagation must be (local) minima of the Bethe free energy. Perhaps surprisingly, the converse need not be the case: minima can be unstable (cid:12)xed points. We illustrate this with an example and discuss implications.

paragraphs: The paper examines the relationship between loopy belief propagation and the Bethe free energy. These provide two perspectives on the same inference problem: an iterative algorithm and an optimization objective. The authors investigate what the stability of an algorithmic fixed point implies about its position in the objective's landscape.

They transform constrained Bethe free-energy minimization into an unconstrained saddle-point problem. Both converging double-loop algorithms and ordinary loopy belief propagation can then be interpreted as attempts to solve that problem. This shared formulation allows stability analysis to connect the behavior of the iterations with the character of the corresponding stationary solutions.

The main conclusion is directional: stable fixed points of loopy belief propagation must be local minima of the Bethe free energy. The reverse implication does not always hold, because a minimum can correspond to an unstable fixed point. The authors illustrate this with an example. Thus, identifying a local minimum alone does not establish that ordinary belief-propagation iterations will remain stable around it.
summary.tldr: Stable loopy-belief-propagation fixed points are local Bethe free-energy minima, but some such minima can be unstable fixed points.

title: Stable Fixed Points of Loopy Belief Propagation Are Local Minima of the Bethe Free Energy

abstract: We propose a family of kernels based on the Binet-Cauchy theorem and its ex- tension to Fredholm operators. This includes as special cases all currently known kernels derived from the behavioral framework, diffusion processes, marginalized kernels, kernels on graphs, and the kernels on sets arising from the subspace angle approach. Many of these kernels can be seen as the extrema of a new continuum of kernel functions, which leads to numerous new special cases. As an application, we apply the new class of kernels to the problem of clustering of video sequences with encouraging results.
originalAbstract: We propose a family of kernels based on the Binet-Cauchy theorem and its ex- tension to Fredholm operators. This includes as special cases all currently known kernels derived from the behavioral framework, diffusion processes, marginalized kernels, kernels on graphs, and the kernels on sets arising from the subspace angle approach. Many of these kernels can be seen as the extrema of a new continuum of kernel functions, which leads to numerous new special cases. As an application, we apply the new class of kernels to the problem of clustering of video sequences with encouraging results.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a family of kernel functions built from the Binet-Cauchy theorem and its extension to Fredholm operators. Its main contribution is a common mathematical construction that encompasses several previously developed approaches. The family includes the then-known kernels derived from the behavioral framework, diffusion processes, marginalized kernels, graphs, and subspace-angle methods for sets.

Many of these existing constructions appear as extreme cases within a new continuum of kernel functions. This relationship does more than place them under one name: it supplies intermediate possibilities and generates numerous new special cases. The framework therefore offers both a unifying account and a way to obtain additional kernels.

The authors apply the new kernel family to clustering video sequences and report encouraging results. That application gives a concrete use for the broader construction. The stated outcome combines mathematical generality with an initial empirical demonstration: diverse kernel approaches can be related through this family, and members of the family can support video clustering.
summary.tldr: Binet-Cauchy kernels unify several existing kernel families, generate new cases, and show encouraging video-clustering results.

title: Binet-Cauchy Kernels

abstract: In this paper we analyze the relationship between the computational capabilities of randomly connected networks of threshold gates in the timeseries domain and their dynamical properties. In particular we propose a complexity measure which we find to assume its highest values near the edge of chaos, i.e. the transition from ordered to chaotic dynamics. Furthermore we show that the proposed complexity measure predicts the computational capabilities very well: only near the edge of chaos are such networks able to perform complex computations on time series. Additionally a simple synaptic scaling rule for self-organized criticality is presented and analyzed.
originalAbstract: In this paper we analyze the relationship between the computational capabilities of randomly connected networks of threshold gates in the timeseries domain and their dynamical properties. In particular we propose a complexity measure which we find to assume its highest values near the edge of chaos, i.e. the transition from ordered to chaotic dynamics. Furthermore we show that the proposed complexity measure predicts the computational capabilities very well: only near the edge of chaos are such networks able to perform complex computations on time series. Additionally a simple synaptic scaling rule for self-organized criticality is presented and analyzed.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how the dynamics of a recurrent network relate to its ability to compute with time series. The networks consist of randomly connected threshold gates. The authors focus on the boundary between ordered and chaotic behavior, asking whether that transition identifies networks with particularly useful computational properties.

They propose a complexity measure and find that it reaches its highest values near this boundary. They also report that the measure predicts computational capability well. Within the network setting studied, complex time-series computations are possible only near the transition, tying the dynamical regime to the kinds of temporal processing the networks can perform.

The paper additionally presents and analyzes a simple synaptic scaling rule for self-organized criticality. This adds a mechanism for adjusting network connections toward the relevant dynamical condition to the analysis of why that condition matters. Together, the results connect a measurable property of network dynamics, observed computational capacity, and a rule for organizing the network’s operating regime.
summary.tldr: For the studied recurrent threshold networks, a complexity measure peaks near the edge of chaos and predicts time-series computational ability.

title: At the Edge of Chaos: Real-time Computations and Self-Organized Criticality in Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: To escape from the curse of dimensionality, we claim that one can learn non-local functions, in the sense that the value and shape of the learned function at x must be inferred using examples that may be far from x. With this objective, we present a non-local non-parametric density esti- mator. It builds upon previously proposed Gaussian mixture models with regularized covariance matrices to take into account the local shape of the manifold. It also builds upon recent work on non-local estimators of the tangent plane of a manifold, which are able to generalize in places with little training data, unlike traditional, local, non-parametric models.
originalAbstract: To escape from the curse of dimensionality, we claim that one can learn non-local functions, in the sense that the value and shape of the learned function at x must be inferred using examples that may be far from x. With this objective, we present a non-local non-parametric density esti- mator. It builds upon previously proposed Gaussian mixture models with regularized covariance matrices to take into account the local shape of the manifold. It also builds upon recent work on non-local estimators of the tangent plane of a manifold, which are able to generalize in places with little training data, unlike traditional, local, non-parametric models.

paragraphs: This paper addresses density estimation when high dimensionality makes nearby training examples scarce. The authors argue for learning non-local functions: the value and shape of a function at one location should be inferred using examples that may be far away. Their proposed nonparametric density estimator is designed around this use of information beyond the immediate neighborhood.

The estimator builds on Gaussian mixture models whose covariance matrices are regularized to reflect the local shape of a manifold. That shape describes how the data are arranged near a location. The method also draws on non-local estimators of manifold tangent planes, which characterize the local directions in which the manifold extends.

The important connection is that local geometric structure can itself be inferred non-locally. The cited tangent-plane estimators can generalize in regions containing little training data, unlike the traditional local nonparametric models discussed by the authors. The paper combines these ideas into a density estimator motivated by escaping the curse of dimensionality; the abstract presents that motivation as a claim, rather than a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: A non-local density estimator combines manifold-shaped Gaussian components with geometry inferred from potentially distant examples to address sparse high-dimensional data.

title: Non-Local Manifold Parzen Windows

abstract: We design a new learning algorithm for the Set Covering Machine from a PAC-Bayes perspective and propose a PAC-Bayes risk bound which is minimized for classifiers achieving a non trivial margin-sparsity trade-off.
originalAbstract: We design a new learning algorithm for the Set Covering Machine from a PAC-Bayes perspective and propose a PAC-Bayes risk bound which is minimized for classifiers achieving a non trivial margin-sparsity trade-off.
title: A PAC-Bayes approach to the Set Covering Machine

abstract: Neural probabilistic language models (NPLMs) have been shown to be competitive with and occasionally superior to the widely-used n-gram language models. The main drawback of NPLMs is their extremely long training and testing times. Morin and Bengio have proposed a hierarchical language model built around a binary tree of words that was two orders of magnitude faster than the non-hierarchical language model it was based on. However, it performed considerably worse than its non-hierarchical counterpart in spite of using a word tree created using expert knowledge. We introduce a fast hierarchical language model along with a simple feature-based algorithm for automatic construction of word trees from the data. We then show that the resulting models can outperform non-hierarchical models and achieve state-of-the-art performance.
originalAbstract: Neural probabilistic language models (NPLMs) have been shown to be competitive with and occasionally superior to the widely-used n-gram language models. The main drawback of NPLMs is their extremely long training and testing times. Morin and Bengio have proposed a hierarchical language model built around a binary tree of words that was two orders of magnitude faster than the non-hierarchical language model it was based on. However, it performed considerably worse than its non-hierarchical counterpart in spite of using a word tree created using expert knowledge. We introduce a fast hierarchical language model along with a simple feature-based algorithm for automatic construction of word trees from the data. We then show that the resulting models can outperform non-hierarchical models and achieve state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Neural probabilistic language models can compete with familiar n-gram models, but their training and prediction costs can make them difficult to use. This paper addresses that computational problem through a hierarchy of words. The motivation is to retain the predictive strengths of neural language modeling while making the model faster to train and evaluate.

An earlier hierarchical approach organized words into a binary tree and achieved a large speed improvement, but its predictive performance suffered despite using expert knowledge to construct the tree. The proposed work introduces both a fast hierarchical language model and a simple algorithm that automatically builds word trees from features in the data. The organization of the vocabulary therefore becomes part of the proposed solution.

The authors show that the resulting models can outperform non-hierarchical models and achieve performance they describe as state of the art. The finding matters because it demonstrates that the earlier accuracy penalty need not accompany every hierarchical design. In the reported work, automatic tree construction supports a model that combines computational efficiency with strong prediction.
summary.tldr: A fast hierarchical language model automatically builds word trees from data and can outperform non-hierarchical models.

title: A Scalable Hierarchical Distributed Language Model

abstract: We study worst-case bounds on the quality of any fixed point assignment of the max-product algorithm for Markov Random Fields (MRF). We start proving a bound independent of the MRF structure and parameters. Afterwards, we show how this bound can be improved for MRFs with particular structures such as bipartite graphs or grids. Our results provide interesting insight into the behavior of max-product. For example, we prove that max-product provides very good results (at least 90% of the optimal) on MRFs with large variable-disjoint cycles (MRFs in which all cycles are variable-disjoint, namely that they do not share any edge and in which each cycle contains at least 20 variables).
originalAbstract: We study worst-case bounds on the quality of any fixed point assignment of the max-product algorithm for Markov Random Fields (MRF). We start proving a bound independent of the MRF structure and parameters. Afterwards, we show how this bound can be improved for MRFs with particular structures such as bipartite graphs or grids. Our results provide interesting insight into the behavior of max-product. For example, we prove that max-product provides very good results (at least 90% of the optimal) on MRFs with large variable-disjoint cycles (MRFs in which all cycles are variable-disjoint, namely that they do not share any edge and in which each cycle contains at least 20 variables).

paragraphs: The max-product algorithm produces assignments for Markov random fields, but assessing an assignment’s quality requires comparing it with the optimum. This paper studies worst-case guarantees for assignments associated with any fixed point of the algorithm. The question is how good such a result must be, even in unfavorable cases.

The authors first prove a bound that does not depend on the field’s particular graph structure or parameter values. They then show that structural information can improve the guarantee, including for bipartite graphs and grids. This gives a progression from a broadly applicable bound to stronger conclusions for specified families of models.

One concrete result guarantees at least 90 percent of the optimal value for fields whose cycles satisfy the stated disjointness condition and each contain at least 20 variables. The abstract describes those cycles as variable-disjoint. This is a conditional guarantee about fixed-point assignment quality. It illustrates how the organization and size of cycles can support a much stronger assessment of max-product’s output.
summary.tldr: Worst-case bounds characterize max-product fixed-point quality, with stronger guarantees for specific graph structures and sufficiently large disjoint cycles.

title: Worst-case bounds on the quality of max-product fixed-points

abstract: The goal of this paper is to investigate the advantages and disadvantages of learning in Banach spaces over Hilbert spaces. While many works have been carried out in generalizing Hilbert methods to Banach spaces, in this paper, we consider the simple problem of learning a Parzen window classifier in a reproducing kernel Banach space (RKBS)---which is closely related to the notion of embedding probability measures into an RKBS---in order to carefully understand its pros and cons over the Hilbert space classifier. We show that while this generalization yields richer distance measures on probabilities compared to its Hilbert space counterpart, it however suffers from serious computational drawback limiting its practical applicability, which therefore demonstrates the need for developing efficient learning algorithms in Banach spaces.
originalAbstract: The goal of this paper is to investigate the advantages and disadvantages of learning in Banach spaces over Hilbert spaces. While many works have been carried out in generalizing Hilbert methods to Banach spaces, in this paper, we consider the simple problem of learning a Parzen window classifier in a reproducing kernel Banach space (RKBS)---which is closely related to the notion of embedding probability measures into an RKBS---in order to carefully understand its pros and cons over the Hilbert space classifier. We show that while this generalization yields richer distance measures on probabilities compared to its Hilbert space counterpart, it however suffers from serious computational drawback limiting its practical applicability, which therefore demonstrates the need for developing efficient learning algorithms in Banach spaces.

paragraphs: The paper examines what is gained and lost when learning methods move from Hilbert spaces to Banach spaces. Rather than surveying every possible learning task, it studies a specific example: a Parzen window classifier in a reproducing kernel Banach space. This focused comparison is intended to make the benefits and costs of the generalization clear.

The classifier is closely connected to embedding probability measures into the space. Through this viewpoint, the authors show that the Banach-space construction provides a richer collection of distance measures between probability distributions than its Hilbert-space counterpart. The additional flexibility therefore concerns how distributions can be represented and compared within the learning method.

That representational gain comes with a serious computational drawback in the approach studied, limiting practical applicability. The result presents a concrete tradeoff between richer probability comparisons and the difficulty of carrying out the associated learning computation. The authors use this finding to motivate efficient learning algorithms for Banach spaces, whose development would be needed to make fuller practical use of the added flexibility.
summary.tldr: A Banach-space classifier offers richer distribution distances but faces serious computational obstacles in the formulation studied.

title: Learning in Hilbert vs. Banach Spaces: A Measure Embedding Viewpoint

abstract: We propose an efficient Bayesian nonparametric model for discovering hierarchical community structure in social networks. Our model is a tree-structured mixture of potentially exponentially many stochastic blockmodels. We describe a family of greedy agglomerative model selection algorithms whose worst case scales quadratically in the number of vertices of the network, but independent of the number of communities. Our algorithms are two orders of magnitude faster than the infinite relational model, achieving comparable or better accuracy.
originalAbstract: We propose an efficient Bayesian nonparametric model for discovering hierarchical community structure in social networks. Our model is a tree-structured mixture of potentially exponentially many stochastic blockmodels. We describe a family of greedy agglomerative model selection algorithms whose worst case scales quadratically in the number of vertices of the network, but independent of the number of communities. Our algorithms are two orders of magnitude faster than the infinite relational model, achieving comparable or better accuracy.

paragraphs: Social networks can contain communities organized at several levels, so discovering their structure involves more than assigning every vertex to a single flat grouping. This paper proposes a Bayesian nonparametric model for finding such hierarchical organization. Its representation combines community models within a tree, allowing the hierarchy itself to be part of the network description.

Specifically, the model is a tree-structured mixture of potentially exponentially many stochastic blockmodels. The large collection of possible blockmodels gives the representation considerable scope, while the paper supplies a family of greedy agglomerative algorithms for selecting a model. These algorithms build the organization through successive merging decisions.

The stated worst-case computational scaling is quadratic in the number of network vertices and independent of the number of communities. That separates the cost of the proposed selection procedure from the potentially large number of groups. The authors report algorithms two orders of magnitude faster than the infinite relational model, with comparable or better accuracy, supporting the practical value of their hierarchical construction.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian hierarchical community model pairs a rich tree representation with algorithms reported to be much faster than the infinite relational model.

title: Bayesian Hierarchical Community Discovery

abstract: We propose a general framework for reconstructing and denoising single entries of incomplete and noisy entries. We describe: effective algorithms for deciding if and entry can be reconstructed and, if so, for reconstructing and denoising it; and a priori bounds on the error of each entry, individually. In the noiseless case our algorithm is exact. For rank-one matrices, the new algorithm is fast, admits a highly-parallel implementation, and produces an error minimizing estimate that is qualitatively close to our theoretical and the state-of-the-art Nuclear Norm and OptSpace methods.
originalAbstract: We propose a general framework for reconstructing and denoising single entries of incomplete and noisy entries. We describe: effective algorithms for deciding if and entry can be reconstructed and, if so, for reconstructing and denoising it; and a priori bounds on the error of each entry, individually. In the noiseless case our algorithm is exact. For rank-one matrices, the new algorithm is fast, admits a highly-parallel implementation, and produces an error minimizing estimate that is qualitatively close to our theoretical and the state-of-the-art Nuclear Norm and OptSpace methods.

paragraphs: Matrix completion usually evaluates reconstruction of an entire low-rank matrix, but a user may care about one particular missing entry. This paper develops a framework for deciding whether that entry is recoverable and estimating its uncertainty. The focus is local accuracy within an incomplete, noisy matrix.

The authors provide algorithms for entry reconstructability, reconstruction, and denoising, along with prior error bounds for each individual entry. In the noiseless case, reconstruction is exact. For rank-one matrices, the resulting algorithm is fast and supports substantial parallelization.

The rank-one estimator minimizes error in the studied formulation and performs comparably to strong nuclear-norm and OptSpace approaches in the reported comparison. The contribution adds entry-specific reasoning to low-rank recovery: some entries can be well determined even when a global summary is uninformative, and uncertainty can be attached to the actual quantity a downstream user wants.
summary.tldr: Entry-wise matrix-completion methods determine recoverability, reconstruct individual values, and provide local error bounds, with efficient rank-one algorithms.

title: Error-Minimizing Estimates and Universal Entry-Wise Error Bounds for Low-Rank Matrix Completion

abstract: Learning dynamic models from observed data has been a central issue in many scientific studies or engineering tasks. The usual setting is that data are collected sequentially from trajectories of some dynamical system operation. In quite a few modern scientific modeling tasks, however, it turns out that reliable sequential data are rather difficult to gather, whereas out-of-order snapshots are much easier to obtain. Examples include the modeling of galaxies, chronic diseases such Alzheimer's, or certain biological processes. Existing methods for learning dynamic model from non-sequence data are mostly based on Expectation-Maximization, which involves non-convex optimization and is thus hard to analyze. Inspired by recent advances in spectral learning methods, we propose to study this problem from a different perspective: moment matching and spectral decomposition. Under that framework, we identify reasonable assumptions on the generative process of non-sequence data, and propose learning algorithms based on the tensor decomposition method \cite{anandkumar2012tensor} to \textit{provably} recover first-order Markov models and hidden Markov models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first formal guarantee on learning from non-sequence data. Preliminary simulation results confirm our theoretical findings.
originalAbstract: Learning dynamic models from observed data has been a central issue in many scientific studies or engineering tasks. The usual setting is that data are collected sequentially from trajectories of some dynamical system operation. In quite a few modern scientific modeling tasks, however, it turns out that reliable sequential data are rather difficult to gather, whereas out-of-order snapshots are much easier to obtain. Examples include the modeling of galaxies, chronic diseases such Alzheimer's, or certain biological processes. Existing methods for learning dynamic model from non-sequence data are mostly based on Expectation-Maximization, which involves non-convex optimization and is thus hard to analyze. Inspired by recent advances in spectral learning methods, we propose to study this problem from a different perspective: moment matching and spectral decomposition. Under that framework, we identify reasonable assumptions on the generative process of non-sequence data, and propose learning algorithms based on the tensor decomposition method \cite{anandkumar2012tensor} to \textit{provably} recover first-order Markov models and hidden Markov models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first formal guarantee on learning from non-sequence data. Preliminary simulation results confirm our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Learning a dynamic model usually relies on observations recorded in sequence. This paper considers settings where reliable sequences are difficult to obtain but unordered snapshots are more accessible. The challenge is to recover information about a changing process even though the observations do not arrive as a recorded trajectory.

The authors approach this problem through moment matching and spectral decomposition. They identify assumptions on how non-sequence observations are generated, then develop tensor-decomposition algorithms for recovering first-order Markov models and hidden Markov models. The assumptions are essential: the recovery guarantee concerns data generated under the specified framework, rather than arbitrary collections of unordered observations.

The paper contrasts this approach with existing expectation-maximization methods, whose nonconvex optimization makes theoretical analysis difficult. Its principal contribution is a provable recovery result for learning from non-sequence data, described by the authors as the first formal guarantee of this kind to their knowledge. Preliminary simulations support the theoretical findings, providing an initial empirical check of the proposed learning approach.
summary.tldr: Tensor-decomposition algorithms provably recover Markov and hidden Markov models from unordered observations under stated generative assumptions.

title: Learning Hidden Markov Models from Non-sequence Data via Tensor Decomposition

abstract: Scene recognition is one of the hallmark tasks of computer vision, allowing definition of a context for object recognition. Whereas the tremendous recent progress in object recognition tasks is due to the availability of large datasets like ImageNet and the rise of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for learning high-level features, performance at scene recognition has not attained the same level of success. This may be because current deep features trained from ImageNet are not competitive enough for such tasks. Here, we introduce a new scene-centric database called Places with over 7 million labeled pictures of scenes. We propose new methods to compare the density and diversity of image datasets and show that Places is as dense as other scene datasets and has more diversity. Using CNN, we learn deep features for scene recognition tasks, and establish new state-of-the-art results on several scene-centric datasets. A visualization of the CNN layers' responses allows us to show differences in the internal representations of object-centric and scene-centric networks.

paragraphs: Recognizing a scene means identifying the broader visual setting, which can also provide context for recognizing objects. The paper observes that progress in scene recognition had not matched progress in object recognition. It suggests that features learned from object-focused ImageNet data may be insufficiently suited to scene tasks, motivating a dataset centered on scenes.

The authors introduce Places, containing more than seven million labeled scene pictures. They also propose ways to compare the density and diversity of image datasets. Under these comparisons, Places has density comparable to other scene datasets while offering greater diversity. This evaluates the collection along dimensions beyond its raw image count.

Using Places to train convolutional networks, the authors learn features that establish new state-of-the-art results on several scene-focused datasets. Visualizations of layer responses also reveal differences between the internal representations of object-focused and scene-focused networks. The results connect the choice of training images to both recognition performance and the kinds of representations learned inside a network.
summary.tldr: Places supplies over seven million labeled scene images and enables scene-trained CNN features with leading reported recognition results.

title: Learning Deep Features for Scene Recognition using Places Database

abstract: We present two new methods for inference in Gaussian process (GP) models with general nonlinear likelihoods. Inference is based on a variational framework where a Gaussian posterior is assumed and the likelihood is linearized about the variational posterior mean using either a Taylor series expansion or statistical linearization. We show that the parameter updates obtained by these algorithms are equivalent to the state update equations in the iterative extended and unscented Kalman filters respectively, hence we refer to our algorithms as extended and unscented GPs. The unscented GP treats the likelihood as a 'black-box' by not requiring its derivative for inference, so it also applies to non-differentiable likelihood models. We evaluate the performance of our algorithms on a number of synthetic inversion problems and a binary classification dataset.

paragraphs: Gaussian process models with nonlinear likelihoods can require approximate inference. This paper develops two methods within a variational framework that assumes a Gaussian posterior. Both simplify the nonlinear likelihood around the current variational posterior mean, giving a common starting point for updating the approximation to the unknown quantities.

The methods differ in how they construct that simplification. One uses a Taylor expansion, while the other uses statistical linearization. The authors show that the resulting parameter updates match the state-update equations of iterative extended and unscented Kalman filters, respectively. This equivalence motivates the names extended and unscented Gaussian processes and connects the proposed inference algorithms to established filtering updates.

A practical feature of the unscented method is that it does not require derivatives of the likelihood. It can therefore treat the likelihood as a black box and applies to nondifferentiable likelihood models as well. The authors evaluate the methods on synthetic inversion problems and a binary classification dataset. The stated contribution is the inference construction and its applicability, rather than an abstract-level claim of superior performance.
summary.tldr: Two variational GP inference methods connect to Kalman-filter updates, with the unscented version supporting derivative-free likelihood inference.

title: Extended and Unscented Gaussian Processes

abstract: Supervised topic models simultaneously model the latent topic structure of large collections of documents and a response variable associated with each document. Existing inference methods are based on either variational approximation or Monte Carlo sampling. This paper presents a novel spectral decomposition algorithm to recover the parameters of supervised latent Dirichlet allocation (sLDA) models. The Spectral-sLDA algorithm is provably correct and computationally efficient. We prove a sample complexity bound and subsequently derive a sufficient condition for the identifiability of sLDA. Thorough experiments on a diverse range of synthetic and real-world datasets verify the theory and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the algorithm.

This paper presents a novel spectral decomposition algorithm to recover the parameters of supervised latent Dirichlet allocation (sLDA) models. paragraphs: Supervised topic models connect two kinds of information: the hidden topics within documents and a response associated with each document. Learning these models requires recovering parameters that describe that joint structure. The paper introduces Spectral-sLDA, a spectral decomposition algorithm for supervised latent Dirichlet allocation, providing an alternative to inference based on variational approximation or Monte Carlo sampling.

The authors establish correctness and computational efficiency for the algorithm. They also prove a sample complexity bound, which addresses the amount of data needed for parameter recovery. From this analysis, they derive a sufficient condition for identifiability: a condition under which the model's parameters can be distinguished. Sufficiency means that satisfying the condition provides a guarantee, without claiming it is the only possible route to identification.

Experiments across synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical analysis and demonstrate practical effectiveness. The contribution combines a parameter-recovery algorithm with guarantees about recovery and identifiability, connecting an alternative computational method to evidence that it works in the evaluated document-modeling settings.
summary.tldr: Spectral-sLDA recovers supervised topic-model parameters with correctness and sample-complexity guarantees, supported by synthetic and real-data experiments.

title: Spectral Methods for Supervised Topic Models

abstract: We study the fundamental limits to communication-efficient distributed methods for convex learning and optimization, under different assumptions on the information available to individual machines, and the types of functions considered. We identify cases where existing algorithms are already worst-case optimal, as well as cases where room for further improvement is still possible. Among other things, our results indicate that without similarity between the local objective functions (due to statistical data similarity or otherwise) many communication rounds may be required, even if the machines have unbounded computational power.
originalAbstract: We study the fundamental limits to communication-efficient distributed methods for convex learning and optimization, under different assumptions on the information available to individual machines, and the types of functions considered. We identify cases where existing algorithms are already worst-case optimal, as well as cases where room for further improvement is still possible. Among other things, our results indicate that without similarity between the local objective functions (due to statistical data similarity or otherwise) many communication rounds may be required, even if the machines have unbounded computational power.

paragraphs: Distributed learning divides work among machines, but those machines still need to exchange information to solve a shared problem. This paper studies fundamental limits on that communication for convex learning and optimization. Its analysis varies both the information available locally and the kinds of objective functions being optimized.

The results separate settings where existing algorithms already attain the best possible worst-case communication behavior from settings where further improvement remains possible. Worst-case optimality means that no method covered by the corresponding assumptions can uniformly avoid the identified difficulty. This distinction helps determine whether reducing communication calls for a better algorithm or stronger assumptions about the problem.

A central finding concerns similarity between machines’ local objectives. Without such similarity, many communication rounds may be necessary even when local computation is unlimited. Similarity may arise from statistically similar data or other structure. The result shows why additional processing power alone may not remove the coordination bottleneck: information held across machines can still need repeated exchange.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies communication limits in distributed convex optimization, showing that dissimilar local objectives can require many rounds despite unlimited local computation.

title: Communication Complexity of Distributed Convex Learning and Optimization

abstract: We propose a novel deep neural network architecture for semi-supervised semantic segmentation using heterogeneous annotations. Contrary to existing approaches posing semantic segmentation as region-based classification, our algorithm decouples classification and segmentation, and learns a separate network for each task. In this architecture, labels associated with an image are identified by classification network, and binary segmentation is subsequently performed for each identified label by segmentation network. The decoupled architecture enables us to learn classification and segmentation networks separately based on the training data with image-level and pixel-wise class labels, respectively. It facilitates to reduce search space for segmentation effectively by exploiting class-specific activation maps obtained from bridging layers. Our algorithm shows outstanding performance compared to other semi-supervised approaches even with much less training images with strong annotations in PASCAL VOC dataset.

Our algorithm shows outstanding performance compared to other semi-supervised approaches even with much less training images with strong annotations in PASCAL VOC dataset.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns class labels to individual image pixels, but training data can provide different levels of detail. Some images identify only which classes are present, while others label pixels. This paper designs a neural architecture that uses both forms of annotation by separating image classification from segmentation.

A classification network first identifies the labels associated with an image. A separate segmentation network then performs binary segmentation for each identified label, deciding which pixels belong to that class. The networks can be learned separately from image-level and pixel-level labels, respectively. Bridging layers supply class-specific activation maps that help narrow the segmentation search space.

On PASCAL VOC, the authors report strong performance relative to other semi-supervised methods despite using substantially fewer images with detailed annotations. The finding supports the architectural choice to give the two annotation types distinct roles. Image-level supervision helps establish what is present, while the segmentation component uses detailed supervision to learn where an identified class appears.
summary.tldr: Separate classification and segmentation networks use mixed annotation types to deliver strong segmentation results with fewer pixel-labeled training images.

title: Decoupled Deep Neural Network for Semi-supervised Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Deep neural networks have received a considerable attention due to the success of their training for real world machine learning applications. They are also of great interest to the understanding of sensory processing in cortical sensory hierarchies. The purpose of this work is to advance our theoretical understanding of the computational benefits of these architectures. Using a simple model of clustered noisy inputs and a simple learning rule, we provide analytically derived recursion relations describing the propagation of the signals along the deep network. By analysis of these equations, and defining performance measures, we show that these model networks have optimal depths. We further explore the dependence of the optimal architecture on the system parameters.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why depth can be computationally useful and how much depth a network should have. Rather than analyzing an unrestricted neural network, it studies a simple model with clustered, noisy inputs and a simple learning rule. That controlled setting makes it possible to derive mathematical descriptions of signal propagation.

The authors obtain recursion relations that describe how signals change as they pass through successive layers. They then define performance measures and analyze those equations to determine how network depth affects performance. This approach ties architectural choices to the evolution of signals inside the model, rather than treating the number of layers as an unexplained design parameter.

The analysis shows that these model networks have optimal depths. The authors also explore how the preferred architecture changes with system parameters. The result therefore supports a parameter-dependent balance in network depth within the studied setting. It contributes to theoretical understanding of deep computation while also relating to interest in hierarchical sensory processing in the cortex.
summary.tldr: An analytically tractable model shows that deep networks can have optimal depths that depend on the system's parameters.

title: Optimal Architectures in a Solvable Model of Deep Networks

abstract: The recent success of deep neural networks relies on massive amounts of labeled data. For a target task where labeled data is unavailable, domain adaptation can transfer a learner from a different source domain. In this paper, we propose a new approach to domain adaptation in deep networks that can jointly learn adaptive classifiers and transferable features from labeled data in the source domain and unlabeled data in the target domain. We relax a shared-classifier assumption made by previous methods and assume that the source classifier and target classifier differ by a residual function. We enable classifier adaptation by plugging several layers into deep network to explicitly learn the residual function with reference to the target classifier. We fuse features of multiple layers with tensor product and embed them into reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces to match distributions for feature adaptation. The adaptation can be achieved in most feed-forward models by extending them with new residual layers and loss functions, which can be trained efficiently via back-propagation. Empirical evidence shows that the new approach outperforms state of the art methods on standard domain adaptation benchmarks.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation transfers a learner from a labeled source domain to a target domain without labels. This paper addresses both the features used for prediction and the classifier that acts on them. It relaxes the assumption that source and target must share an identical classifier, instead assuming that their classifiers differ by a residual function.

Additional network layers explicitly learn that residual, allowing the classification rule to adapt. For feature adaptation, the method combines features from multiple layers using a tensor product and embeds them in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces to match distributions. These components jointly address differences in representations and in the classifiers associated with the two domains.

The approach can be incorporated into most feed-forward networks by adding residual layers and suitable losses, with training performed through backpropagation. Experiments on standard domain adaptation benchmarks show improvements over the state-of-the-art methods evaluated. The contribution is a joint adaptation strategy whose extra classifier flexibility is expressed through the stated residual relationship between source and target.
summary.tldr: Residual Transfer Networks jointly adapt features and classifiers using labeled source data and unlabeled target data.

title: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation with Residual Transfer Networks

abstract: We develop a probabilistic framework for deep learning based on the Deep Rendering Mixture Model (DRMM), a new generative probabilistic model that explicitly capture variations in data due to latent task nuisance variables. We demonstrate that max-sum inference in the DRMM yields an algorithm that exactly reproduces the operations in deep convolutional neural networks (DCNs), providing a first principles derivation. Our framework provides new insights into the successes and shortcomings of DCNs as well as a principled route to their improvement. DRMM training via the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm is a powerful alternative to DCN back-propagation, and initial training results are promising. Classification based on the DRMM and other variants outperforms DCNs in supervised digit classification, training 2-3x faster while achieving similar accuracy. Moreover, the DRMM is applicable to semi-supervised and unsupervised learning tasks, achieving results that are state-of-the-art in several categories on the MNIST benchmark and comparable to state of the art on the CIFAR10 benchmark.

paragraphs: This paper develops a probabilistic explanation of deep learning through the Deep Rendering Mixture Model, or DRMM. The model explicitly represents hidden nuisance variables: sources of variation in the data that are incidental to the task. This gives the framework a way to describe how observed data vary while separating those variations from the information needed for a prediction.

The central theoretical connection is that max-sum inference in this model exactly reproduces the operations of deep convolutional networks. This provides a derivation of those operations from a probabilistic model. The framework also supports training through Expectation-Maximization, offering an alternative to the backpropagation used to train convolutional networks.

The authors describe the initial training results as promising. In supervised digit classification, they report training two to three times faster while reaching similar accuracy. They also apply the framework to learning with limited or absent labels, reporting leading results in several MNIST categories and results comparable to leading methods on CIFAR10. These findings support both the explanatory framework and its practical training approach.
summary.tldr: A generative probabilistic model derives convolutional-network operations and offers an alternative training approach with promising classification results.

title: A Probabilistic Framework for Deep Learning

abstract: We study active learning where the labeler can not only return incorrect labels but also abstain from labeling. We consider different noise and abstention conditions of the labeler. We propose an algorithm which utilizes abstention responses, and analyze its statistical consistency and query complexity under fairly natural assumptions on the noise and abstention rate of the labeler. This algorithm is adaptive in a sense that it can automatically request less queries with a more informed or less noisy labeler. We couple our algorithm with lower bounds to show that under some technical conditions, it achieves nearly optimal query complexity.
originalAbstract: We study active learning where the labeler can not only return incorrect labels but also abstain from labeling. We consider different noise and abstention conditions of the labeler. We propose an algorithm which utilizes abstention responses, and analyze its statistical consistency and query complexity under fairly natural assumptions on the noise and abstention rate of the labeler. This algorithm is adaptive in a sense that it can automatically request less queries with a more informed or less noisy labeler. We couple our algorithm with lower bounds to show that under some technical conditions, it achieves nearly optimal query complexity.

paragraphs: Active learning concerns how a learner chooses which examples to ask someone to label. This paper studies a setting in which those requests do not always produce reliable answers: the labeler may give an incorrect label or decline to label an example at all. Both behaviors affect how much useful information the learner obtains from its queries.

The proposed algorithm uses abstention responses as part of learning. A refusal therefore becomes an input to the procedure rather than merely an unanswered request. The authors analyze statistical consistency and query complexity under assumptions about the labeler's noise and abstention rates. These address whether learning succeeds with sufficient information and how many requests it requires.

The algorithm adapts automatically to the labeler, potentially using fewer queries when responses are more informed or less noisy. The paper also establishes lower bounds against which to judge its query requirements. Under additional technical conditions, the algorithm comes close to those bounds, supporting a qualified claim of nearly optimal query complexity.
summary.tldr: An active learning algorithm uses both labels and abstentions, adapting its query requirements to labeler quality under stated conditions.

title: Active Learning from Imperfect Labelers

abstract: Several mechanisms to focus attention of a neural network on selected parts of its input or memory have been used successfully in deep learning models in recent years. Attention has improved image classification, image captioning, speech recognition, generative models, and learning algorithmic tasks, but it had probably the largest impact on neural machine translation. Recently, similar improvements have been obtained using alternative mechanisms that do not focus on a single part of a memory but operate on all of it in parallel, in a uniform way. Such mechanism, which we call active memory, improved over attention in algorithmic tasks, image processing, and in generative modelling. So far, however, active memory has not improved over attention for most natural language processing tasks, in particular for machine translation. We analyze this shortcoming in this paper and propose an extended model of active memory that matches existing attention models on neural machine translation and generalizes better to longer sentences. We investigate this model and explain why previous active memory models did not succeed. Finally, we discuss when active memory brings most benefits and where attention can be a better choice.

paragraphs: Attention helps a neural network focus on selected parts of its input or memory. This paper examines an alternative called active memory, which operates uniformly across the memory in parallel. Earlier active-memory mechanisms had shown benefits in several areas, yet had not surpassed attention on most language tasks, especially machine translation.

The authors investigate this gap and propose an extended active-memory model. The central question is whether processing memory broadly can provide the capabilities that make selective attention useful for translation. Their analysis also addresses why earlier versions of active memory fell short, linking the proposed extension to a specific weakness in previous approaches.

The extended model matches existing attention models on neural machine translation and generalizes better to longer sentences in the reported comparison. This makes active memory a credible alternative in the studied setting, without establishing that it replaces attention everywhere. The paper also discusses circumstances in which active memory offers the greatest benefits and circumstances in which attention may remain preferable. Its contribution is both an improved model and an examination of the choice between these mechanisms.
summary.tldr: An extended active-memory model matches attention on machine translation and generalizes better to longer sentences in the reported comparison.

title: Can Active Memory Replace Attention?

abstract: We consider the parametric learning problem, where the objective of the learner is determined by a parametric loss function. Employing empirical risk minimization with possibly regularization, the inferred parameter vector will be biased toward the training samples. Such bias is measured by the cross validation procedure in practice where the data set is partitioned into a training set used for training and a validation set, which is not used in training and is left to measure the out-of-sample performance. A classical cross validation strategy is the leave-one-out cross validation (LOOCV) where one sample is left out for validation and training is done on the rest of the samples that are presented to the learner, and this process is repeated on all of the samples. LOOCV is rarely used in practice due to the high computational complexity. In this paper, we first develop a computationally efficient approximate LOOCV (ALOOCV) and provide theoretical guarantees for its performance. Then we use ALOOCV to provide an optimization algorithm for finding the regularizer in the empirical risk minimization framework. In our numerical experiments, we illustrate the accuracy and efficiency of ALOOCV as well as our proposed framework for the optimization of the regularizer.

paragraphs: Parameters fitted by empirical risk minimization are influenced by their training data, so their performance must be assessed out of sample. Leave-one-out cross-validation repeatedly trains on every sample except one, but the repeated fitting makes it expensive. This paper develops a computationally efficient approximation to that procedure.

The proposed approximate leave-one-out cross-validation method, ALOOCV, comes with theoretical performance guarantees. The authors then use it within an optimization algorithm for choosing the regularizer in empirical risk minimization, connecting efficient performance estimation to the design of the fitted model.

Numerical experiments illustrate both the accuracy and efficiency of the approximation and the usefulness of regularizer optimization. The abstract supplies no specific datasets, speedups, or approximation-error values. Its contribution is the combination of a justified validation approximation and a method that uses that approximation to tune regularization, rather than an assertion that validation is unnecessary.
summary.tldr: Approximate leave-one-out validation makes regularizer selection more computationally practical.

title: On Optimal Generalizability in Parametric Learning

abstract: The inference of the causal relationship between a pair of observed variables is a fundamental problem in science, and most existing approaches are based on one single causal model. In practice, however, observations are often collected from multiple sources with heterogeneous causal models due to certain uncontrollable factors, which renders causal analysis results obtained by a single model skeptical. In this paper, we generalize the Additive Noise Model (ANM) to a mixture model, which consists of a finite number of ANMs, and provide the condition of its causal identifiability. To conduct model estimation, we propose Gaussian Process Partially Observable Model (GPPOM), and incorporate independence enforcement into it to learn latent parameter associated with each observation. Causal inference and clustering according to the underlying generating mechanisms of the mixture model are addressed in this work. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

paragraphs: Inferring a causal relationship between two variables becomes harder when observations come from different sources governed by different mechanisms. A single causal model may then give a misleading account of the combined data. This paper addresses that heterogeneity by allowing several underlying causal mechanisms within one model.

The authors extend the additive noise model to a finite mixture of such models and provide a condition under which its causal direction is identifiable. They introduce a Gaussian Process Partially Observable Model to estimate the mixture. The estimation procedure enforces independence while learning a latent parameter associated with each observation, connecting individual observations to the model’s hidden structure.

The approach addresses two related goals: inferring the causal relationship and clustering observations according to the mechanisms that generated them. Grouping by mechanism makes the heterogeneous structure part of the analysis rather than forcing every observation into one relationship. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the approach’s effectiveness, while the identifiability claim remains tied to the condition established in the paper.
summary.tldr: A mixture of additive noise models supports causal inference and mechanism-based clustering when observations arise from heterogeneous sources.

title: Causal Inference and Mechanism Clustering of A Mixture of Additive Noise Models

abstract: Kleinberg (2002) stated three axioms that any clustering procedure should satisfy and showed there is no clustering procedure that simultaneously satisfies all three. One of these, called the consistency axiom, requires that when the data is modified in a helpful way, i.e. if points in the same cluster are made more similar and those in different ones made less similar, the algorithm should output the same clustering. To circumvent this impossibility result, research has focused on considering clustering procedures that have a clustering quality measure (or a cost) and showing that a modification of Kleinberg’s axioms that takes cost into account lead to feasible clustering procedures. In this work, we take a different approach, based on the observation that the consistency axiom fails to be satisfied when the “correct” number of clusters changes. We modify this axiom by making use of cost functions to determine the correct number of clusters, and require that consistency holds only if the number of clusters remains unchanged. We show that single linkage satisfies the modified axioms, and if the input is well-clusterable, some popular procedures such as k-means also satisfy the axioms, taking a step towards explaining the success of these objective functions for guiding the design of algorithms.

paragraphs: Kleinberg's impossibility result shows that three proposed requirements for clustering cannot all hold simultaneously. One requirement, consistency, says a clustering should stay unchanged when members of each group become more similar and different groups become less similar. This paper examines why that seemingly helpful modification can still create a conflict.

The authors identify changes in the appropriate number of clusters as a source of the problem. They use cost functions to determine that number and revise consistency so it applies only when the number remains unchanged. This makes the requirement conditional on the grouping scale staying stable, rather than demanding the same partition across every qualifying modification.

They prove that single linkage satisfies the revised axioms. For inputs that are well-clusterable, some other popular procedures, including k-means, also satisfy them. The distinction matters: the k-means result depends on the structure of the input. The work offers a compatible set of requirements and helps explain why familiar clustering objectives can guide successful algorithms.
summary.tldr: Conditioning clustering consistency on an unchanged cluster count yields compatible axioms satisfied by single linkage and, on well-clusterable inputs, k-means.

title: Clustering Redemption–Beyond the Impossibility of Kleinberg’s Axioms

abstract: Variational inference is increasingly being addressed with stochastic optimization. In this setting, the gradient's variance plays a crucial role in the optimization procedure, since high variance gradients lead to poor convergence. A popular approach used to reduce gradient's variance involves the use of control variates. Despite the good results obtained, control variates developed for variational inference are typically looked at in isolation. In this paper we clarify the large number of control variates that are available by giving a systematic view of how they are derived. We also present a Bayesian risk minimization framework in which the quality of a procedure for combining control variates is quantified by its effect on optimization convergence rates, which leads to a very simple combination rule. Results show that combining a large number of control variates this way significantly improves the convergence of inference over using the typical gradient estimators or a reduced number of control variates.

paragraphs: Variational inference often relies on stochastic optimization, where gradients are estimated using randomness. High variance in those estimates can make optimization converge poorly. Control variates reduce that variability, but methods developed for variational inference have typically been considered individually. This paper asks how a large collection of them can be used together effectively.

The authors first give a systematic account of how available control variates are derived. They then introduce a Bayesian risk minimization framework for combining them. The framework evaluates a combination procedure through its effect on optimization convergence rates, connecting the statistical quality of the gradient estimate to the progress of the inference algorithm.

That analysis yields a simple combination rule. Reported results show that combining many control variates with this rule significantly improves convergence compared with typical gradient estimators or smaller collections of control variates. The contribution therefore goes beyond listing variance-reduction techniques: it supplies a principled way to combine them and demonstrates benefits for the optimization process they are intended to improve.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian framework yields a simple rule for combining many control variates, significantly improving variational-inference convergence in reported results.

title: Using Large Ensembles of Control Variates for Variational Inference

abstract: Despite its omnipresence in robotics application, the nature of spatial knowledge and the mechanisms that underlie its emergence in autonomous agents are still poorly understood. Recent theoretical works suggest that the Euclidean structure of space induces invariants in an agent’s raw sensorimotor experience. We hypothesize that capturing these invariants is beneficial for sensorimotor prediction and that, under certain exploratory conditions, a motor representation capturing the structure of the external space should emerge as a byproduct of learning to predict future sensory experiences. We propose a simple sensorimotor predictive scheme, apply it to different agents and types of exploration, and evaluate the pertinence of these hypotheses. We show that a naive agent can capture the topology and metric regularity of its sensor’s position in an egocentric spatial frame without any a priori knowledge, nor extraneous supervision.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how an agent might acquire spatial knowledge through its own movements and sensory observations. Its starting point is the idea that the Euclidean structure of the environment creates regularities in raw sensorimotor experience. Learning those regularities could therefore help an agent predict what it will sense after acting.

The authors hypothesize that, under suitable exploratory conditions, a representation of external spatial structure can emerge within a motor representation as a byproduct of prediction. They test this idea using a simple sensorimotor prediction scheme across different agents and forms of exploration. Spatial organization is thus evaluated as something learned through the prediction task, without separate spatial supervision.

The results show that a naive agent can capture both the topology and metric regularity of its sensor’s position in an agent-centered reference frame. These correspond to spatial organization and regularity in spatial distances. The demonstrated emergence requires no prior spatial knowledge or external supervision. The finding supports the proposed connection between sensorimotor prediction and spatial representation, with exploration conditions remaining part of the hypothesis.
summary.tldr: Under suitable exploration conditions, predicting sensory consequences can produce an agent-centered spatial representation without spatial supervision.

title: Unsupervised Emergence of Egocentric Spatial Structure from Sensorimotor Prediction

abstract: Continual learning aims to improve the ability of modern learning systems to deal with non-stationary distributions, typically by attempting to learn a series of tasks sequentially. Prior art in the field has largely considered supervised or reinforcement learning tasks, and often assumes full knowledge of task labels and boundaries. In this work, we propose an approach (CURL) to tackle a more general problem that we will refer to as unsupervised continual learning. The focus is on learning representations without any knowledge about task identity, and we explore scenarios when there are abrupt changes between tasks, smooth transitions from one task to another, or even when the data is shuffled. The proposed approach performs task inference directly within the model, is able to dynamically expand to capture new concepts over its lifetime, and incorporates additional rehearsal-based techniques to deal with catastrophic forgetting. We demonstrate the efficacy of CURL in an unsupervised learning setting with MNIST and Omniglot, where the lack of labels ensures no information is leaked about the task. Further, we demonstrate strong performance compared to prior art in an i.i.d setting, or when adapting the technique to supervised tasks such as incremental class learning.
