paragraphs: Continual learning concerns systems that keep learning as the data they encounter changes. Many approaches assume that tasks come with labels or clearly marked boundaries. CURL studies a less supervised setting: learning representations without being told which task an example belongs to, including streams with abrupt changes, gradual transitions, or shuffled observations.

CURL performs task inference inside the model rather than receiving task identities externally. It can also expand during learning to represent new concepts. Rehearsal-based techniques help address catastrophic forgetting, the loss of previously learned information as new data arrives. Together, these components address recognizing changing structure, accommodating it, and retaining earlier knowledge.

The authors demonstrate the approach on MNIST and Omniglot without labels, preventing those labels from revealing task information. They also report strong performance compared with earlier work when observations are independently and identically distributed and when the method is adapted to supervised incremental class learning. These findings suggest that the framework’s usefulness extends beyond a single ordering of tasks, while its central contribution remains representation learning without supplied task identity.
summary.tldr: CURL learns representations from changing unlabeled data by inferring tasks internally, expanding for new concepts, and rehearsing to reduce forgetting.

title: Continual Unsupervised Representation Learning

abstract: This paper proposes a method to ease the unsupervised learning of object landmark detectors. Similarly to previous methods, our approach is fully unsupervised in a sense that it does not require or make any use of annotated landmarks for the target object category. Contrary to previous works, we do however assume that a landmark detector, which has already learned a structured representation for a given object category in a fully supervised manner, is available. Under this setting, our main idea boils down to adapting the given pre-trained network to the target object categories in a fully unsupervised manner. To this end, our method uses the pre-trained network as a core which remains frozen and does not get updated during training, and learns, in an unsupervised manner, only a projection matrix to perform the adaptation to the target categories. By building upon an existing structured representation learned in a supervised manner, the optimization problem solved by our method is much more constrained with significantly less parameters to learn which seems to be important for the case of unsupervised learning. We show that our method surpasses fully unsupervised techniques trained from scratch as well as a strong baseline based on fine-tuning, and produces state-of-the-art results on several datasets. Code can be found at tiny.cc/GitHub-Unsupervised

paragraphs: The paper learns object landmarks without annotated landmarks for the target category. Its starting point is an explicit source of prior supervision: an available detector that has already learned a structured representation from labeled examples of another object category. The task is to adapt that existing structure to new categories without target landmark labels.

The pretrained network remains frozen throughout adaptation. Only a projection matrix is learned, using an unsupervised objective. This greatly reduces the number of trainable parameters and constrains the optimization problem. The authors suggest that these restrictions are important for unsupervised learning, where the target annotations needed to directly guide a more flexible adaptation are unavailable.

The method surpasses fully unsupervised approaches trained from scratch and a strong fine-tuning baseline, with state-of-the-art results reported on several datasets. The findings support transferring an existing structured representation through a small learned adaptation. The target learning is unsupervised, but the overall approach depends on access to a detector previously trained with supervision.
summary.tldr: A frozen supervised landmark detector can be adapted to unlabeled target categories by learning only a projection matrix.

title: Object landmark discovery through unsupervised adaptation

abstract: Synthetic visual data can provide practicically infinite diversity and rich labels, while avoiding ethical issues with privacy and bias. However, for many tasks, current models trained on synthetic data generalize poorly to real data. The task of 3D human pose estimation is a particularly interesting example of this sim2real problem, because learning-based approaches perform reasonably well given real training data, yet labeled 3D poses are extremely difficult to obtain in the wild, limiting scalability. In this paper, we show that standard neural-network approaches, which perform poorly when trained on synthetic RGB images, can perform well when the data is pre-processed to extract cues about the person’s motion, notably as optical flow and the motion of 2D keypoints. Therefore, our results suggest that motion can be a simple way to bridge a sim2real gap when video is available. We evaluate on the 3D Poses in the Wild dataset, the most challenging modern benchmark for 3D pose estimation, where we show full 3D mesh recovery that is on par with state-of-the-art methods trained on real 3D sequences, despite training only on synthetic humans from the SURREAL dataset.

paragraphs: Synthetic humans provide richly labeled training data for 3D pose estimation, where obtaining real-world 3D labels is difficult. Yet models trained on synthetic color images often transfer poorly to real images. This paper investigates whether representing motion can help bridge that gap between simulated training data and real observations.

The authors preprocess the data to extract optical flow and the movement of two-dimensional keypoints. Standard neural-network approaches that perform poorly when trained on synthetic RGB images can perform well with these motion cues. The finding suggests that changing the information presented to the network can make synthetic training more useful when video is available.

Evaluation on the 3D Poses in the Wild dataset shows full 3D mesh recovery comparable to state-of-the-art methods trained on real 3D sequences. The proposed approach trains only on synthetic humans from SURREAL. These results support motion as a simple transfer strategy for the evaluated setting, with the availability of video being a stated condition for using the relevant cues.
summary.tldr: Motion cues help models trained only on synthetic humans recover real-world 3D meshes at performance comparable to evaluated methods trained on real sequences.

title: Sim2real transfer learning for 3D human pose estimation: motion to the rescue

abstract: The instability of Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) training has frequently been attributed to gradient descent. Consequently, recent methods have aimed to tailor the models and training procedures to stabilise the discrete updates. In contrast, we study the continuous-time dynamics induced by GAN training. Both theory and toy experiments suggest that these dynamics are in fact surprisingly stable. From this perspective, we hypothesise that instabilities in training GANs arise from the integration error in discretising the continuous dynamics. We experimentally verify that well-known ODE solvers (such as Runge-Kutta) can stabilise training - when combined with a regulariser that controls the integration error. Our approach represents a radical departure from previous methods which typically use adaptive optimisation and stabilisation techniques that constrain the functional space (e.g. Spectral Normalisation). Evaluation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet shows that our method outperforms several strong baselines, demonstrating its efficacy.

paragraphs: GAN training is often unstable, and many methods modify models or discrete updates to control that instability. This paper instead examines the continuous-time dynamics underlying training. Its theory and toy experiments suggest those dynamics can be surprisingly stable, motivating a closer look at how numerical updates approximate them.

The authors hypothesize that discretization introduces integration errors responsible for training instability. They investigate established ordinary differential equation solvers, including Runge–Kutta methods, as training procedures. Experiments show that these solvers can stabilize training when combined with a regularizer that controls integration error. The combination is part of the reported result, rather than a claim that any ODE solver alone suffices.

Evaluations on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet outperform several strong baselines. The findings support numerical integration as a useful perspective for designing GAN training methods. They also provide experimental evidence consistent with the proposed explanation of instability, while the broader claim that discretization error causes GAN training instability remains framed as a hypothesis.
summary.tldr: ODE solvers combined with integration-error regularization stabilize GAN training, supporting the hypothesis that discretization contributes to instability.

title: Training Generative Adversarial Networks by Solving Ordinary Differential Equations

abstract: Many results in recent years established polynomial time learnability of various models via neural networks algorithms (e.g. \cite{andoni2014learning, daniely2016toward, daniely2017sgd, cao2019generalization, ziwei2019polylogarithmic, zou2019improved, ma2019comparative, du2018gradient, arora2019fine, song2019quadratic, oymak2019towards, ge2019mildly, brutzkus2018sgd}). However, unless the model is linear separable~\cite{brutzkus2018sgd}, or the activation is a polynomial~\cite{ge2019mildly}, these results require very large networks -- much more than what is needed for the mere existence of a good predictor. In this paper we prove that SGD on depth two neural networks can memorize samples, learn polynomials with bounded weights, and learn certain kernel spaces, with {\em near optimal} network size, sample complexity, and runtime. In particular, we show that SGD on depth two network with $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{m}{d}\right)$ hidden neurons (and hence $\tilde{O}(m)$ parameters) can memorize $m$ random labeled points in $\sphere^{d-1}$.

paragraphs: A network can be large enough to represent a good predictor without being easy for a training algorithm to find. Many earlier theoretical learning guarantees bridged that gap by requiring networks much larger than representation alone demanded. This paper investigates whether stochastic gradient descent can succeed with network sizes closer to what the task intrinsically requires.

The authors prove guarantees for depth-two neural networks on several tasks: memorizing samples, learning polynomials with bounded weights, and learning certain kernel spaces. Across these settings, they obtain near-optimal network size, sample complexity, and runtime. The contribution concerns the resources needed by a concrete learning algorithm, rather than only the existence of suitable network parameters.

A specific memorization result uses roughly m divided by d hidden neurons to fit m randomly labeled points on the sphere in d dimensions, up to logarithmic factors. The total parameter count is roughly m, again up to logarithmic factors. This shows that successful optimization need not require the very large excess parameter counts used in many prior guarantees for the tasks studied.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that stochastic gradient descent can memorize and learn specified function classes with depth-two networks using nearly optimal resources.

title: Neural Networks Learning and Memorization with (almost) no Over-Parameterization

abstract: Automatic differentiation, as implemented today, does not have a simple mathematical model adapted to the needs of modern machine learning. In this work we articulate the relationships between differentiation of programs as implemented in practice, and differentiation of nonsmooth functions. To this end we provide a simple class of functions, a nonsmooth calculus, and show how they apply to stochastic approximation methods. We also evidence the issue of artificial critical points created by algorithmic differentiation and show how usual methods avoid these points with probability one.
originalAbstract: Automatic differentiation, as implemented today, does not have a simple mathematical model adapted to the needs of modern machine learning. In this work we articulate the relationships between differentiation of programs as implemented in practice, and differentiation of nonsmooth functions. To this end we provide a simple class of functions, a nonsmooth calculus, and show how they apply to stochastic approximation methods. We also evidence the issue of artificial critical points created by algorithmic differentiation and show how usual methods avoid these points with probability one.

paragraphs: Automatic differentiation computes derivatives by following the operations in a program. This paper asks how that practical procedure relates to mathematical differentiation when the function being computed is nonsmooth. The distinction matters because a program's derivative calculations need a sound interpretation if they are to support an analysis of learning algorithms.

The authors develop a mathematical framework consisting of a class of functions and a calculus for handling their nonsmooth behavior. They connect this framework to stochastic approximation methods, bringing program differentiation and the analysis of iterative learning into the same account. The contribution is therefore a way to reason about computations already used in machine learning.

A central finding concerns artificial critical points created by algorithmic differentiation: points that appear critical because of the differentiation procedure. The paper identifies this issue and shows that the usual methods covered by its analysis avoid those points with probability one. This connects a potential mathematical complication to its consequences for stochastic learning, rather than simply treating every computed derivative as an ordinary smooth derivative.
summary.tldr: The paper provides a nonsmooth mathematical framework for automatic differentiation and explains why usual learning methods almost surely avoid the artificial critical points it can create.

title: A mathematical model for automatic differentiation in machine learning

abstract: We consider a covariate shift problem where one has access to several different training datasets for the same learning problem and a small validation set which possibly differs from all the individual training distributions. The distribution shift is due, in part, to \emph{unobserved} features in the datasets. The objective, then, is to find the best mixture distribution over the training datasets (with only observed features) such that training a learning algorithm using this mixture has the best validation performance. Our proposed algorithm, \textsf{Mix\&Match}, combines stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with optimistic tree search and model re-use (evolving partially trained models with samples from different mixture distributions) over the space of mixtures, for this task. We prove a novel high probability bound on the final SGD iterate without relying on a global gradient norm bound, and use it to show the advantages of model re-use. Additionally, we provide simple regret guarantees for our algorithm with respect to recovering the optimal mixture, given a total budget of SGD evaluations. Finally, we validate our algorithm on two real-world datasets.

paragraphs: When several datasets address the same prediction problem, their best combination may depend on the population where the model will be evaluated. This paper considers a small validation set whose distribution may differ from every available training dataset. Some of the shift arises from features that are not observed.

Mix&Match searches for mixture weights over the training datasets that yield the best validation performance. It combines stochastic gradient descent with optimistic tree search over possible mixtures. Crucially, it reuses partially trained models, continuing their training with samples from different mixtures instead of treating every candidate as a completely separate training run.

The authors prove a high-probability bound for the final SGD iterate without assuming a global gradient-norm bound, and use it to establish advantages of model reuse. They also provide simple-regret guarantees for finding the optimal mixture under a fixed budget of SGD evaluations. Evaluation on two real-world datasets supports the approach. The contribution makes training-data composition an optimization problem while explicitly accounting for the computational cost of searching.
summary.tldr: Mix&Match searches training-data mixtures with tree search and reusable SGD models, providing guarantees under a fixed training budget.

title: Mix and Match: An Optimistic Tree-Search Approach for Learning Models from Mixture Distributions

abstract: In this paper, we propose a new accelerated stochastic first-order method called clipped-SSTM for smooth convex stochastic optimization with heavy-tailed distributed noise in stochastic gradients and derive the first high-probability complexity bounds for this method closing the gap in the theory of stochastic optimization with heavy-tailed noise. Our method is based on a special variant of accelerated Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) and clipping of stochastic gradients. We extend our method to the strongly convex case and prove new complexity bounds that outperform state-of-the-art results in this case. Finally, we extend our proof technique and derive the first non-trivial high-probability complexity bounds for SGD with clipping without light-tails assumption on the noise.

Our method is based on a special variant of accelerated Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) and clipping of stochastic gradients. We extend our method to the strongly convex case and prove new complexity bounds that outperform state-of-the-art results in this case. Finally, we extend our proof technique and derive the first non-trivial high-probability complexity bounds for SGD with clipping without light-tails assumption on the noise.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization uses noisy gradient estimates to improve an objective. Heavy-tailed noise makes reliable guarantees challenging because unusually large gradient errors can matter. This paper studies smooth convex objectives in that setting and introduces clipped-SSTM, a method combining a special accelerated stochastic gradient procedure with gradient clipping.

Clipping limits the magnitude of stochastic gradient updates, while acceleration is built into the underlying optimization method. The authors derive high-probability complexity bounds for clipped-SSTM under heavy-tailed gradient noise. Such bounds describe computational requirements with a probabilistic guarantee, addressing a theoretical gap identified in the abstract.

The method is extended to strongly convex objectives, where the new complexity bounds improve on prior results. The proof technique also yields nontrivial high-probability bounds for ordinary stochastic gradient descent with clipping without assuming light-tailed noise. The contribution is thus both an accelerated algorithm and an analysis applicable to a simpler clipped method, with claims tied to the stated optimization settings.
summary.tldr: Clipped-SSTM combines acceleration and gradient clipping to obtain high-probability optimization guarantees under heavy-tailed gradient noise.

title: Stochastic Optimization with Heavy-Tailed Noise via Accelerated Gradient Clipping

abstract: We present a transductive learning algorithm that takes as input training examples from a distribution P and arbitrary (unlabeled) test examples, possibly chosen by an adversary. This is unlike prior work that assumes that test examples are small perturbations of P. Our algorithm outputs a selective classifier, which abstains from predicting on some examples. By considering selective transductive learning, we give the first nontrivial guarantees for learning classes of bounded VC dimension with arbitrary train and test distributions—no prior guarantees were known even for simple classes of functions such as intervals on the line. In particular, for any function in a class C of bounded VC dimension, we guarantee a low test error rate and a low rejection rate with respect to P. Our algorithm is efficient given an Empirical Risk Minimizer (ERM) for C. Our guarantees hold even for test examples chosen by an unbounded white-box adversary. We also give guarantees for generalization, agnostic, and unsupervised settings.

By considering selective transductive learning, we give the first nontrivial guarantees for learning classes of bounded VC dimension with arbitrary train and test distributions—no prior guarantees were known even for simple classes of functions such as intervals on the line. We also give guarantees for generalization, agnostic, and unsupervised settings.

paragraphs: Many approaches to adversarial learning assume that test inputs are small modifications of ordinary examples. This paper considers a broader setting: training examples come from a distribution P, while the unlabeled test examples can be arbitrary. The learner receives those test inputs in advance, making the problem transductive rather than requiring predictions for unseen future inputs.

The algorithm produces a selective classifier, which can decline to predict on some examples. This option enables guarantees for function classes with bounded VC dimension, a measure of their expressive capacity. The guarantees combine low test error with a low rejection rate measured against P. The reference distribution matters: the rejection guarantee does not say that few arbitrary adversarial inputs must be accepted or rejected.

The algorithm is efficient when an empirical risk minimizer for the function class is available. Its guarantees cover even an adversary with unlimited computation and full knowledge of the learner. The paper also establishes results for generalization, agnostic learning, and unsupervised settings, extending the role of selective prediction beyond small-perturbation robustness.
summary.tldr: Selective transductive learning provides guarantees for arbitrary adversarial test inputs by allowing abstention while keeping rejection low on the training distribution.

title: Beyond Perturbations: Learning Guarantees with Arbitrary Adversarial Test Examples

abstract: Continual Learning has inspired a plethora of approaches and evaluation settings; however, the majority of them overlooks the properties of a practical scenario, where the data stream cannot be shaped as a sequence of tasks and offline training is not viable. We work towards General Continual Learning (GCL), where task boundaries blur and the domain and class distributions shift either gradually or suddenly. We address it through mixing rehearsal with knowledge distillation and regularization; our simple baseline, Dark Experience Replay, matches the network's logits sampled throughout the optimization trajectory, thus promoting consistency with its past. By conducting an extensive analysis on both standard benchmarks and a novel GCL evaluation setting (MNIST-360), we show that such a seemingly simple baseline outperforms consolidated approaches and leverages limited resources. We further explore the generalization capabilities of our objective, showing its regularization being beneficial beyond mere performance.
originalAbstract: Continual Learning has inspired a plethora of approaches and evaluation settings; however, the majority of them overlooks the properties of a practical scenario, where the data stream cannot be shaped as a sequence of tasks and offline training is not viable. We work towards General Continual Learning (GCL), where task boundaries blur and the domain and class distributions shift either gradually or suddenly. We address it through mixing rehearsal with knowledge distillation and regularization; our simple baseline, Dark Experience Replay, matches the network's logits sampled throughout the optimization trajectory, thus promoting consistency with its past. By conducting an extensive analysis on both standard benchmarks and a novel GCL evaluation setting (MNIST-360), we show that such a seemingly simple baseline outperforms consolidated approaches and leverages limited resources. We further explore the generalization capabilities of our objective, showing its regularization being beneficial beyond mere performance.

paragraphs: Continual learning studies how a model learns from changing data while retaining useful previous knowledge. Many evaluation settings organize that data into distinct tasks. This paper instead targets General Continual Learning, where task boundaries are unclear, distributions can change gradually or abruptly, and collecting data for offline training is not a viable option.

The proposed baseline, Dark Experience Replay, combines rehearsal, knowledge distillation, and regularization. Its central mechanism matches the network's logits, or prediction scores, recorded at different points during training. Reusing these past outputs encourages the current network to remain consistent with earlier versions of itself. Historical predictions thus become a learning signal alongside experience from the changing stream.

The authors evaluate the method on standard benchmarks and a new setting called MNIST-360. They report that this simple combination outperforms established approaches while using limited resources. They also investigate generalization and find benefits from the regularization beyond the main performance comparison. The results make consistency with past predictions a strong baseline for learning under blurred task boundaries.
summary.tldr: Dark Experience Replay improves continual learning by rehearsing experience and matching past prediction scores as data distributions change.

title: Dark Experience for General Continual Learning: a Strong, Simple Baseline

abstract: Finding the k largest or smallest elements from a collection of scores, i.e., top-k operation, is an important model component widely used in information retrieval, machine learning, and data mining. However, if the top-k operation is implemented in an algorithmic way, e.g., using bubble algorithm, the resulted model cannot be trained in an end-to-end way using prevalent gradient descent algorithms. This is because these implementations typically involve swapping indices, whose gradient cannot be computed. Moreover, the corresponding mapping from the input scores to the indicator vector of whether this element belongs to the top-k set is essentially discontinuous. To address the issue, we propose a smoothed approximation, namely SOFT (Scalable Optimal transport-based diFferenTiable) top-k operator. Specifically, our SOFT top-k operator approximates the output of top-k operation as the solution of an Entropic Optimal Transport (EOT) problem. The gradient of the SOFT operator can then be efficiently approximated based on the optimality conditions of EOT problem. We then apply the proposed operator to k-nearest neighbors algorithm and beam search algorithm. The numerical experiment demonstrates their achieve improved performance.

paragraphs: Selecting the k highest or lowest scores is a common step in machine learning systems. However, a hard top-k selection creates a difficulty for gradient-based training: a small score change can abruptly change which items are selected. Implementations that swap indices also do not provide the gradients needed to train the surrounding model end to end.

The paper introduces SOFT top-k, a smooth approximation to this selection operation. It expresses the approximate selection as the solution of an entropic optimal transport problem. This gives the system a smoother relationship between input scores and selection outputs, making it possible to obtain useful gradients through the selection step.

The authors efficiently approximate those gradients using the transport problem's optimality conditions. They apply the operator to k-nearest neighbors and beam search, reporting improved performance in numerical experiments. The contribution is a way to incorporate an approximate top-k decision into gradient-based learning, allowing selection-dependent components to participate in training rather than leaving the hard selection step without a usable gradient.
summary.tldr: SOFT top-k uses entropic optimal transport to approximate hard selection with an operation that supports gradient-based training.

title: Differentiable Top-k with Optimal Transport

abstract: In Meta-Reinforcement Learning (meta-RL) an agent is trained on a set of tasks to prepare for and learn faster in new, unseen, but related tasks. The training tasks are usually hand-crafted to be representative of the expected distribution of target tasks and hence all used in training. We show that given a set of training tasks, learning can be both faster and more effective (leading to better performance in the target tasks), if the training tasks are appropriately selected. We propose a task selection algorithm based on information theory, which optimizes the set of tasks used for training in meta-RL, irrespectively of how they are generated. The algorithm establishes which training tasks are both sufficiently relevant for the target tasks, and different enough from one another. We reproduce different meta-RL experiments from the literature and show that our task selection algorithm improves the final performance in all of them.

Training tasks are often designed to resemble the expected target tasks, and then all are used. This paper asks whether choosing among the available tasks can improve both learning speed and eventual target-task performance.

The authors propose an information-theoretic selection algorithm that balances two considerations. Selected tasks should be relevant enough to the target tasks, while also differing sufficiently from one another. This makes task selection a joint problem of usefulness and variety, rather than simply accepting the entire available collection as the training set.

The selection procedure operates on a given set of tasks regardless of how those tasks were generated. The authors reproduce several meta-reinforcement-learning experiments from prior work and report better final performance in every reproduced experiment. Their results show that appropriate selection can make training faster and more effective, supporting the idea that the composition of training experience is itself an important part of meta-learning.
summary.tldr: Information-theoretic task selection improves meta-reinforcement learning by choosing training tasks that combine target relevance with diversity.

title: Information-theoretic Task Selection for Meta-Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Tracking objects of interest in a video is one of the most popular and widely applicable problems in computer vision. However, with the years, a Cambrian explosion of use cases and benchmarks has fragmented the problem in a multitude of different experimental setups. As a consequence, the literature has fragmented too, and now novel approaches proposed by the community are usually specialised to fit only one specific setup. To understand to what extent this specialisation is necessary, in this work we present UniTrack, a solution to address five different tasks within the same framework. UniTrack consists of a single and task-agnostic appearance model, which can be learned in a supervised or self-supervised fashion, and multiple ``heads'' that address individual tasks and do not require training. We show how most tracking tasks can be solved within this framework, and that the same appearance model can be successfully used to obtain results that are competitive against specialised methods for most of the tasks considered. The framework also allows us to analyse appearance models obtained with the most recent self-supervised methods, thus extending their evaluation and comparison to a larger variety of important problems.

paragraphs: Video tracking has split into many tasks and benchmarks, encouraging researchers to build methods specialized for particular experimental setups. This paper asks how much of that specialization is actually necessary for representing what objects look like. Its focus is whether one appearance model can serve several different tracking tasks.

The authors introduce UniTrack, which addresses five tasks within a shared framework. It combines a single appearance model with separate task-specific heads that require no training. The shared appearance model can itself be learned through either supervised or self-supervised training. This separation allows task-specific tracking procedures to use the same learned visual representation.

UniTrack obtains results competitive with specialized methods on most of the tasks considered. That finding supports sharing appearance models across multiple tracking settings without claiming that every task performs equally well. The framework also gives researchers a way to compare recent self-supervised appearance models across a wider range of tracking problems, extending evaluation beyond one specialized setup.
summary.tldr: UniTrack uses one shared appearance model and untrained task-specific heads to achieve competitive results on most of five tracking tasks.

title: Do Different Tracking Tasks Require Different Appearance Models?

abstract: Data deletion algorithms aim to remove the influence of deleted data points from trained models at a cheaper computational cost than fully retraining those models. However, for sequences of deletions, most prior work in the non-convex setting gives valid guarantees only for sequences that are chosen independently of the models that are published. If people choose to delete their data as a function of the published models (because they don’t like what the models reveal about them, for example), then the update sequence is adaptive. In this paper, we give a general reduction from deletion guarantees against adaptive sequences to deletion guarantees against non-adaptive sequences, using differential privacy and its connection to max information. Combined with ideas from prior work which give guarantees for non-adaptive deletion sequences, this leads to extremely flexible algorithms able to handle arbitrary model classes and training methodologies, giving strong provable deletion guarantees for adaptive deletion sequences. We show in theory how prior work for non-convex models fails against adaptive deletion sequences, and use this intuition to design a practical attack against the SISA algorithm of Bourtoule et al. [2021] on CIFAR-10, MNIST, Fashion-MNIST.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove a data point's influence from a trained model without paying the full cost of retraining. A complication arises when deletion requests depend on models already released. Someone might request deletion after seeing what a model reveals about them, so the model and the sequence of requests become connected.

This paper addresses that adaptive setting. It develops a general reduction that lets guarantees for deletion sequences chosen independently of published models support guarantees for adaptive sequences. The reduction uses differential privacy and its connection to max information to manage the dependence introduced by observing model outputs.

Combined with existing approaches for non-adaptive deletion, the result supports flexible algorithms with provable adaptive deletion guarantees across arbitrary model classes and training methods. The authors also show theoretically why earlier non-convex approaches can fail under adaptive requests. They turn that reasoning into a practical attack on SISA using CIFAR-10, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST, demonstrating why the distinction between adaptive and non-adaptive requests matters.
summary.tldr: The paper uses differential privacy to extend machine-unlearning guarantees to deletion requests that depend on previously published models.

title: Adaptive Machine Unlearning

abstract: We study the problem of reconstructing a causal graphical model from data in the presence of latent variables. The main problem of interest is recovering the causal structure over the latent variables while allowing for general, potentially nonlinear dependencies. In many practical problems, the dependence between raw observations (e.g. pixels in an image) is much less relevant than the dependence between certain high-level, latent features (e.g. concepts or objects), and this is the setting of interest. We provide conditions under which both the latent representations and the underlying latent causal model are identifiable by a reduction to a mixture oracle. These results highlight an intriguing connection between the well-studied problem of learning the order of a mixture model and the problem of learning the bipartite structure between observables and unobservables. The proof is constructive, and leads to several algorithms for explicitly reconstructing the full graphical model. We discuss efficient algorithms and provide experiments illustrating the algorithms in practice.

paragraphs: In many datasets, the causal relationships of interest concern hidden concepts rather than raw measurements. For an image, those concepts might be objects, while the observations are pixels. This paper studies recovery of the causal graph over latent variables while allowing the relationships involved to be general and potentially nonlinear.

The authors provide conditions under which both the latent representations and their causal model are identifiable. They establish this through a reduction to a mixture oracle. The central connection links determining the order of a mixture model with recovering the bipartite graph that connects observed variables to unobserved ones. This offers a route from mixture information to hidden graphical structure.

The proof is constructive, so the identifiability argument also leads to algorithms for explicitly reconstructing the full graphical model. The paper discusses efficient algorithms and includes experiments illustrating their use. Its contribution is therefore both a recovery result and an algorithmic pathway. The stated conditions are essential to interpreting the result: recovery of latent causal structure is established within that setting, rather than asserted for arbitrary observational data.
summary.tldr: Under stated identifiability conditions, mixture-oracle information enables constructive recovery of latent representations and their causal graph.

title: Learning latent causal graphs via mixture oracles

abstract: How can artificial agents learn to solve many diverse tasks in complex visual environments without any supervision? We decompose this question into two challenges: discovering new goals and learning to reliably achieve them. Our proposed agent, Latent Explorer Achiever (LEXA), addresses both challenges by learning a world model from image inputs and using it to train an explorer and an achiever policy via imagined rollouts. Unlike prior methods that explore by reaching previously visited states, the explorer plans to discover unseen surprising states through foresight, which are then used as diverse targets for the achiever to practice. After the unsupervised phase, LEXA solves tasks specified as goal images zero-shot without any additional learning. LEXA substantially outperforms previous approaches to unsupervised goal reaching, both on prior benchmarks and on a new challenging benchmark with 40 test tasks spanning across four robotic manipulation and locomotion domains. LEXA further achieves goals that require interacting with multiple objects in sequence. Project page: https://orybkin.github.io/lexa/

paragraphs: Learning many tasks without supervision requires an agent to find worthwhile goals and learn how to reach them. LEXA separates these responsibilities between an explorer and an achiever. Both learn through imagined trajectories generated by a world model trained from images, allowing the agent to practice using its learned account of the environment.

The explorer uses foresight to seek surprising states that have not yet been visited. Those discoveries become diverse targets for the achiever. This gives goal discovery and goal practice distinct roles: exploration expands the collection of targets, while the achiever learns to reliably reach them.

After unsupervised training, LEXA can attempt tasks specified by goal images without further learning. The authors report substantial improvements over previous unsupervised goal-reaching approaches on existing benchmarks and a new benchmark containing 40 tasks across four robotic manipulation and locomotion domains. They also report success on goals requiring sequential interaction with multiple objects. These findings show that the learned abilities can support both varied targets and goals involving several interactions.
summary.tldr: LEXA learns to discover and achieve diverse visual goals through world-model imagination, then tackles goal-image tasks without additional learning.

title: Discovering and Achieving Goals via World Models

abstract: Emphatic algorithms have shown great promise in stabilizing and improving reinforcement learning by selectively emphasizing the update rule. Although the emphasis fundamentally depends on an interest function which defines the intrinsic importance of each state, most approaches simply adopt a uniform interest over all states (except where a hand-designed interest is possible based on domain knowledge). In this paper, we investigate adaptive methods that allow the interest function to dynamically vary over states and iterations. In particular, we leverage meta-gradients to automatically discover online an interest function that would accelerate the agent’s learning process. Empirical evaluations on a wide range of environments show that adapting the interest is key to provide significant gains. Qualitative analysis indicates that the learned interest function emphasizes states of particular importance, such as bottlenecks, which can be especially useful in a transfer learning setting.

paragraphs: Emphatic reinforcement learning changes how strongly different learning updates are weighted. Its emphasis depends on an interest function that assigns importance to states. Most approaches use the same interest everywhere unless domain knowledge supports a manually designed alternative. This paper investigates learning that interest function automatically as the agent trains.

The proposed methods allow interest to vary across both states and training iterations. They use meta-gradients to discover an interest function online with the aim of accelerating learning. This makes the allocation of learning emphasis itself adjustable, rather than fixing every state's importance before the learning process begins.

Across a wide range of evaluated environments, adapting interest produces significant gains. Qualitative analysis shows that learned interest highlights particularly important states, including bottlenecks. Such emphasis can be especially useful in transfer learning, according to the study. The findings support adaptive state importance as a useful component of emphatic methods, with the empirical gains tied to the environments and learning settings examined.
summary.tldr: Learning which states deserve greater emphasis improves emphatic reinforcement learning across the evaluated environments.

title: Adaptive Interest for Emphatic Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recently, graph neural networks have been gaining a lot of attention to simulate dynamical systems due to their inductive nature leading to zero-shot generalizability. Similarly, physics-informed inductive biases in deep-learning frameworks have been shown to give superior performance in learning the dynamics of physical systems. There is a growing volume of literature that attempts to combine these two approaches. Here, we evaluate the performance of thirteen different graph neural networks, namely, Hamiltonian and Lagrangian graph neural networks, graph neural ODE, and their variants with explicit constraints and different architectures. We briefly explain the theoretical formulation highlighting the similarities and differences in the inductive biases and graph architecture of these systems. Then, we evaluate them on spring, pendulum, and gravitational and 3D deformable solid systems to compare the performance in terms of rollout error, conserved quantities such as energy and momentum, and generalizability to unseen system sizes. Our study demonstrates that GNNs with additional inductive biases, such as explicit constraints and decoupling of kinetic and potential energies, exhibit significantly enhanced performance. Further, all the physics-informed GNNs exhibit zero-shot generalizability to system sizes an order of magnitude larger than the training system, thus providing a promising route to simulate large-scale realistic systems.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks and physics-informed models both offer useful structure for learning dynamical systems. This paper compares thirteen graph neural networks to examine how different combinations of physical assumptions and graph architectures affect simulation performance. The models include Hamiltonian networks, Lagrangian networks, graph neural ordinary differential equations, and variants with explicit constraints.

The authors explain the theoretical formulations and evaluate the models on spring, pendulum, gravitational, and three-dimensional deformable solid systems. Their comparisons consider rollout error, preservation of quantities such as energy and momentum, and transfer to unseen system sizes. These criteria examine both predictive accuracy over trajectories and whether predictions retain relevant physical structure.

The study finds significantly enhanced performance from additional inductive biases, including explicit constraints and separating kinetic from potential energy. All the evaluated physics-informed graph networks also generalize without additional training to systems an order of magnitude larger than their training systems. These empirical findings support the potential of combining graph structure with physical knowledge for larger simulations, while distinguishing the design choices associated with stronger performance.
summary.tldr: A comparison of thirteen graph networks finds that additional physical structure improves simulation and supports transfer to substantially larger systems.

title: Unravelling the Performance of Physics-informed Graph Neural Networks for Dynamical Systems

abstract: A critical problem in the field of post hoc explainability is the lack of a common foundational goal among methods. For example, some methods are motivated by function approximation, some by game theoretic notions, and some by obtaining clean visualizations. This fragmentation of goals causes not only an inconsistent conceptual understanding of explanations but also the practical challenge of not knowing which method to use when.In this work, we begin to address these challenges by unifying eight popular post hoc explanation methods (LIME, C-LIME, KernelSHAP, Occlusion, Vanilla Gradients, Gradients × Input, SmoothGrad, and Integrated Gradients). We show that these methods all perform local function approximation of the black-box model, differing only in the neighbourhood and loss function used to perform the approximation. This unification enables us to (1) state a no free lunch theorem for explanation methods, demonstrating that no method can perform optimally across all neighbourhoods, and (2) provide a guiding principle to choose among methods based on faithfulness to the black-box model. We empirically validate these theoretical results using various real-world datasets, model classes, and prediction tasks.By bringing diverse explanation methods into a common framework, this work (1) advances the conceptual understanding of these methods, revealing their shared local function approximation objective, properties, and relation to one another, and (2) guides the use of these methods in practice, providing a principled approach to choose among methods and paving the way for the creation of new ones.

paragraphs: Post hoc explanation methods often appear to pursue different goals, making it difficult to understand their relationships or choose between them. This paper places eight popular methods in a common framework, including LIME, KernelSHAP, Occlusion, gradient-based explanations, SmoothGrad, and Integrated Gradients. The shared task is approximating a black-box model locally.

Within this framework, the methods differ in the neighborhood where they approximate the model and the loss function used to judge that approximation. Those choices make the intended meaning of faithfulness more explicit: an explanation is evaluated against particular model behavior around an input. The framework therefore connects method selection to the behavior one wants the explanation to reproduce.

The authors prove a no-free-lunch result showing that no explanation method is optimal across all neighborhoods. They also derive a principle for choosing methods based on faithfulness and validate their theoretical results across datasets, model classes, and prediction tasks. The contribution gives both a conceptual account of existing methods and a principled basis for selecting among them.
summary.tldr: Eight explanation methods share a local approximation objective, and choosing among them depends on the neighborhood and faithfulness criterion that matter.

title: Which Explanation Should I Choose? A Function Approximation Perspective to Characterizing Post Hoc Explanations

abstract: Long-term fairness is an important factor of consideration in designing and deploying learning-based decision systems in high-stake decision-making contexts. Recent work has proposed the use of Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) to formulate decision-making with long-term fairness requirements in dynamically changing environments, and demonstrated major challenges in directly deploying heuristic and rule-based policies that worked well in static environments. We show that policy optimization methods from deep reinforcement learning can be used to find strictly better decision policies that can often achieve both higher overall utility and less violation of the fairness requirements, compared to previously-known strategies. In particular, we propose new methods for imposing fairness requirements in policy optimization by regularizing the advantage evaluation of different actions. Our proposed methods make it easy to impose fairness constraints without reward engineering or sacrificing training efficiency. We perform detailed analyses in three established case studies, including attention allocation in incident monitoring, bank loan approval, and vaccine distribution in population networks.

paragraphs: A decision policy can affect the environment in ways that change future outcomes and fairness. Rules that work well in a static setting may therefore struggle when applied repeatedly. This paper studies long-term fairness through Markov decision processes, which represent decisions and their consequences in dynamically changing environments.

The authors use deep reinforcement learning to optimize policies and introduce fairness requirements through advantage regularization. Advantage evaluations assess the relative appeal of different actions; regularizing them makes fairness part of the policy update process. The proposed methods allow fairness constraints to be imposed without engineering a new reward or sacrificing training efficiency.

The paper reports that policy optimization can find strictly better policies than previously known strategies, often achieving both higher overall utility and fewer fairness violations. Detailed analyses cover incident-monitoring attention allocation, bank loan approval, and vaccine distribution in population networks. These results support learning policies with long-term consequences in view, while preserving the qualification that simultaneous gains in utility and fairness occur often rather than universally.
summary.tldr: Regularizing action advantages incorporates long-term fairness into policy optimization and often improves both utility and fairness in the studied settings.

title: Policy Optimization with Advantage Regularization for Long-Term Fairness in Decision Systems

abstract: Inferring causal structure poses a combinatorial search problem that typically involves evaluating structures with a score or independence test. The resulting search is costly, and designing suitable scores or tests that capture prior knowledge is difficult. In this work, we propose to amortize causal structure learning. Rather than searching over structures, we train a variational inference model to directly predict the causal structure from observational or interventional data. This allows our inference model to acquire domain-specific inductive biases for causal discovery solely from data generated by a simulator, bypassing both the hand-engineering of suitable score functions and the search over graphs. The architecture of our inference model emulates permutation invariances that are crucial for statistical efficiency in structure learning, which facilitates generalization to significantly larger problem instances than seen during training. On synthetic data and semisynthetic gene expression data, our models exhibit robust generalization capabilities when subject to substantial distribution shifts and significantly outperform existing algorithms, especially in the challenging genomics domain. Our code and models are publicly available at: https://github.com/larslorch/avici

The architecture of our inference model emulates permutation invariances that are crucial for statistical efficiency in structure learning, which facilitates generalization to significantly larger problem instances than seen during training. On synthetic data and semisynthetic gene expression data, our models exhibit robust generalization capabilities when subject to substantial distribution shifts and significantly outperform existing algorithms, especially in the challenging genomics domain. Our code and models are publicly available at: https://github.com/larslorch/avici

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships usually requires searching through many possible graphs and evaluating them with scores or statistical tests. This becomes expensive as the problem grows, and incorporating domain knowledge into those evaluations is difficult. The paper proposes learning a reusable inference model that predicts causal structure directly from observational data or data collected through interventions.

The model learns from simulator-generated examples, allowing domain-specific expectations about causal relationships to enter through training data. This moves the effort from repeatedly searching over graphs to training a predictor that can be applied to new datasets. Its architecture also respects permutation invariances: changes in ordering that should not change the underlying inference. The authors connect this design to statistical efficiency and generalization to substantially larger problems than those used during training.

On synthetic and semisynthetic gene-expression data, the models generalize robustly under substantial distribution shifts and significantly outperform existing algorithms, especially in genomics. These findings support amortized inference as a practical alternative to repeated causal-graph search in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: A simulator-trained model predicts causal graphs directly and shows strong generalization across larger problems and distribution shifts.

title: Amortized Inference for Causal Structure Learning

abstract: Bandits with knapsacks (BwK) is an influential model of sequential decision-making under uncertainty that incorporates resource consumption constraints. In each round, the decision-maker observes an outcome consisting of a reward and a vector of nonnegative resource consumptions, and the budget of each resource is decremented by its consumption. In this paper we introduce a natural generalization of the stochastic BwK problem that allows non-monotonic resource utilization. In each round, the decision-maker observes an outcome consisting of a reward and a vector of resource drifts that can be positive, negative or zero, and the budget of each resource is incremented by its drift. Our main result is a Markov decision process (MDP) policy that has constant regret against a linear programming (LP) relaxation when the decision-maker knows the true outcome distributions. We build upon this to develop a learning algorithm that has logarithmic regret against the same LP relaxation when the decision-maker does not know the true outcome distributions. We also present a reduction from BwK to our model that shows our regret bound matches existing results.

paragraphs: Bandits with knapsacks combines learning which actions earn rewards with constraints on resource use. In the standard formulation, each action consumes nonnegative amounts of resources, so budgets only decline. This paper generalizes the stochastic problem to allow resources to increase, decrease, or remain unchanged after an action.

The new formulation represents each outcome using a reward and resource drifts, which are added to the available budgets. The authors first consider a decision-maker who knows the true outcome distributions. For that setting, they construct a Markov decision process policy with constant regret relative to a linear programming relaxation.

They then use this result to build an algorithm for unknown outcome distributions, obtaining logarithmic regret against the same relaxation. The comparison target matters: the guarantees are explicitly measured against that linear programming benchmark. A reduction from ordinary bandits with knapsacks shows that the regret bound matches existing results. The work extends resource-constrained learning to replenishable resources while connecting its guarantees to the established consumption-only setting.
summary.tldr: A bandit model allowing resource replenishment admits logarithmic learning regret against a linear programming relaxation.

title: Non-monotonic Resource Utilization in the Bandits with Knapsacks Problem

abstract: The recent availability of large datasets in bio-medicine has inspired the development of representation learning methods for multiple healthcare applications. Despite advances in predictive performance, the clinical utility of such methods is limited when exposed to real-world data. This study develops model diagnostic measures to detect potential pitfalls before deployment without assuming access to external data. Specifically, we focus on modeling realistic data shifts in electrophysiological signals (EEGs) via data transforms and extend the conventional task-based evaluations with analyses of a) the model's latent space and b) predictive uncertainty under these transforms. We conduct experiments on multiple EEG feature encoders and two clinically relevant downstream tasks using publicly available large-scale clinical EEGs. Within this experimental setting, our results suggest that measures of latent space integrity and model uncertainty under the proposed data shifts may help anticipate performance degradation during deployment.

paragraphs: Strong predictive performance on an available EEG dataset may not reveal how a model will behave under changes encountered in practice. This study develops diagnostics intended to expose potential problems before deployment without requiring an external dataset. It focuses on changes to electrophysiological signals that can be modeled through realistic data transformations.

The evaluation examines more than downstream task performance. It also studies the model’s latent space, the internal representation produced from EEG inputs, and its predictive uncertainty after the transformations. These additional views ask whether the learned representation remains intact and how confidence behaves when the input distribution changes.

The authors test multiple EEG feature encoders on two clinically relevant tasks using large public clinical EEG datasets. Within those experiments, latent-space integrity and uncertainty measures under the proposed shifts appear useful for anticipating performance degradation. The finding supports their potential as predeployment diagnostics, while remaining a qualified result tied to the transformations, models, and tasks studied.
summary.tldr: EEG transformations reveal representation and uncertainty changes that may help anticipate deployment-time performance degradation without external data.

title: Evaluating Latent Space Robustness and Uncertainty of EEG-ML Models under Realistic Distribution Shifts

abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors. In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code will be available.

paragraphs: Accurate 3D object detectors can require substantial computation. This paper studies knowledge distillation for pillar- and voxel-based detectors, training smaller students with guidance from stronger teachers. It first examines model compression and reduced input resolution to construct students with useful accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs, then benchmarks existing 2D distillation methods on six teacher-student pairs.

The proposed pipeline improves distillation in two ways. It transfers prediction information only at a few pivotal positions selected using the teacher’s classification responses. It also initializes students through teacher-guided weight inheritance, helping pass along the teacher’s feature-extraction ability. These choices target both the information transferred during training and the student’s starting point.

A separate most-efficient model runs at 51 frames per second on an NVIDIA A100, 2.2 times faster than PointPillar with higher accuracy. These results demonstrate favorable tradeoffs across distinct student configurations.
summary.tldr: Selective distillation and teacher-guided initialization produce 3D detectors with strong accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs on Waymo.

title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Product ranking is the core problem for revenue-maximizing online retailers. To design proper product ranking algorithms, various consumer choice models are proposed to characterize the consumers' behaviors when they are provided with a list of products. However, existing works assume that each consumer purchases at most one product or will keep viewing the product list after purchasing a product, which does not agree with the common practice in real scenarios. In this paper, we assume that each consumer can purchase multiple products at will. To model consumers' willingness to view and purchase, we set a random attention span and purchase budget, which determines the maximal amount of products that he/she views and purchases, respectively. Under this setting, we first design an optimal ranking policy when the online retailer can precisely model consumers' behaviors. Based on the policy, we further develop the Multiple-Purchase-with-Budget UCB (MPB-UCB) algorithms with $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret that estimate consumers' behaviors and maximize revenue simultaneously in online settings. Experiments on both synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets prove the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: An online retailer's product ordering affects revenue, but ranking depends on how shoppers browse and buy. This paper studies a model in which customers can purchase multiple products while facing separate limits on viewing and purchasing. Random attention spans determine how many products they view, and random purchase budgets determine how many they buy.

Under this behavioral model, the authors first derive an optimal ranking policy when customer behavior is known precisely. They then develop Multiple-Purchase-with-Budget UCB algorithms for the online setting, where the retailer must estimate that behavior while choosing rankings. Learning customer behavior and earning revenue therefore happen together.

The online algorithms have regret growing on the order of the square root of the number of rounds, up to logarithmic factors. Experiments on synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets support their effectiveness. The theoretical results apply within the stated attention-and-budget model, which explicitly accommodates multiple purchases and bounded browsing. This provides a ranking framework for behavior that simpler single-purchase assumptions do not capture.
summary.tldr: The paper derives optimal and online-learning product rankings for a customer model with multiple purchases, random attention spans, and purchase budgets.

title: Product Ranking for Revenue Maximization with Multiple Purchases

abstract: We analyze feature learning in infinite-width neural networks trained with gradient flow through a self-consistent dynamical field theory. We construct a collection of deterministic dynamical order parameters which are inner-product kernels for hidden unit activations and gradients in each layer at pairs of time points, providing a reduced description of network activity through training. These kernel order parameters collectively define the hidden layer activation distribution, the evolution of the neural tangent kernel, and consequently output predictions. We show that the field theory derivation recovers the recursive stochastic process of infinite-width feature learning networks obtained from Yang & Hu with Tensor Programs. For deep linear networks, these kernels satisfy a set of algebraic matrix equations. For nonlinear networks, we provide an alternating sampling procedure to self-consistently solve for the kernel order parameters. We provide comparisons of the self-consistent solution to various approximation schemes including the static NTK approximation, gradient independence assumption, and leading order perturbation theory, showing that each of these approximations can break down in regimes where general self-consistent solutions still provide an accurate description. Lastly, we provide experiments in more realistic settings which demonstrate that the loss and kernel dynamics of CNNs at fixed feature learning strength is preserved across different widths on a CIFAR classification task.

paragraphs: This paper studies how features change during gradient-flow training in infinite-width neural networks. Rather than tracking every neuron individually, it describes training through deterministic kernels: inner products of hidden activations and gradients across layers and pairs of times. Together, these quantities determine activation distributions, neural tangent kernel evolution, and predictions.

The authors derive a self-consistent dynamical field theory that recovers an existing infinite-width feature-learning process. For deep linear networks, the kernels satisfy algebraic matrix equations. For nonlinear networks, an alternating sampling procedure solves for them self-consistently, so the quantities describing different aspects of network activity agree with the dynamics they collectively generate.

Comparisons show that the static neural tangent kernel approximation, gradient independence assumption, and leading-order perturbation theory can each fail in regimes where the self-consistent solution remains accurate. Additional CNN experiments on a CIFAR classification task find preserved loss and kernel dynamics across widths when feature-learning strength is fixed. These results support tracking evolving kernels when simpler approximations no longer capture training behavior.
summary.tldr: A self-consistent field theory tracks evolving kernels during wide-network feature learning, remaining accurate in regimes where simpler approximations fail.

title: Self-Consistent Dynamical Field Theory of Kernel Evolution in Wide Neural Networks

abstract: To act safely and ethically in the real world, agents must be able to reason about harm and avoid harmful actions. However, to date there is no statistical method for measuring harm and factoring it into algorithmic decisions. In this paper we propose the first formal definition of harm and benefit using causal models. We show that any factual definition of harm is incapable of identifying harmful actions in certain scenarios, and show that standard machine learning algorithms that cannot perform counterfactual reasoning are guaranteed to pursue harmful policies following distributional shifts. We use our definition of harm to devise a framework for harm-averse decision making using counterfactual objective functions. We demonstrate this framework on the problem of identifying optimal drug doses using a dose-response model learned from randomised control trial data. We find that the standard method of selecting doses using treatment effects results in unnecessarily harmful doses, while our counterfactual approach identifies doses that are significantly less harmful without sacrificing efficacy.

paragraphs: Deciding whether an action causes harm requires more than observing its outcome: it can require comparing that outcome with what would have happened under another action. This paper formalizes harm and benefit using causal models, making counterfactual comparisons part of the decision-making objective.

The authors show that definitions based only on factual outcomes fail to identify harmful actions in certain scenarios. They also establish a result in which standard learning algorithms lacking counterfactual reasoning are guaranteed to pursue harmful policies following distribution shifts. These findings motivate a framework that explicitly optimizes counterfactual objectives to make decisions averse to harm.

The framework is demonstrated through drug-dose selection using a dose-response model learned from randomized trial data. In that analysis, selecting doses through standard treatment-effect methods produces unnecessarily harmful choices. The counterfactual approach identifies significantly less harmful doses without sacrificing efficacy. The example illustrates how evaluating benefit and harm through causal alternatives can change a decision even when maintaining treatment effectiveness remains a goal.
summary.tldr: A causal definition of harm supports counterfactual decision objectives that identify less harmful drug doses without reduced efficacy in the paper's demonstration.

title: Counterfactual harm

abstract: While deep learning models have shown remarkable performance in various tasks, they are susceptible to learning non-generalizable _spurious features_ rather than the core features that are genuinely correlated to the true label. In this paper, beyond existing analyses of linear models, we theoretically examine the learning process of a two-layer nonlinear convolutional neural network in the presence of spurious features. Our analysis suggests that imbalanced data groups and easily learnable spurious features can lead to the dominance of spurious features during the learning process. In light of this, we propose a new training algorithm called **PDE** that efficiently enhances the model's robustness for a better worst-group performance. PDE begins with a group-balanced subset of training data and progressively expands it to facilitate the learning of the core features. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmark datasets confirm the superior performance of our method on models such as ResNets and Transformers. On average, our method achieves a $2.8$ \% improvement in worst-group accuracy compared with the state-of-the-art method, while enjoying up to $10\times$ faster training efficiency.

paragraphs: Neural networks can learn convenient features that correlate with labels in training but fail to generalize. This paper investigates how such spurious features gain influence during learning. Its theoretical analysis considers a two-layer nonlinear convolutional network and suggests that imbalanced data groups, together with easily learned spurious features, can cause those features to dominate the training process.

The proposed algorithm, Progressive Data Expansion or PDE, starts training with a group-balanced subset of the available data. It then gradually expands that subset to encourage learning of the core features associated with the label. The approach changes how training examples are introduced over time, using the initial balance to address the learning dynamics identified by the analysis.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks report improved robustness with architectures including ResNets and Transformers. Compared with the state-of-the-art method, PDE achieves an average 2.8% improvement in worst-group accuracy and up to tenfold faster training. Worst-group performance focuses attention on the groups most poorly served by the model, making the reported gains relevant to robustness under spurious correlations.
summary.tldr: Progressive Data Expansion starts with balanced groups and gradually adds data to improve worst-group performance against spurious correlations.

title: Robust Learning with Progressive Data Expansion Against Spurious Correlation

abstract: The backtracking line-search is an effective technique to automatically tune the step-size in smooth optimization. It guarantees similar performance to using the theoretically optimal step-size. Many approaches have been developed to instead tune per-coordinate step-sizes, also known as diagonal preconditioners, but none of the existing methods are provably competitive with the optimal per-coordinate step-sizes. We propose multidimensional backtracking, an extension of the backtracking line-search to find good diagonal preconditioners for smooth convex problems. Our key insight is that the gradient with respect to the step-sizes, also known as hyper-gradients, yields separating hyperplanes that let us search for good preconditioners using cutting-plane methods. As black-box cutting-plane approaches like the ellipsoid method are computationally prohibitive, we develop an efficient algorithm tailored to our setting. Multidimensional backtracking is provably competitive with the best diagonal preconditioner and requires no manual tuning.

paragraphs: Backtracking line search automatically chooses a step size for optimization and can match the performance of a theoretically optimal choice. Giving each coordinate its own step size offers a more flexible update, but makes the search harder. This paper develops multidimensional backtracking for smooth convex problems, with guarantees relative to the best diagonal preconditioner.

A diagonal preconditioner is the collection of these individual coordinate step sizes. The authors' key observation is that gradients with respect to the step sizes, called hyper-gradients, provide separating hyperplanes. These boundaries allow cutting-plane methods to narrow the search for good choices. Because generic cutting-plane algorithms would be too expensive, the paper develops an efficient algorithm tailored to this problem.

The resulting method requires no manual tuning and is provably competitive with the best diagonal preconditioner. That guarantee extends the automatic-selection principle of ordinary backtracking to a multidimensional choice. Its stated scope is smooth convex optimization, where the analysis supports comparing automatically selected coordinate scales with the strongest diagonal choice.
summary.tldr: Multidimensional backtracking automatically selects coordinate-wise step sizes with guarantees against the best diagonal preconditioner for smooth convex problems.

title: Searching for Optimal Per-Coordinate Step-sizes with Multidimensional Backtracking

abstract: Given a visual scene, humans have strong intuitions about how a scene can evolve over time under given actions. The intuition, often termed visual intuitive physics, is a critical ability that allows us to make effective plans to manipulate the scene to achieve desired outcomes without relying on extensive trial and error. In this paper, we present a framework capable of learning 3D-grounded visual intuitive physics models from videos of complex scenes with fluids. Our method is composed of a conditional Neural Radiance Field (NeRF)-style visual frontend and a 3D point-based dynamics prediction backend, using which we can impose strong relational and structural inductive bias to capture the structure of the underlying environment. Unlike existing intuitive point-based dynamics works that rely on the supervision of dense point trajectory from simulators, we relax the requirements and only assume access to multi-view RGB images and (imperfect) instance masks acquired using color prior. This enables the proposed model to handle scenarios where accurate point estimation and tracking are hard or impossible. We generate datasets including three challenging scenarios involving fluid, granular materials, and rigid objects in the simulation. The datasets do not include any dense particle information so most previous 3D-based intuitive physics pipelines can barely deal with that. We show our model can make long-horizon future predictions by learning from raw images and significantly outperforms models that do not employ an explicit 3D representation space. We also show that once trained, our model can achieve strong generalization in complex scenarios under extrapolate settings.
