paragraphs: Graph neural networks can make confident predictions on inputs unlike their training data. RAGNOR detects such out-of-distribution inputs using the norms, or magnitudes, of learned embeddings. It works after the original network has been trained and supports both individual-node and whole-graph detection tasks.

Raw embedding magnitudes are difficult to interpret on graphs. Anomalous neighbors can contaminate local information, different classes or structural roles can have different magnitude scales, and sparsely connected nodes may offer too few reference points. RAGNOR addresses these issues through global Z-score normalization, median-based aggregation of local information, and blending information across multiple graph hops.

These operations turn raw norm signals into outlier scores while requiring no retraining and adding minimal overhead. Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report detection performance that is competitive with or better than the compared alternatives. The method's practical contribution is a modular way to adapt a simple embedding signal to relational data, making it suitable for integration into existing graph-processing pipelines.
summary.tldr: RAGNOR refines graph embedding magnitudes into outlier scores using normalization and robust neighborhood aggregation without retraining the GNN.

title: Refining Norms: A Post-hoc Framework for OOD Detection in Graph Neural Networks

abstract: The *balanced loss* is a widely adopted objective for multi-class classification under class imbalance. By assigning equal importance to all classes, regardless of their frequency, it promotes fairness and ensures that minority classes are not overlooked. However, directly minimizing the balanced classification loss is typically intractable, which makes the design of effective surrogate losses a central question. This paper introduces and studies two advanced surrogate loss families: Generalized Logit-Adjusted (GLA) loss functions and Generalized Class-Aware weighted (GCA) losses. GLA losses generalize Logit-Adjusted losses, which shift logits based on class priors, to the broader general cross-entropy loss family. GCA loss functions extend the standard class-weighted losses, which scale losses inversely by class frequency, by incorporating class-dependent confidence margins and extending them to the general cross-entropy family. We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of consistency for both loss families. We show that GLA losses are Bayes-consistent, but only $H$-consistent for complete (i.e., unbounded) hypothesis sets. Moreover, their $H$-consistency bounds depend inversely on the minimum class probability, scaling at least as $1/\mathsf p _{\min}$. In contrast, GCA losses are $H$-consistent for any hypothesis set that is bounded or complete, with $H$-consistency bounds that scale more favorably as $1/\sqrt{\mathsf p _{\min}}$, offering significantly stronger theoretical guarantees in imbalanced settings. We report the results of experiments demonstrating that, empirically, both the GCA losses with calibrated class-dependent confidence margins and GLA losses can greatly outperform straightforward class-weighted losses as well as the LA losses. GLA generally performs slightly better in common benchmarks, whereas GCA exhibits a slight edge in highly imbalanced settings. Thus, we advocate for both GLA and GCA losses as principled, theoretically sound, and state-of-the-art surrogates for balanced classification under class imbalance.

paragraphs: Balanced classification gives each class equal importance even when some classes have far fewer examples. Because directly optimizing its error is usually intractable, training relies on substitute objectives. This paper develops two families: Generalized Logit-Adjusted losses, which adjust prediction scores using class frequencies, and Generalized Class-Aware weighted losses, which combine class weighting with class-specific confidence margins.

The theory distinguishes optimal prediction with unrestricted flexibility from consistency within a particular hypothesis set. GLA losses are Bayes-consistent, but their hypothesis-set consistency holds only for complete, unbounded sets. GCA losses have that consistency for bounded or complete sets. Their bounds also deteriorate more slowly as the rarest class becomes rarer: inverse square-root dependence on its probability, compared with at least inverse dependence for GLA.

Experiments show that both families can substantially outperform straightforward class weighting and standard logit adjustment. GLA generally has a small advantage on common benchmarks, while GCA has a small advantage under severe imbalance. Thus, the stronger GCA guarantees do not translate into universal empirical superiority; the findings support both families, with different theoretical and observed strengths.
summary.tldr: Two generalized loss families improve balanced classification, with GCA offering stronger hypothesis-set guarantees and GLA often slightly better benchmark performance.

title: Improved Balanced Classification with Theoretically Grounded Loss Functions

abstract: Simulating collective decision-making involves more than aggregating individual behaviors; it emerges from dynamic interactions among individuals. While large language models (LLMs) offer strong potential for social simulation, achieving quantitative alignment with real-world data remains a key challenge. To bridge this gap, we propose the \textbf{M}ean-\textbf{F}ield \textbf{LLM} (\textbf{MF-LLM}) framework, the first to incorporate mean field theory into LLM-based social simulation. MF-LLM models bidirectional interactions between individuals and the population through an iterative process, generating population signals to guide individual decisions, which in turn update the signals. This interplay produces coherent trajectories of collective behavior. To improve alignment with real-world data, we introduce \textbf{IB-Tune}, a novel fine-tuning method inspired by the \textbf{I}nformation \textbf{B}ottleneck principle, which retains population signals most predictive of future actions while filtering redundant history. Evaluated on a real-world social dataset, MF-LLM reduces KL divergence to human population distributions by \textbf{47\%} compared to non-mean-field baselines, enabling accurate trend forecasting and effective intervention planning. MF-LLM models bidirectional interactions between individuals and the population through an iterative process, generating population signals to guide individual decisions, which in turn update the signals. This interplay produces coherent trajectories of collective behavior. paragraphs: MF-LLM models collective behavior as a feedback process between individuals and their population. Simply aggregating independently generated decisions misses how people respond to the surrounding group. The framework incorporates mean field theory into language-model social simulation so that population-level signals guide individual decisions, and those decisions subsequently change the signals.

This loop creates evolving trajectories of collective behavior. title: MF-LLM: Simulating Population Decision Dynamics via a Mean-Field Large Language Model Framework

abstract: Pre-training large language models (LLMs) on vast text corpora enhances natural language processing capabilities but risks encoding social biases, particularly gender bias. While parameter-modification methods like fine-tuning mitigate bias, they are resource-intensive, unsuitable for closed-source models, and lack adaptability to evolving societal norms. Instruction-based approaches offer flexibility but often compromise general performance on normal tasks. To address these limitations, we propose $\textit{FaIRMaker}$, an automated and model-independent framework that employs an $\textbf{auto-search and refinement}$ paradigm to adaptively generate Fairwords, which act as instructions to reduce gender bias and enhance response quality. $\textit{FaIRMaker}$ enhances the debiasing capacity by enlarging the Fairwords search space while preserving the utility and making it applicable to closed-source models by training a sequence-to-sequence model that adaptively refines Fairwords into effective debiasing instructions when facing gender-related queries and performance-boosting prompts for neutral inputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that $\textit{FaIRMaker}$ effectively mitigates gender bias while preserving task integrity and ensuring compatibility with both open- and closed-source LLMs.

paragraphs: Language models can absorb gender biases from their training text. Changing their parameters to reduce those biases requires resources and access that closed-source models may not provide. Instructions offer another route, but the paper identifies a practical tension: instructions intended to reduce bias can also hurt performance on ordinary tasks.

FaIRMaker addresses this tension through automated search and refinement of instructions called Fairwords. It expands the space of candidate instructions and trains a sequence-to-sequence model to refine them adaptively. For gender-related queries, the resulting instructions aim to reduce bias; for neutral inputs, they aim to improve task performance.

This design places the adaptation in an instruction-generating framework that can work across models, including those whose parameters are inaccessible. The reported experiments find that FaIRMaker mitigates gender bias while preserving task integrity in both open- and closed-source language models. The contribution is therefore an adaptive way to combine bias mitigation with useful responses, rather than applying the same intervention indiscriminately to every query.
summary.tldr: FaIRMaker automatically searches for and refines instructions that reduce gender bias while preserving performance on ordinary tasks.

title: Auto-Search and Refinement: An Automated Framework for Gender Bias Mitigation in Large Language Models

abstract: We find that the cross-entropy loss curves of neural language models empirically adhere to a scaling law with learning rate (LR) annealing over training steps: $$L(s) = L_0 + A\cdot S_1^{-\alpha} - C\cdot S_2,$$ where $L(s)$ is the validation loss at step $s$, $S_1$ is the area under the LR curve, $S_2$ is the LR annealing area, and $L_0$, $A$, $C$, $\alpha$ are constant parameters. This formulation accounts for two main effects: (1) power-law scaling over data size, and (2) the additional loss reduction during LR annealing. Unlike previous studies that only fit losses at final steps, our formulation captures the entire training curve, allowing for parameter fitting using losses from any training step. Applying the scaling law with LR annealing and fitting only one or two training curves, we can accurately predict the loss at any given step under any learning rate scheduler (LRS). This approach significantly reduces computational cost in formulating scaling laws while providing more accuracy and expressiveness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our findings hold across a range of hyper-parameters and model architectures and can extend to scaling effect of model sizes. Moreover, our formulation provides accurate theoretical insights into empirical results observed in numerous previous studies, particularly those focusing on LR schedule and annealing. We believe that this work is promising to enhance the understanding of LLM training dynamics while democratizing scaling laws, and it is helpful to guide both research and industrial participants in refining training strategies for further LLMs.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an empirical scaling law for language-model validation loss throughout training. It explicitly includes the learning-rate schedule, addressing both progress accumulated during training and the additional loss reduction associated with lowering the learning rate. The aim is to describe the full trajectory instead of fitting only final training outcomes.

The formula combines a constant loss term, a power-law term based on the area under the learning-rate curve, and a subtractive term based on the annealing area. Because the formula applies across training steps, intermediate loss measurements can contribute to parameter fitting. The authors report that fitting one or two training curves allows accurate prediction across steps and learning-rate schedules.

Extensive experiments support the relationship across a range of hyperparameters and architectures, with an extension to model-size scaling. The formulation also explains empirical patterns reported in earlier work on learning-rate schedules and annealing. Its practical value is reducing the computation needed to estimate scaling behavior while representing how scheduling choices alter training progress; the evidence remains an empirical finding across the tested settings.
summary.tldr: An empirical scaling law incorporates learning-rate accumulation and annealing to predict language-model loss throughout training.

title: Scaling Law with Learning Rate Annealing

abstract: We study *gradient descent* (GD) with a constant stepsize for $\ell_2$-regularized logistic regression with linearly separable data. Classical theory suggests small stepsizes to ensure monotonic reduction of the optimization objective, achieving exponential convergence in $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\kappa)$ steps with $\kappa$ being the condition number. Surprisingly, we show that this can be *accelerated* to $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{\kappa})$ by simply using a large stepsize---for which the objective evolves *nonmonotonically*. The acceleration brought by large stepsizes extends to minimizing the population risk for separable distributions, improving on the best-known upper bounds on the number of steps to reach a near-optimum. Finally, we characterize the largest stepsize for the local convergence of GD, which also determines the global convergence in special scenarios. Our results extend the analysis of Wu et al. (2024) from convex settings with minimizers at infinity to strongly convex cases with finite minimizers.

paragraphs: Gradient descent is often analyzed with small steps that reduce the objective at every update. This paper examines a setting where allowing temporary increases can accelerate convergence: logistic regression with L2 regularization and linearly separable data. The method remains ordinary gradient descent with a constant step size; the change is to use a sufficiently large step.

For this setting, the authors improve the iteration dependence from approximately the condition number to its square root, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The larger steps produce a nonmonotonic objective trajectory, so steady improvement at each update is not required for the faster overall rate. They also extend the acceleration result to population-risk minimization for separable distributions, improving the best-known upper bounds for reaching a near-optimum.

The paper further characterizes the largest step size permitting local convergence. In special scenarios, this threshold also determines global convergence. These results extend earlier large-step analysis from convex problems whose minimizers lie at infinity to strongly convex problems with finite minimizers, clarifying where this acceleration can occur.
summary.tldr: For L2-regularized logistic regression on separable data, large constant steps accelerate gradient descent despite nonmonotonic objective values.

title: Large Stepsizes Accelerate Gradient Descent for Regularized Logistic Regression

abstract: Commuting Origin-destination (OD) flows, capturing daily population mobility of citizens, are vital for sustainable development across cities around the world. However, it is challenging to obtain the data due to the high cost of travel surveys and privacy concerns. Surprisingly, we find that satellite imagery, publicly available across the globe, contains rich urban semantic signals to support high-quality OD flow generation, with over 98\% expressiveness of traditional multisource hard-to-collect urban sociodemographic, economics, land use, and point of interest data. This inspires us to design a novel data generator, GlODGen (Global-scale OriginDestination Flow Generator), which can generate OD flow data for any cities of interest around the world. Specifically, GlODGen first leverages Vision-Language Geo-Foundation Models to extract urban semantic signals related to human mobility from satellite imagery. These features are then combined with population data to form region-level representations, which are used to generate OD flows via graph diffusion models. Extensive experiments on 4 continents and 6 representative cities show that GlODGen has great generalizability across diverse urban environments on different continents and can generate OD flow data for global cities highly consistent with real-world mobility data. We implement GlODGen as an automated tool, seamlessly integrating data acquisition and curation, urban semantic feature extraction, and OD flow generation together. It has been released at https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/generate-od-pubtools.

paragraphs: Commuting origin-destination flows describe daily movement between areas, but collecting them through travel surveys is costly and raises privacy concerns. This paper investigates publicly available satellite imagery as a source of information for generating these flows. The authors report that its urban semantic signals provide over 98% of the expressiveness of traditional, harder-to-collect multisource urban data.

It combines those features with population data to represent individual regions. A graph diffusion model then generates flows between regions. This pipeline connects visible urban structure and population information to the relationships needed to model commuting.

Experiments cover six representative cities across four continents and report strong generalization across varied urban environments, with generated flows highly consistent with observed mobility data. The released automated tool integrates data acquisition, curation, feature extraction, and flow generation. The stated ambition is worldwide applicability; the empirical evidence comes from the cities and continents evaluated.
summary.tldr: GlODGen combines satellite-derived urban features, population data, and graph diffusion to generate commuting flows across diverse cities.

title: Satellites Reveal Mobility: A Commuting Origin-destination Flow Generator for Global Cities

abstract: We present SciArena, an open and collaborative platform for evaluating foundation models on scientific literature-grounded tasks. Unlike traditional benchmarks for scientific literature understanding and synthesis, SciArena engages the research community directly, following the Chatbot Arena evaluation approach of community voting on model comparisons.By leveraging collective intelligence, SciArena offers a community-driven evaluation of model performance on open-ended scientific tasks that demand literature-grounded, long-form responses.The platform currently supports 44 open-source and proprietary foundation models and has collected over 19,000 votes from human researchers across diverse scientific domains. Our analysis of the data collected so far confirms its high quality.We discuss the results and insights based on the model ranking leaderboard.To further promote research in building model-based automated evaluation systems for literature tasks, we release SciArena-Eval, a meta-evaluation benchmark based on our collected preference data. The benchmark measures the accuracy of models in judging answer quality by comparing their pairwise assessments with human votes. Our experiments highlight the benchmark’s challenges and emphasize the need for more reliable automated evaluation methods.

paragraphs: Scientific literature tasks often require long-form synthesis rather than an answer that can be checked against one fixed solution. SciArena evaluates foundation models on these open-ended tasks through comparisons judged by researchers. Following an arena-style approach, it uses community votes to assess the quality of literature-grounded responses and build a model leaderboard.

At the point described in the paper, the platform supports 44 open-source and proprietary models and has collected more than 19,000 researcher votes across scientific domains. The authors analyze the collected data, report evidence of its high quality, and discuss insights from the resulting rankings. The platform makes researchers’ comparative judgments central to evaluation.

The paper also introduces SciArena-Eval, which uses those preferences to evaluate automated judges. A model’s pairwise answer assessments are compared with human votes to measure how well it reproduces researcher judgments. Experiments show that this is challenging, motivating more reliable automated evaluation. The two contributions therefore address both assessing scientific assistants and testing systems that would assess those assistants automatically.
summary.tldr: SciArena uses researcher preferences to evaluate literature-grounded model responses and to benchmark automated judges against human assessments.

title: SciArena: An Open Evaluation Platform for Non-Verifiable Scientific Literature-Grounded Tasks

abstract: Multivariate time series (MTS) classification has attracted increasing attention across various domains. Existing methods either decompose MTS into separate univariate series, ignoring inter-variable dependencies, or jointly model all variables, which may lead to over-smoothing and loss of semantic structure. These limitations become particularly pronounced when dealing with complex and heterogeneous variable types. To address these challenges, we propose SwinGroupNet (SGN), which explores a novel perspective for constructing variable interaction and temporal dependency. Specifically, SGN processes multi-scale time series using (1) Variable Group Embedding (VGE), which partitions variables into groups and performs independent group-wise embedding; (2) Multi-Scale Group Window Mixing (MGWM), which reconstructs variable interactions by modeling both intra-group and inter-group dependencies while extracting multi-scale temporal features; and (3) Periodic Window Shifting and Merging (PWSM), which exploits inherent periodic patterns to enable hierarchical temporal interaction and feature aggregation. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets from multiple domains demonstrate that SGN consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, with an average improvement of 4.2% over existing methods. We release the source code at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SGN.

paragraphs: Multivariate time series contain several variables changing together over time. Classifying them requires capturing relationships among variables without erasing their distinct structure. Treating every variable independently misses those relationships, while modeling everything jointly can over-smooth the representation. SwinGroupNet, or SGN, addresses this tension by organizing interactions through groups and temporal windows.

Variable Group Embedding first partitions the variables and represents each group independently. Multi-Scale Group Window Mixing then models relationships both within groups and between groups while extracting temporal features at several scales. Periodic Window Shifting and Merging uses periodic patterns to support interaction and aggregation across a temporal hierarchy.

This architecture gives variable relationships and temporal structure separate but connected roles in the representation. Across benchmark datasets from multiple domains, the authors report consistently state-of-the-art performance and an average improvement of 4.2% over existing methods. The findings support grouped, hierarchical processing as an effective approach for the evaluated classification tasks, particularly where variable types and their interactions are complex and heterogeneous.
summary.tldr: SGN combines variable grouping with multi-scale and periodically shifted windows to improve multivariate time-series classification.

title: SGN: Shifted Window-Based Hierarchical Variable Grouping for Multivariate Time Series Classification

abstract: Video Large Language Models have demonstrated strong video understanding capabilities, yet their practical deployment is hindered by substantial inference costs caused by redundant video tokens. Existing pruning techniques fail to effectively exploit the spatiotemporal redundancy present in video data. To bridge this gap, we perform a systematic analysis of video redundancy from two perspectives: temporal context and visual context. Leveraging these insights, we propose Dynamic Density Pruning for Fast Video LLMs termed FastVID. Specifically, FastVID dynamically partitions videos into temporally ordered segments to preserve temporal structure and applies a density-based token pruning strategy to maintain essential spatial and temporal information. Our method significantly reduces computational overhead while maintaining temporal and visual integrity. Extensive evaluations show that FastVID achieves state-of-the-art performance across various short- and long-video benchmarks on leading Video LLMs, including LLaVA-OneVision, LLaVA-Video, Qwen2-VL, and Qwen2.5-VL. Notably, on LLaVA-OneVision-7B, FastVID effectively prunes $\textbf{90.3\%}$ of video tokens, reduces FLOPs to $\textbf{8.3\%}$, and accelerates the prefilling stage by $\textbf{7.1}\times$, while maintaining $\textbf{98.0\%}$ of the original accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/LunarShen/FastVID.

paragraphs: Video language models spend substantial computation processing video tokens that contain overlapping information. FastVID studies this redundancy through both temporal context and visual context. Its goal is to remove unnecessary tokens while retaining the information needed to understand what appears in a video and how it changes over time.

The method dynamically divides a video into segments that remain in temporal order. It then uses density-based token pruning to preserve essential spatial and temporal information. Combining segmentation with pruning addresses the structure of video redundancy, rather than treating every token as an isolated candidate for removal.

These results demonstrate a substantial measured efficiency gain, with the reported speedup specifically applying to the prefilling stage.
summary.tldr: FastVID prunes redundant video tokens while preserving temporal structure, substantially accelerating prefilling with limited measured accuracy loss.

title: FastVID: Dynamic Density Pruning for Fast Video Large Language Models

abstract: We present a novel framework for \(\varepsilon\)-optimally solving two-player zero-sum partially observable stochastic games (zs-POSGs). These games pose a major challenge due to the absence of a principled connection with dynamic programming (DP) techniques developed for two-player zero-sum stochastic games (zs-SGs). Prior attempts at transferring solution methods have lacked a lossless reduction—defined here as a transformation that preserves value functions, equilibrium strategies, and optimality structure—thereby limiting generalisation to ad hoc algorithms. This work introduces the first lossless reduction from zs-POSGs to transition-independent zs-SGs, enabling the principled application of a broad class of DP-based methods. We show empirically that point-based value iteration (PBVI) algorithms, applied via this reduction, produce \(\varepsilon\)-optimal strategies across a range of benchmark domains, consistently matching or outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. Our results open a systematic pathway for algorithmic and theoretical transfer from SGs to partially observable settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies two-player zero-sum stochastic games in which players have only partial observations. The aim is to compute strategies within an epsilon tolerance of optimality. A central obstacle has been the lack of a principled connection to dynamic-programming methods developed for stochastic games, making earlier transfers of those methods dependent on ad hoc constructions.

The authors introduce what they describe as the first lossless reduction to transition-independent zero-sum stochastic games. Lossless has a specific meaning here: the transformation preserves value functions, equilibrium strategies, and optimality structure. These preserved properties matter because they let solution methods operate on the transformed game while retaining the strategic content of the original problem.

Using this reduction, the authors apply point-based value iteration and empirically obtain epsilon-optimal strategies across several benchmark domains. Performance consistently matches or exceeds existing state-of-the-art methods in those evaluations. The broader contribution is a systematic connection between the two game settings, enabling a class of dynamic-programming techniques and associated theoretical ideas to transfer to partially observable problems.
summary.tldr: A lossless game reduction enables dynamic-programming methods to compute empirically epsilon-optimal strategies in partially observable zero-sum games.

title: \(\varepsilon\)-Optimally Solving Two-Player Zero-Sum POSGs

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance on reasoning benchmarks like math and logic. While many works have largely assumed well-defined tasks, real-world queries are often underspecified and only solvable by acquiring missing information. We formalize this information-gathering problem as a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) with missing variable assignments. Using a special case where only one necessary variable assignment is missing, we can evaluate an LLM's ability to identify the minimal necessary question to ask. We present QuestBench, a set of underspecified reasoning tasks solvable by asking at most one question, which includes: (1) Logic-Q: logical reasoning tasks with one missing proposition, (2) Planning-Q: PDDL planning problems with partially-observed initial states, (3) GSM-Q: human-annotated grade school math problems with one unknown variable, and (4) GSME-Q: equation-based version of GSM-Q. The LLM must select the correct clarification question from multiple options. While current models excel at GSM-Q and GSME-Q, they achieve only 40-50% accuracy on Logic-Q and Planning-Q. Analysis shows that the ability to solve well-specified reasoning problems is not sufficient for success on our benchmark: models struggle to identify the right question even when they can solve the fully specified version. This highlights the need for specifically optimizing models' information acquisition capabilities.

The benchmark contains logic problems, planning tasks with partially observed starting states, grade-school mathematics, and equation-based versions of those mathematics problems. Each task can be resolved by asking at most one question. Models select the appropriate clarification from multiple options, allowing the evaluation to focus on identifying the necessary information.

Current models perform strongly on the mathematics variants but reach only 40–50% accuracy on the logic and planning tasks. Further analysis shows failures even when a model can solve the corresponding fully specified problem. The findings distinguish reasoning with available facts from choosing which fact to acquire and motivate training specifically for information acquisition.
summary.tldr: QuestBench shows that solving complete reasoning problems does not ensure an LLM can identify the right clarification question.

title: QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?

abstract: Variational inference (VI) is a popular approach in Bayesian inference, that looks for the best approximation of the posterior distribution within a parametric family, minimizing a loss that is typically the (reverse) Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. In this paper, we focus on the following parametric family: mixtures of isotropic Gaussians (i.e., with diagonal covariance matrices proportional to the identity) and uniform weights. We develop a variational framework and provide efficient algorithms suited for this family. In contrast with mixtures of Gaussian with generic covariance matrices, this choice presents a balance between accurate approximations of multimodal Bayesian posteriors, while being memory and computationally efficient. Our algorithms implement gradient descent on the location of the mixture components (the modes of the Gaussians), and either (an entropic) Mirror or Bures descent on their variance parameters. We illustrate the performance of our algorithms on numerical experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops variational inference using equally weighted mixtures of isotropic Gaussian distributions. Each component has a covariance proportional to the identity, so its spread is the same in every direction. Combining several such components offers a way to approximate a posterior with multiple modes while keeping each individual component simple.

The motivation is a balance between representational flexibility and computational cost. Gaussian mixtures with general covariance matrices allow more elaborate component shapes, but require more memory and computation. The chosen family retains multiple adjustable centers and variance parameters without giving every component a full covariance structure. The authors develop a variational framework and algorithms specifically for this family.

Their algorithms use gradient descent to update component locations and either entropic mirror descent or Bures descent to update variances. Numerical experiments illustrate performance. The contribution is an efficient optimization approach for this particular approximation family, aimed at capturing multimodal Bayesian posteriors through mixtures of simple components rather than increasing the complexity of each component.
summary.tldr: The paper develops efficient variational-inference algorithms using equally weighted isotropic Gaussian mixtures to approximate multimodal posteriors.

title: Variational Inference with Mixtures of Isotropic Gaussians

abstract: Sparse Perception Models (SPMs) adopt a query-driven paradigm that forgoes explicit dense BEV or volumetric construction, enabling highly efficient computation and accelerated inference. In this paper, we introduce SQS, a novel query-based splatting pre-training specifically designed to advance SPMs in autonomous driving. SQS introduces a plug-in module that predicts 3D Gaussian representations from sparse queries during pre-training, leveraging self-supervised splatting to learn fine-grained contextual features through the reconstruction of multi-view images and depth maps. During fine-tuning, the pre-trained Gaussian queries are seamlessly integrated into downstream networks via query interaction mechanisms that explicitly connect pre-trained queries with task-specific queries, effectively accommodating the diverse requirements of occupancy prediction and 3D object detection. Extensive experiments on autonomous driving benchmarks demonstrate that SQS delivers considerable performance gains across multiple query-based 3D perception tasks, notably in occupancy prediction and 3D object detection, outperforming prior state-of-the-art pre-training approaches by a significant margin (i.e., +1.3 mIoU on occupancy prediction and +1.0 NDS on 3D detection).

paragraphs: Sparse perception models use queries to interpret driving scenes without explicitly building dense bird's-eye-view or volumetric representations. This supports efficient computation and inference. The paper introduces SQS, a pre-training method designed to improve the contextual information learned by those sparse queries before they are used for specific three-dimensional perception tasks.

During pre-training, a plug-in module predicts 3D Gaussian representations from the queries. Self-supervised splatting reconstructs images from multiple views and depth maps, encouraging the queries to capture fine-grained scene context. The findings support reconstruction-based pre-training as a way to enrich sparse representations, with query interactions providing the link from the shared pre-training task to distinct downstream objectives.
summary.tldr: SQS pre-trains sparse scene queries through Gaussian splatting and reconstruction, improving occupancy prediction and 3D object detection.

title: SQS: Enhancing Sparse Perception Models via Query-based Splatting in Autonomous Driving

abstract: Recent work indicates that low-dimensional dynamics of neural and behavioral data are often preserved across days and subjects. However, extracting these preserved dynamics remains challenging: high-dimensional neural population activity and the recorded neuron populations vary across recording sessions. While existing modeling tools can improve alignment between neural and behavioral data, they often operate on a per-subject basis or discretize behavior into categories, disrupting its natural continuity and failing to capture the underlying dynamics. We introduce $\underline{\text{C}}$ontrastive $\underline{\text{A}}$ligned $\underline{\text{N}}$eural $\underline{\text{D}}$$\underline{\text{Y}}$namics (CANDY), an end‑to‑end framework that aligns neural and behavioral data using rank-based contrastive learning, adapted for continuous behavioral variables, to project neural activity from different sessions onto a shared low-dimensional embedding space. CANDY fits a shared linear dynamical system to the aligned embeddings, enabling an interpretable model of the conserved temporal structure in the latent space. We validate CANDY on synthetic and real-world datasets spanning multiple species, behaviors, and recording modalities. Our results show that CANDY is able to learn aligned latent embeddings and preserved dynamics across neural recording sessions and subjects, and it achieves improved cross-session behavior decoding performance. We further show that the latent linear dynamical system generalizes to new sessions and subjects, achieving comparable or even superior behavior decoding performance to models trained from scratch. These advances enable robust cross‑session behavioral decoding and offer a path towards identifying shared neural dynamics that underlie behavior across individuals and recording conditions. The code and two-photon imaging data of striatal neural activity that we acquired here are available at https://github.com/schnitzer-lab/CANDY-public.git.

Tests on synthetic and real data span species, behaviors, and recording modalities. CANDY improves cross-session decoding, and its latent dynamics transfer to new sessions and subjects with performance comparable to or better than models trained from scratch. This supports reuse of conserved neural-behavioral structure despite changes in the recorded neurons and acquisition conditions.
summary.tldr: CANDY aligns neural recordings across sessions and learns shared interpretable behavioral dynamics.

title: Extracting task-relevant preserved dynamics from contrastive aligned neural recordings

abstract: In online allocation problems, an algorithm must choose from a set of options at each step, where each option incurs a set of costs/rewards associated with a set of $d$ agents. The goal is to minimize/maximize a function of the accumulated costs/rewards assigned to the agents over the course of the entire allocation process. Such problems are common in combinatorial optimization, including minimization problems such as machine scheduling and network routing, as well as maximization problems such as fair allocation for welfare maximization. In this paper, we develop a general learning-augmented algorithmic framework for online allocation problems that produces a nearly optimal solution using only a single $d$-dimensional vector of learned weights. Using this general framework, we derive learning-augmented online algorithms for a broad range of application problems in routing, scheduling, and fair allocation. Our main tool is convex programming duality, which may also have further implications for learning-augmented algorithms in the future.

paragraphs: Online allocation involves making a sequence of choices whose consequences accumulate across multiple agents. A scheduling choice can add work to a machine, while a routing choice can add cost to part of a network. The objective concerns the final distribution of costs or rewards, even though the algorithm must choose at each step.

This paper develops a general framework that incorporates learned information through a single vector of weights, with one component per agent. The authors show how this compact input can support nearly optimal allocation. Their main mathematical tool is convex programming duality, which connects the allocation problem to an alternative optimization formulation used to guide decisions.

The framework yields algorithms for routing, scheduling, and fair allocation, covering both cost minimization and reward maximization. Its contribution is a shared approach across these applications: learned guidance does not need to describe an entire sequence of decisions. A small set of weights can provide the information used by the framework to achieve its stated solution quality.
summary.tldr: A general online allocation framework uses one learned weight per agent to obtain nearly optimal solutions across routing, scheduling, and fair allocation.

title: A Learning-Augmented Approach to Online Allocation Problems

abstract: Agent systems based on large language models (LLMs) have shown great potential in complex reasoning tasks, but building efficient and generalizable workflows remains a major challenge. Most existing approaches rely on manually designed processes, which limits their adaptability across different tasks. While a few methods attempt automated workflow generation, they are often tied to specific datasets or query types and make limited use of intermediate feedback, reducing system robustness and reasoning depth. Moreover, their operations are typically predefined and inflexible. To address these limitations, we propose **DyFlow**, a dynamic workflow generation framework that adaptively constructs and adjusts reasoning procedures based on task requirements and real-time intermediate feedback, thereby enhancing cross-task generalization. DyFlow consists of two core components: a designer and an executor. The designer decomposes complex problems into a sequence of sub-goals defined by high-level objectives and dynamically plans the next steps based on intermediate outputs and feedback. These plans are then carried out by the executor, which executes each operation using dynamic operators with context-aware parameterization, enabling flexible and semantically grounded reasoning. We systematically evaluate DyFlow across diverse domains, including social reasoning, biomedical tasks, mathematical problem solving, and code generation. Results demonstrate that DyFlow significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving substantial Pass@k improvements and exhibiting robust generalization across diverse domains.

paragraphs: DyFlow addresses how language-model agents organize complex reasoning. A manually fixed workflow can fit one task while adapting poorly to another. Even automated workflow builders may remain tied to particular query types or make little use of intermediate results. The paper makes workflow construction an ongoing process informed by the task and the feedback generated while solving it.

The framework separates responsibilities between a designer and an executor. The designer breaks a problem into sub-goals expressed as high-level objectives, then uses intermediate outputs to decide what should happen next. The executor carries out those plans using dynamic operators whose parameters depend on context. This makes both the sequence of operations and their execution responsive to the developing solution.

Evaluations cover social reasoning, biomedical tasks, mathematics, and code generation. The authors report substantial Pass@k improvements over existing baselines and robust generalization across the tested domains. These findings support the value of revising reasoning procedures during execution, particularly when a single predefined workflow may not match the needs of different problems.
summary.tldr: DyFlow lets a designer and executor adapt an agent's reasoning workflow using task requirements and intermediate feedback.

title: DyFlow: Dynamic Workflow Framework for Agentic Reasoning

abstract: We use abstract algebra to derive new algorithms for fast cross-validation, online learning, and parallel learning. To use these algorithms on a classification model, we must show that the model has appropriate algebraic structure. It is easy to give algebraic structure to some models, and we do this explicitly for Bayesian classifiers and a novel variation of decision stumps called HomStumps. But not all classifiers have an obvious structure, so we introduce the Free HomTrainer. This can be used to give a “generic” algebraic structure to any classifier. We use the Free HomTrainer to give algebraic structure to bagging and boosting. In so doing, we derive novel online and parallel algorithms, and present the first fast cross-validation schemes for these classifiers.
originalAbstract: We use abstract algebra to derive new algorithms for fast cross-validation, online learning, and parallel learning. To use these algorithms on a classification model, we must show that the model has appropriate algebraic structure. It is easy to give algebraic structure to some models, and we do this explicitly for Bayesian classifiers and a novel variation of decision stumps called HomStumps. But not all classifiers have an obvious structure, so we introduce the Free HomTrainer. This can be used to give a “generic” algebraic structure to any classifier. We use the Free HomTrainer to give algebraic structure to bagging and boosting. In so doing, we derive novel online and parallel algorithms, and present the first fast cross-validation schemes for these classifiers.

paragraphs: Cross-validation, online training, and parallel training organize learning in different ways, but this paper develops algorithms for all three through abstract algebra. The central idea is to identify algebraic structure in a classifier's training process. Once an appropriate structure is established, the generic algorithms can be applied to that classification model.

For some models, this structure is straightforward to supply. The authors explicitly construct it for Bayesian classifiers and for HomStumps, a new variation of decision stumps. Other classifiers do not expose an obvious structure. To address that obstacle, the paper introduces the Free HomTrainer, a construction that can provide a generic algebraic structure to any classifier.

The authors apply the Free HomTrainer to bagging and boosting. This leads to new online and parallel algorithms, together with what they describe as the first fast cross-validation schemes for these classifiers. The broader contribution is a reusable route from mathematical structure to training algorithms. Applying that route still requires establishing the relevant structure, either directly or through the generic construction.
summary.tldr: Algebraic structure provides a common route to fast cross-validation, online learning, and parallel training, including new methods for bagging and boosting.

title: Algebraic classifiers: a generic approach to fast cross-validation, online training, and parallel training

abstract: We propose a scalable nonparametric Bayesian regression model based on a mixture of Gaussian process (GP) experts and the inducing points formalism underpinning sparse GP approximations. Each expert is augmented with a set of inducing points, and the allocation of data points to experts is defined probabilistically based on their proximity to the experts. This allocation mechanism enables a fast variational inference procedure for learning of the inducing inputs and hyperparameters of the experts. When using K experts, our method can run K^2 times faster and use K^2 times less memory than popular sparse methods such as the FITC approximation. Furthermore, it is easy to parallelize and handles non-stationarity straightforwardly. Our experiments show that on medium-sized datasets (of around 10^4 training points) it trains up to 5 times faster than FITC while achieving comparable accuracy. On a large dataset of 10^5 training points, our method significantly outperforms six competitive baselines while requiring only a few hours of training.

Each expert is augmented with a set of inducing points, and the allocation of data points to experts is defined probabilistically based on their proximity to the experts. This allocation mechanism enables a fast variational inference procedure for learning of the inducing inputs and hyperparameters of the experts. When using K experts, our method can run K^2 times faster and use K^2 times less memory than popular sparse methods such as the FITC approximation. Furthermore, it is easy to parallelize and handles non-stationarity straightforwardly. Our experiments show that on medium-sized datasets (of around 10^4 training points) it trains up to 5 times faster than FITC while achieving comparable accuracy. On a large dataset of 10^5 training points, our method significantly outperforms six competitive baselines while requiring only a few hours of training.

paragraphs: The paper proposes scalable Bayesian regression through a mixture of Gaussian process experts. Each expert has its own inducing points, the compact representation used in sparse Gaussian process approximations. Data are assigned probabilistically according to proximity to the experts, making allocation an explicit part of the model.

This allocation supports fast variational inference for learning both inducing inputs and expert hyperparameters. The model is easy to parallelize and handles non-stationarity directly. With K experts, the method can achieve K² reductions in runtime and memory relative to popular sparse approaches such as FITC. This is a possible scaling advantage, distinct from the measured speedups in the experiments.

On datasets with around 10,000 training points, the method trains up to five times faster than FITC while attaining comparable accuracy. On a dataset with 100,000 training points, it substantially outperforms six competitive baselines with a few hours of training. These results support the practical value of combining local expert allocation with sparse approximation.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic allocation among sparse Gaussian process experts enables efficient inference and strong regression results on large datasets.

title: Fast Allocation of Gaussian Process Experts

abstract: We present a series of learning algorithms and theoretical guarantees for designing accurate ensembles of structured prediction tasks. This includes several randomized and deterministic algorithms devised by converting on-line learning algorithms to batch ones, and a boosting-style algorithm applicable in the context of structured prediction with a large number of labels. We give a detailed study of all these algorithms, including the description of new on-line-to-batch conversions and learning guarantees. We also report the results of extensive experiments with these algorithms in several structured prediction tasks.
originalAbstract: We present a series of learning algorithms and theoretical guarantees for designing accurate ensembles of structured prediction tasks. This includes several randomized and deterministic algorithms devised by converting on-line learning algorithms to batch ones, and a boosting-style algorithm applicable in the context of structured prediction with a large number of labels. We give a detailed study of all these algorithms, including the description of new on-line-to-batch conversions and learning guarantees. We also report the results of extensive experiments with these algorithms in several structured prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Structured prediction concerns outputs whose parts have relationships, making ensemble design more involved than combining isolated class decisions. This paper develops a collection of learning algorithms for constructing accurate ensembles in that setting. It pairs the algorithmic proposals with theoretical guarantees about learning.

Several methods come from converting online learning algorithms into batch procedures. Online learning updates a predictor sequentially, while a batch procedure produces a predictor from an available training collection. The paper develops new conversions for this purpose and includes both randomized and deterministic algorithms, providing multiple routes from sequential learning procedures to structured prediction ensembles.

Another contribution is a boosting-style algorithm that applies when the structured prediction setting has many labels. The authors provide a detailed study of the proposed methods and their guarantees, together with extensive experiments on several structured prediction tasks. The contribution therefore combines ensemble construction, analysis, and empirical evaluation, giving a family of approaches for learning with structured outputs rather than a single prescribed ensemble procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper develops structured prediction ensembles through new online-to-batch conversions and a boosting-style method, supported by learning guarantees and experiments.

title: Ensemble Methods for Structured Prediction

abstract: Gaussian processes (GP) provide an attractive machine learning model due to their non-parametric form, their flexibility to capture many types of observation data, and their generic inference procedures. Sparse GP inference algorithms address the cubic complexity of GPs by focusing on a small set of pseudo-samples. To date, such approaches have focused on the simple case of Gaussian observation likelihoods. This paper develops a variational sparse solution for GPs under general likelihoods by providing a new characterization of the gradients required for inference in terms of individual observation likelihood terms. In addition, we propose a simple new approach for optimizing the sparse variational approximation using a fixed point computation. We demonstrate experimentally that the fixed point operator acts as a contraction in many cases and therefore leads to fast convergence. An experimental evaluation for count regression, classification, and ordinal regression illustrates the generality and advantages of the new approach.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer flexible models, but their cubic computational complexity creates a scaling problem. Sparse methods address this by concentrating computation on a smaller collection of pseudo-samples. This paper extends that strategy beyond Gaussian observation likelihoods, aiming to preserve sparse inference when the form of the observed data calls for other likelihoods.

The authors derive a variational sparse solution using a new expression for the gradients needed during inference. Those gradients are characterized through individual observation likelihood terms. They also propose optimizing the sparse approximation through a fixed-point computation, giving the approach a concrete iterative procedure for finding the approximation.

Experiments show that the fixed-point operator behaves as a contraction in many cases, which leads to rapid convergence in those cases. Evaluations on count regression, classification, and ordinal regression illustrate the breadth and advantages of the method. The stated convergence evidence is empirical and qualified, while the broader contribution is a sparse variational framework for generalized GP observation models.
summary.tldr: A sparse variational GP method supports general likelihoods and uses fixed-point optimization that converges quickly in many tested cases.

title: Sparse Variational Inference for Generalized GP Models

abstract: To scale Gaussian processes (GPs) to large data sets we introduce the robust Bayesian Committee Machine (rBCM), a practical and scalable product-of-experts model for large-scale distributed GP regression. Unlike state-of-the-art sparse GP approximations, the rBCM is conceptually simple and does not rely on inducing or variational parameters. The key idea is to recursively distribute computations to independent computational units and, subsequently, recombine them to form an overall result. Efficient closed-form inference allows for straightforward parallelisation and distributed computations with a small memory footprint. The rBCM is independent of the computational graph and can be used on heterogeneous computing infrastructures, ranging from laptops to clusters. With sufficient computing resources our distributed GP model can handle arbitrarily large data sets.

Unlike state-of-the-art sparse GP approximations, the rBCM is conceptually simple and does not rely on inducing or variational parameters. The key idea is to recursively distribute computations to independent computational units and, subsequently, recombine them to form an overall result. Efficient closed-form inference allows for straightforward parallelisation and distributed computations with a small memory footprint. The rBCM is independent of the computational graph and can be used on heterogeneous computing infrastructures, ranging from laptops to clusters. With sufficient computing resources our distributed GP model can handle arbitrarily large data sets.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process regression needs scalable computation to handle large datasets. This paper introduces the robust Bayesian Committee Machine, or rBCM, as a distributed product-of-experts model. The approach builds an overall prediction by combining results from separate computational units.

The main design recursively divides computation among independent units and then recombines their outputs. Inference has an efficient closed form, which supports parallel execution and a small memory footprint. The model also avoids inducing parameters and variational parameters, giving it a different computational structure from the sparse Gaussian-process approximations discussed in the abstract.

A further property is independence from the computational graph: the model is not tied to one particular arrangement of the computation. This supports use on heterogeneous infrastructure, from laptops to clusters. The authors state that arbitrarily large datasets can be handled when sufficient computing resources are available. That qualification is central to the scalability claim: the contribution provides a way to distribute the workload as resources grow, rather than a fixed-resource guarantee for unlimited data.
summary.tldr: The robust Bayesian Committee Machine scales Gaussian-process regression by recursively distributing computation and combining expert predictions.

title: Distributed Gaussian Processes

abstract: Dimensionality reduction is a popular approach for dealing with high dimensional data that leads to substantial computational savings. Random projections are a simple and effective method for universal dimensionality reduction with rigorous theoretical guarantees. In this paper, we theoretically study the problem of differentially private empirical risk minimization in the projected subspace (compressed domain). We ask: is it possible to design differentially private algorithms with small excess risk given access to only projected data? In this paper, we answer this question in affirmative, by showing that for the class of generalized linear functions, given only the projected data and the projection matrix, we can obtain excess risk bounds of $O(w(Theta)^2/3/n^1/3) under eps-differential privacy, and O((w(Theta)/n)^1/2)$ under (eps,delta)-differential privacy, where n is the sample size and w(Theta) is the Gaussian width of the parameter space that we optimize over. A simple consequence of these results is that, for a large class of ERM problems, in the traditional setting (i.e., with access to the original data), under eps-differential privacy, we improve the worst-case risk bounds of Bassily et al. (FOCS 2014).

paragraphs: Random projections reduce data dimensionality and can make learning computationally cheaper. This paper asks whether accurate, differentially private empirical risk minimization remains possible when the learner has access only to projected data and the projection matrix. The question combines two requirements: learning from compressed inputs and protecting privacy.

For generalized linear functions, the authors establish excess-risk bounds in this compressed setting. Writing n for the sample size and w(Theta) for the Gaussian width of the parameter space, the stated bounds scale as O(w(Theta)^(2/3)/n^(1/3)) under epsilon-differential privacy and O((w(Theta)/n)^(1/2)) under approximate differential privacy. These expressions connect the guarantees to sample size and the geometry of the parameter space.

The results answer the compressed-learning question affirmatively for the specified function class. They also have a consequence for learning with access to the original data: for a large class of empirical risk minimization problems, the analysis improves previously established worst-case risk bounds under epsilon-differential privacy. The contribution is theoretical, linking compression, privacy, and statistical accuracy.
summary.tldr: Private learning from random projections admits excess-risk guarantees for generalized linear functions, with bounds governed by parameter-space geometry.

title: Efficient Private Empirical Risk Minimization for High-dimensional Learning

abstract: Probability distributions produced by the cross-entropy loss for ordinal classification problems can possess undesired properties. We propose a straightforward technique to constrain discrete ordinal probability distributions to be unimodal via the use of the Poisson and binomial probability distributions. We evaluate this approach in the context of deep learning on two large ordinal image datasets, obtaining promising results.
originalAbstract: Probability distributions produced by the cross-entropy loss for ordinal classification problems can possess undesired properties. We propose a straightforward technique to constrain discrete ordinal probability distributions to be unimodal via the use of the Poisson and binomial probability distributions. We evaluate this approach in the context of deep learning on two large ordinal image datasets, obtaining promising results.

paragraphs: Ordinal classification predicts categories that have a meaningful order. A model produces probabilities over those categories, so the shape of that distribution is part of its output. This paper observes that distributions learned with cross-entropy can have undesirable properties for ordinal problems and proposes explicitly constraining their shape.

The proposed technique uses Poisson and binomial probability distributions to make the discrete ordinal predictions unimodal. Unimodality means the probabilities form a single peak across the ordered categories. This imposes structure on how probability is distributed across possible answers, going beyond merely producing a probability for each category. The authors present the technique as a straightforward way to incorporate this requirement into deep ordinal classification.

The approach is evaluated on two large ordinal image datasets, with results described as promising. The stated finding supports further use of the proposed distributional constraint in this setting. The contribution centers on making an intended property of ordinal predictions explicit in their probability distributions and demonstrating the approach in deep learning experiments.
summary.tldr: Poisson and binomial constructions enforce unimodal predictions for deep ordinal classification, with promising results on two image datasets.

title: Unimodal Probability Distributions for Deep Ordinal Classification

abstract: In this work we introduce a conditional accelerated lazy stochastic gradient descent algorithm with optimal number of calls to a stochastic first-order oracle and convergence rate $O(1/\epsilon^2)$ improving over the projection-free, Online Frank-Wolfe based stochastic gradient descent of (Hazan and Kale, 2012) with convergence rate $O(1/\epsilon^4)$.
originalAbstract: In this work we introduce a conditional accelerated lazy stochastic gradient descent algorithm with optimal number of calls to a stochastic first-order oracle and convergence rate $O(1/\epsilon^2)$ improving over the projection-free, Online Frank-Wolfe based stochastic gradient descent of (Hazan and Kale, 2012) with convergence rate $O(1/\epsilon^4)$.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a conditional accelerated lazy stochastic gradient descent algorithm. Its stated contribution concerns the amount of optimization work needed to reach a target accuracy. The analysis focuses on calls to a stochastic first-order oracle: a source of gradient information used by the optimization procedure to choose how to update its current solution.

The authors report an optimal number of calls to that oracle and a convergence rate expressed as O(1/epsilon²), where epsilon represents the desired accuracy. They compare this with an earlier projection-free stochastic gradient method based on Online Frank-Wolfe, whose stated rate is O(1/epsilon⁴). The difference is in the exponent governing dependence on accuracy, rather than merely a constant multiplier.

That distinction matters when increasingly precise solutions are required: the reported bound grows less sharply as epsilon becomes smaller. The abstract presents this as a theoretical improvement over the specified earlier method. Its concrete finding is the improved accuracy dependence together with oracle-call optimality; the reported result concerns these optimization guarantees rather than a measured application-specific speedup.
summary.tldr: The proposed stochastic optimization algorithm achieves optimal oracle-call complexity and improves the stated accuracy dependence from O(1/epsilon⁴) to O(1/epsilon²).

title: Conditional Accelerated Lazy Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: In this paper we study a family of variance reduction methods with randomized batch size—at each step, the algorithm first randomly chooses the batch size and then selects a batch of samples to conduct a variance-reduced stochastic update. We give the linear converge rate for this framework for composite functions, and show that the optimal strategy to achieve the best converge rate per data access is to always choose batch size equalling to 1, which is equivalent to the SAGA algorithm. However, due to the presence of cache/disk IO effect in computer architecture, number of data access cannot reflect the running time because of 1) random memory access is much slower than sequential access, 2) when data is too big to fit into memory, disk seeking takes even longer time. After taking these into account, choosing batch size equals to 1 is no longer optimal, so we propose a new algorithm called SAGA++ and theoretically show how to calculate the optimal average batch size. Our algorithm outperforms SAGA and other existing batch and stochastic solvers on real datasets. In addition, we also conduct a precise analysis to compare different update rules for variance reduction methods, showing that SAGA++ converges faster than SVRG in theory.

paragraphs: This paper studies variance-reduced optimization methods that randomly choose a batch size before selecting samples for each update. It establishes linear convergence for this framework on composite functions. When efficiency is measured purely by data accesses, the best strategy is always choosing a batch of one, which recovers the SAGA algorithm.

The authors then account for the cost of accessing data on actual hardware. Random memory access is slower than sequential access, and disk seeking adds further expense when data does not fit in memory. Under this accounting, minimizing the number of accessed samples does not necessarily minimize running time, and a batch size of one is no longer optimal.

The resulting method, SAGA++, comes with a theoretical calculation of the optimal average batch size. Experiments on real datasets show it outperforming SAGA and other batch and stochastic solvers. A separate comparison of variance-reduction update rules also establishes faster theoretical convergence than SVRG. The paper’s central point is that batch selection should reflect both optimization progress and the architecture-dependent cost of obtaining data.
summary.tldr: SAGA++ chooses batches using memory and disk access costs, improving practical performance beyond the single-sample strategy favored by data-access counts.

title: Fast Variance Reduction Method with Stochastic Batch Size

abstract: Phase retrieval algorithms have become an important component in many modern computational imaging systems. For instance, in the context of ptychography and speckle correlation imaging, they enable imaging past the diffraction limit and through scattering media, respectively. Unfortunately, traditional phase retrieval algorithms struggle in the presence of noise. Progress has been made recently on developing more robust algorithms using signal priors, but at the expense of limiting the range of supported measurement models (e.g., to Gaussian or coded diffraction patterns). In this work we leverage the regularization-by-denoising framework and a convolutional neural network denoiser to create prDeep, a new phase retrieval algorithm that is both robust and broadly applicable. We test and validate prDeep in simulation to demonstrate that it is robust to noise and can handle a variety of system models.

paragraphs: Phase retrieval is an important computational step in imaging systems, including applications that image beyond the diffraction limit or through scattering media. Noise makes the reconstruction problem difficult for traditional algorithms. Methods using signal priors can improve robustness, but the paper identifies a tradeoff: some restrict which measurement models they can support.

The proposed prDeep algorithm combines regularization by denoising with a convolutional neural network denoiser. This uses the denoising component to guide the reconstruction while seeking broad applicability across measurement systems. The approach targets both concerns together: resistance to noisy measurements and flexibility in the model describing how those measurements were produced.

The authors test prDeep in simulation and report robustness to noise across a variety of system models. This provides evidence that the proposed combination can address the tradeoff motivating the work. The stated validation is computational, and its significance is the demonstrated ability to use a neural denoiser within phase retrieval without restricting the algorithm to a single tested measurement model.
summary.tldr: prDeep combines a neural denoiser with regularization by denoising to achieve noise-robust phase retrieval across varied simulated system models.

title: prDeep: Robust Phase Retrieval with a Flexible Deep Network

abstract: Stochastic optimization algorithms such as SGDs update the model sequentially with cheap per-iteration costs, making them amenable for large-scale data analysis. However, most of the existing studies focus on the classification accuracy which can not be directly applied to the important problems of maximizing the Area under the ROC curve (AUC) in imbalanced classification and bipartite ranking. In this paper, we develop a novel stochastic proximal algorithm for AUC maximization which is referred to as SPAM. Compared with the previous literature, our algorithm SPAM applies to a non-smooth penalty function, and achieves a convergence rate of O(log t/t) for strongly convex functions while both space and per-iteration costs are of one datum.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization is useful for large datasets because it updates a model sequentially with inexpensive steps. However, methods developed around classification accuracy do not directly solve every evaluation objective. This paper focuses on maximizing area under the ROC curve, or AUC, an objective relevant to imbalanced classification and ranking examples from two classes.

The authors introduce SPAM, a stochastic proximal algorithm designed for AUC maximization. A distinguishing feature is its support for a non-smooth penalty function. This broadens the form of the regularized optimization problem the algorithm can handle while preserving the inexpensive updates that make stochastic methods useful for large-scale analysis.

For strongly convex functions, the paper establishes a convergence rate of O(log t/t), where t tracks iterations. Both memory requirements and per-iteration costs are on the scale of one datum. These claims combine a conditional convergence guarantee with small resource requirements. The strong-convexity condition matters: it specifies the setting for the stated rate rather than asserting that every AUC optimization problem has that behavior.
summary.tldr: SPAM optimizes AUC with non-smooth penalties and single-datum-scale costs, achieving O(log t/t) convergence for strongly convex functions.

title: Stochastic Proximal Algorithms for AUC Maximization

abstract: The performance of off-policy learning, including deep Q-learning and deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG), critically depends on the choice of the exploration policy. Existing exploration methods are mostly based on adding noise to the on-going actor policy and can only explore local regions close to what the actor policy dictates. In this work, we develop a simple meta-policy gradient algorithm that allows us to adaptively learn the exploration policy in DDPG. Our algorithm allows us to train flexible exploration behaviors that are independent of the actor policy, yielding a global exploration that significantly speeds up the learning process. With an extensive study, we show that our method significantly improves the sample-efficiency of DDPG on a variety of reinforcement learning continuous control tasks.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning depends heavily on the behavior used to collect experience. The paper focuses on DDPG, where exploration is commonly produced by adding noise to the current actor's actions. The authors argue that this tends to keep exploration near the behavior the actor already chooses, restricting the range of experience available for learning.

They introduce a meta-policy gradient algorithm that adaptively learns an exploration policy. This policy can develop flexible behavior independently of the actor policy. Separating the two gives exploration room to move beyond local perturbations of the actor's current behavior, which the paper describes as enabling global exploration.

An extensive study on continuous-control reinforcement learning tasks shows significantly improved sample efficiency for DDPG. The method also substantially speeds up learning in the reported results. The contribution is to treat experience collection as behavior that can itself be learned, making the exploration policy an adaptive component rather than tying it directly to noisy versions of the actor.
summary.tldr: A learned exploration policy independent of DDPG's actor improves sample efficiency on continuous-control tasks.

title: Learning to Explore via Meta-Policy Gradient

abstract: While model-based deep reinforcement learning (RL) holds great promise for sample efficiency and generalization, learning an accurate dynamics model is often challenging and requires substantial interaction with the environment. A wide variety of domains have dynamics that share common foundations like the laws of classical mechanics, which are rarely exploited by existing algorithms. In fact, humans continuously acquire and use such dynamics priors to easily adapt to operating in new environments. In this work, we propose an approach to learn task-agnostic dynamics priors from videos and incorporate them into an RL agent. Our method involves pre-training a frame predictor on task-agnostic physics videos to initialize dynamics models (and fine-tune them) for unseen target environments. Our frame prediction architecture, SpatialNet, is designed specifically to capture localized physical phenomena and interactions. Our approach allows for both faster policy learning and convergence to better policies, outperforming competitive approaches on several different environments. We also demonstrate that incorporating this prior allows for more effective transfer between environments.
