paragraphs: Learning an accurate model of an environment can require substantial interaction, even when its dynamics share physical principles with other environments. This paper explores using videos to acquire reusable knowledge of those dynamics before an agent encounters its target task. The aim is to give model-based reinforcement learning a useful starting point.

The method first trains a frame predictor on physics videos that are independent of the target tasks. This predictor initializes dynamics models for previously unseen environments, where the models are then fine-tuned. Its SpatialNet architecture is designed to capture localized physical events and interactions, making those patterns part of the learned prior.

Across several environments, the authors report faster policy learning and convergence to better policies than competitive approaches. They also demonstrate more effective transfer between environments when the prior is included. The findings support learning reusable dynamical information from videos, then adapting it through target-environment learning. The prior contributes knowledge before task-specific interaction while fine-tuning connects that knowledge to the new setting.
summary.tldr: Pretraining a frame predictor on physics videos supplies dynamics priors that improve policy learning and transfer in the tested environments.

title: Task-Agnostic Dynamics Priors for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Motivated by settings in which predictive models may be required to be non-discriminatory with respect to certain attributes (such as race), but even collecting the sensitive attribute may be forbidden or restricted, we initiate the study of fair learning under the constraint of differential privacy. Our first algorithm is a private implementation of the equalized odds post-processing approach of (Hardt et al., 2016). This algorithm is appealingly simple, but must be able to use protected group membership explicitly at test time, which can be viewed as a form of “disparate treatment”. Our second algorithm is a differentially private version of the oracle-efficient in-processing approach of (Agarwal et al., 2018) which is more complex but need not have access to protected group membership at test time. We identify new tradeoffs between fairness, accuracy, and privacy that emerge only when requiring all three properties, and show that these tradeoffs can be milder if group membership may be used at test time. We conclude with a brief experimental evaluation.

paragraphs: Predictive models may need to satisfy fairness requirements involving sensitive attributes even when access to those attributes is restricted. This paper studies fair learning under differential privacy, bringing fairness, predictive accuracy, and privacy into the same design problem. It asks how satisfying all three changes the choices available to a learning algorithm.

The first proposed algorithm privately implements an equalized-odds post-processing method. It is relatively simple, but it must explicitly use protected group membership when making predictions. The second privately adapts an oracle-efficient in-processing method. This alternative is more complex, but it does not require protected group membership at test time.

That distinction becomes central to the paper’s findings. The authors identify tradeoffs that emerge when fairness, accuracy, and privacy are required together, and show that these tradeoffs can be milder when group membership is available at prediction time. A brief experimental evaluation accompanies the analysis. The contribution therefore includes both private algorithms and an explanation of how prediction-time access to sensitive information affects their tradeoffs.
summary.tldr: Two private fair-learning algorithms reveal tradeoffs among fairness, accuracy, and privacy that depend on test-time access to group membership.

title: Differentially Private Fair Learning

abstract: We address the problem of inferring the causal effect of an exposure on an outcome across space, using observational data. The data is possibly subject to unmeasured confounding variables which, in a standard approach, must be adjusted for by estimating a nuisance function. Here we develop a method that eliminates the nuisance function, while mitigating the resulting errors-in-variables. The result is a robust and accurate inference method for spatially varying heterogeneous causal effects. The properties of the method are demonstrated on synthetic as well as real data from Germany and the US.

paragraphs: This paper asks how the causal effect of an exposure on an outcome changes across locations. The data are observational and may contain unmeasured confounding variables. That makes the problem more demanding than describing geographic associations: the aim is to infer effects that can differ across space while addressing the influence of confounding.

A standard approach described in the abstract handles this influence by estimating a nuisance function. The proposed method instead eliminates that function. Doing so introduces an errors-in-variables issue, which the method also mitigates. These two steps are linked: removing the nuisance function simplifies one part of the inference problem while requiring attention to the errors that result.

The authors report a robust and accurate method for estimating spatially varying causal effects. They demonstrate its properties using synthetic data and real data from Germany and the United States. The contribution centers on this combination of nuisance-function elimination and error mitigation, providing an approach specifically aimed at heterogeneous causal effects across space.
summary.tldr: The method estimates spatially varying causal effects by eliminating a confounding-related nuisance function and mitigating the resulting errors-in-variables.

title: Inferring Heterogeneous Causal Effects in Presence of Spatial Confounding

abstract: A standard approach in large scale machine learning is distributed stochastic gradient training, which requires the computation of aggregated stochastic gradients over multiple nodes on a network. Communication is a major bottleneck in such applications, and in recent years, compressed stochastic gradient methods such as QSGD (quantized SGD) and sparse SGD have been proposed to reduce communication. It was also shown that error compensation can be combined with compression to achieve better convergence in a scheme that each node compresses its local stochastic gradient and broadcast the result to all other nodes over the network in a single pass. However, such a single pass broadcast approach is not realistic in many practical implementations. For example, under the popular parameter-server model for distributed learning, the worker nodes need to send the compressed local gradients to the parameter server, which performs the aggregation. The parameter server has to compress the aggregated stochastic gradient again before sending it back to the worker nodes. In this work, we provide a detailed analysis on this two-pass communication model, with error-compensated compression both on the worker nodes and on the parameter server. We show that the error-compensated stochastic gradient algorithm admits three very nice properties: 1) it is compatible with an arbitrary compression technique; 2) it admits an improved convergence rate than the non error-compensated stochastic gradient method such as QSGD and sparse SGD; 3) it admits linear speedup with respect to the number of workers. The empirical study is also conducted to validate our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Distributed stochastic gradient training requires workers to exchange gradient information, making communication a potential bottleneck. Compression reduces the information sent, and error compensation can improve convergence when compression is used. This paper studies that combination in a communication pattern that matches parameter server systems.

In this setting, compression happens twice: workers compress their local gradients before sending them to a server, and the server compresses the aggregated gradient before returning it. An analysis of a single broadcast pass does not capture both stages. DoubleSqueeze analyzes error compensation at the workers and at the server, directly addressing the errors introduced along this two stage communication path.

The theoretical results establish compatibility with arbitrary compression techniques, improved convergence rates over noncompensated approaches such as quantized and sparse SGD, and linear speedup with the number of workers. An empirical study validates the theoretical findings. The contribution makes error compensated compression applicable to the full communication cycle of a parameter server, rather than analyzing only one part of that cycle.
summary.tldr: DoubleSqueeze analyzes error compensated gradient compression at both workers and a parameter server, establishing improved convergence and linear worker speedup.

title: DoubleSqueeze: Parallel Stochastic Gradient Descent with Double-pass Error-Compensated Compression

abstract: Most of today’s distributed machine learning systems assume reliable networks : whenever two machines exchange information (e.g., gradients or models), the network should guarantee the delivery of the message. At the same time, recent work exhibits the impressive tolerance of machine learning algorithms to errors or noise arising from relaxed communication or synchronization. In this paper, we connect these two trends, and consider the following question: Can we design machine learning systems that are tolerant to network unreliability during training? With this motivation, we focus on a theoretical problem of independent interest—given a standard distributed parameter server architecture, if every communication between the worker and the server has a non-zero probability $p$ of being dropped, does there exist an algorithm that still converges, and at what speed? In the context of prior art, this problem can be phrased as distributed learning over random topologies . The technical contribution of this paper is a novel theoretical analysis proving that distributed learning over random topologies can achieve comparable convergence rate to centralized or distributed learning over reliable networks. Further, we prove that the influence of the packet drop rate diminishes with the growth of the number of parameter servers. We map this theoretical result onto a real-world scenario, training deep neural networks over an unreliable network layer, and conduct network simulation to validate the system improvement by allowing the networks to be unreliable.

It studies a parameter-server architecture in which each worker–server communication has a nonzero probability of being lost, making the pattern of successful connections vary during training.

The authors analyze this situation as distributed learning over random topologies. Their theoretical result shows that such learning can achieve convergence rates comparable to centralized training or distributed training over reliable networks. The significance is that reliable delivery need not be taken as an unquestioned prerequisite for the studied training setup. The result supports designing learning and communication together so that training can tolerate some dropped exchanges.
summary.tldr: Distributed training can retain comparable convergence rates despite dropped messages, with packet-loss effects diminishing as the number of parameter servers grows.

title: Distributed Learning over Unreliable Networks

abstract: Recent research shows that sublevel sets of the loss surfaces of overparameterized networks are connected, exactly or approximately. We describe and compare experimentally a panel of methods used to connect two low-loss points by a low-loss curve on this surface. Our methods vary in accuracy and complexity. Most of our methods are based on ”macroscopic” distributional assumptions and are insensitive to the detailed properties of the points to be connected. Some methods require a prior training of a ”global connection model” which can then be applied to any pair of points. The accuracy of the method generally correlates with its complexity and sensitivity to the endpoint detail.

paragraphs: Two neural-network weight vectors can each achieve low loss, raising the question of whether a continuous path between them can also keep loss low. Motivated by research on connected low-loss regions in overparameterized networks, this paper describes and experimentally compares several methods for constructing such paths.

Most of the methods use broad distributional assumptions about the weights and are relatively insensitive to the detailed properties of the endpoints. Some require training a global connection model in advance, which can then be applied to any pair of points. This makes the amount of endpoint-specific information and prior preparation central differences between the approaches.

The comparison finds that connection accuracy generally correlates with method complexity and sensitivity to endpoint details. Thus, the work maps out a tradeoff between broadly applicable distribution-based constructions and methods that use more detailed information. Its contribution is a panel of practical connection strategies and an empirical comparison of how their design choices relate to the quality of the resulting low-loss curves.
summary.tldr: The paper compares methods for connecting low-loss neural-network weights, finding a general tradeoff between connection accuracy, complexity, and endpoint sensitivity.

title: Low-loss connection of weight vectors: distribution-based approaches

abstract: We study the robust one-bit compressed sensing problem whose goal is to design an algorithm that faithfully recovers any sparse target vector $\theta_0\in\mathbb{R}^d$ \emph{uniformly} via $m$ quantized noisy measurements. Specifically, we consider a new framework for this problem where the sparsity is implicitly enforced via mapping a low dimensional representation $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^k$ through a known $n$-layer ReLU generative network $G:\mathbb{R}^k\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^d$ such that $\theta_0 = G(x_0)$. Such a framework poses low-dimensional priors on $\theta_0$ without a known sparsity basis. We propose to recover the target $G(x_0)$ solving an unconstrained empirical risk minimization (ERM). Under a weak \emph{sub-exponential measurement assumption}, we establish a joint statistical and computational analysis. In particular, we prove that the ERM estimator in this new framework achieves a statistical rate of $m=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(kn \log d /\varepsilon^2)$ recovering any $G(x_0)$ uniformly up to an error $\varepsilon$. When the network is shallow (i.e., $n$ is small), we show this rate matches the information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithm factors of $\varepsilon^{-1}$. From the lens of computation, we prove that under proper conditions on the network weights, our proposed empirical risk, despite non-convexity, has no stationary point outside of small neighborhoods around the true representation $x_0$ and its negative multiple; furthermore, we show that the global minimizer of the empirical risk stays within the neighborhood around $x_0$ rather than its negative multiple under further assumptions on weights.

Specifically, we consider a new framework for this problem where the sparsity is implicitly enforced via mapping a low dimensional representation $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^k$ through a known $n$-layer ReLU generative network $G:\mathbb{R}^k\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^d$ such that $\theta_0 = G(x_0)$. Such a framework poses low-dimensional priors on $\theta_0$ without a known sparsity basis. We propose to recover the target $G(x_0)$ solving an unconstrained empirical risk minimization (ERM). Under a weak \emph{sub-exponential measurement assumption}, we establish a joint statistical and computational analysis. In particular, we prove that the ERM estimator in this new framework achieves a statistical rate of $m=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(kn \log d /\varepsilon^2)$ recovering any $G(x_0)$ uniformly up to an error $\varepsilon$. When the network is shallow (i.e., $n$ is small), we show this rate matches the information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithm factors of $\varepsilon^{-1}$. From the lens of computation, we prove that under proper conditions on the network weights, our proposed empirical risk, despite non-convexity, has no stationary point outside of small neighborhoods around the true representation $x_0$ and its negative multiple; furthermore, we show that the global minimizer of the empirical risk stays within the neighborhood around $x_0$ rather than its negative multiple under further assumptions on weights.

paragraphs: One-bit compressed sensing seeks to recover a signal from noisy measurements quantized to a single bit. This paper assumes the target is generated from a k-dimensional representation by a known n-layer ReLU network producing a d-dimensional output. The network supplies low-dimensional structure without requiring a known sparsity basis.

Recovery uses unconstrained empirical risk minimization. Under a sub-exponential measurement assumption, the authors prove uniform recovery to error ε using roughly kn log d/ε² measurements, suppressing additional logarithmic factors. For shallow networks, this matches the information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors in inverse accuracy. Uniformity means the guarantee covers any target represented by the specified generator.

The paper also studies the non-convex optimization landscape. Under suitable conditions on network weights, stationary points are confined to small neighborhoods of the true representation and a negative multiple of it. Further weight assumptions place the global minimizer near the true representation. These conditional results connect measurement requirements with favorable landscape structure, while distinguishing the statistical guarantee from the additional conditions needed for the computational conclusions.
summary.tldr: A known ReLU generator enables conditional uniform recovery guarantees from noisy one-bit measurements, alongside analysis of the non-convex recovery landscape.

title: Robust One-Bit Recovery via ReLU Generative Networks: Near-Optimal Statistical Rate and Global Landscape Analysis

abstract: The objective of a reinforcement learning agent is to behave so as to maximise the sum of a suitable scalar function of state: the reward. These rewards are typically given and immutable. In this paper, we instead consider the proposition that the reward function itself can be a good locus of learned knowledge. To investigate this, we propose a scalable meta-gradient framework for learning useful intrinsic reward functions across multiple lifetimes of experience. Through several proof-of-concept experiments, we show that it is feasible to learn and capture knowledge about long-term exploration and exploitation into a reward function. Furthermore, we show that unlike policy transfer methods that capture “how” the agent should behave, the learned reward functions can generalise to other kinds of agents and to changes in the dynamics of the environment by capturing “what” the agent should strive to do.

This paper investigates whether the reward function can itself store learned knowledge. The authors propose a scalable meta-gradient framework that learns useful intrinsic rewards across multiple lifetimes of experience, making the reward signal an object of learning.

A learned reward can guide what an agent pursues, allowing experience accumulated across lifetimes to influence later learning through the objective supplied to the agent.

It distinguishes this transfer from transferring a policy: a reward describes desirable outcomes, while a policy captures behavior. The experiments support the possibility that knowledge about objectives can remain useful when the agent or its environment changes. The evidence is presented as proof of concept, rather than a universal transfer guarantee.
summary.tldr: Learned intrinsic rewards can capture exploration and exploitation knowledge that transfers across agents and environmental changes in proof-of-concept experiments.

title: What Can Learned Intrinsic Rewards Capture?

abstract: Conventional unsupervised multi-source domain adaptation (UMDA) methods assume all source domains can be accessed directly. However, this assumption neglects the privacy-preserving policy, where all the data and computations must be kept decentralized. There exist three challenges in this scenario: (1) Minimizing the domain distance requires the pairwise calculation of the data from the source and target domains, while the data on the source domain is not available. (2) The communication cost and privacy security limit the application of existing UMDA methods, such as the domain adversarial training. (3) Since users cannot govern the data quality, the irrelevant or malicious source domains are more likely to appear, which causes negative transfer. To address the above problems, we propose a privacy-preserving UMDA paradigm named Knowledge Distillation based Decentralized Domain Adaptation (KD3A), which performs domain adaptation through the knowledge distillation on models from different source domains. The extensive experiments show that KD3A significantly outperforms state-of-the-art UMDA approaches. Moreover, the KD3A is robust to the negative transfer and brings a 100x reduction of communication cost compared with other decentralized UMDA methods.

paragraphs: Learning from several source domains becomes harder when their data and computations must stay decentralized. Conventional unsupervised multi-source domain adaptation assumes direct access to source data. Without that access, methods cannot straightforwardly compare source and target examples, and communication costs constrain how the different participants can cooperate.

KD3A addresses this setting through knowledge distillation from models trained on different source domains. Source models become the means of transferring knowledge for adaptation while respecting the decentralized data constraint. The paper also addresses negative transfer: irrelevant or malicious sources can hurt the target model, especially when users cannot control the quality of the contributing datasets.

The experiments report that KD3A substantially outperforms leading unsupervised multi-source adaptation approaches. They also show robustness to negative transfer and a hundredfold reduction in communication cost relative to other decentralized methods in this setting. These results matter together: useful adaptation must manage source quality as well as the practical cost of obtaining knowledge from distributed participants.
summary.tldr: KD3A adapts through knowledge distillation from decentralized source models, with reported gains in accuracy, negative-transfer robustness, and communication efficiency.

title: KD3A: Unsupervised Multi-Source Decentralized Domain Adaptation via Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Normalizing flows are among the most popular paradigms in generative modeling, especially for images, primarily because we can efficiently evaluate the likelihood of a data point. This is desirable both for evaluating the fit of a model, and for ease of training, as maximizing the likelihood can be done by gradient descent. However, training normalizing flows comes with difficulties as well: models which produce good samples typically need to be extremely deep – which comes with accompanying vanishing/exploding gradient problems. A very related problem is that they are often poorly \emph{conditioned}: since they are parametrized as invertible maps from $\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$, and typical training data like images intuitively is lower-dimensional, the learned maps often have Jacobians that are close to being singular. In our paper, we tackle representational aspects around depth and conditioning of normalizing flows: both for general invertible architectures, and for a particular common architecture, affine couplings. We prove that $\Theta(1)$ affine coupling layers suffice to exactly represent a permutation or $1 \times 1$ convolution, as used in GLOW, showing that representationally the choice of partition is not a bottleneck for depth. We also show that shallow affine coupling networks are universal approximators in Wasserstein distance if ill-conditioning is allowed, and experimentally investigate related phenomena involving padding. Finally, we show a depth lower bound for general flow architectures with few neurons per layer and bounded Lipschitz constant.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows offer efficient likelihood evaluation, but good samples often require deep models that are difficult to train. Another issue is poor conditioning: an invertible transformation can have a Jacobian close to singular when representing data concentrated near lower-dimensional structure. This paper studies how depth and conditioning affect what flow models can represent.

For affine coupling architectures, the authors prove that a constant number of layers can exactly represent a permutation or a 1 × 1 convolution. Thus, the choice of partition is not itself a representational bottleneck for depth in that sense. That qualification connects expressive power to potentially difficult numerical behavior. The paper additionally investigates padding experimentally and proves a depth lower bound for general flow architectures with few neurons per layer and bounded Lipschitz constant. Together, the results distinguish what shallow models can represent when conditioning is unrestricted from what constrained architectures may require in depth.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes how flow depth and conditioning interact, including shallow universality when ill-conditioning is allowed and depth lower bounds under constraints.

title: Representational aspects of depth and conditioning in normalizing flows

abstract: This paper aims to provide understandings for the effect of an over-parameterized model, e.g. a deep neural network, memorizing instance-dependent noisy labels. We first quantify the harms caused by memorizing noisy instances, and show the disparate impacts of noisy labels for sample instances with different representation frequencies. We then analyze how several popular solutions for learning with noisy labels mitigate this harm at the instance level. Our analysis reveals that existing approaches lead to disparate treatments when handling noisy instances. While higher-frequency instances often enjoy a high probability of an improvement by applying these solutions, lower-frequency instances do not. Our analysis reveals new understandings for when these approaches work, and provides theoretical justifications for previously reported empirical observations. This observation requires us to rethink the distribution of label noise across instances and calls for different treatments for instances in different regimes.

paragraphs: An over-parameterized model can memorize incorrect labels, including errors whose likelihood depends on the individual example. This paper analyzes the harm caused by that memorization at the instance level. It shows that the consequences differ according to how frequently an instance’s representation occurs in the data.

The authors then examine several popular approaches for learning with noisy labels. Their analysis finds that these remedies also have uneven effects. Higher-frequency instances often have a high probability of benefiting, while lower-frequency instances do not enjoy the same improvement prospects. This distinguishes the overall usefulness of a noise-handling method from its effectiveness for different kinds of examples.

The theoretical analysis explains when existing approaches work and provides justification for previously reported empirical observations. Its main implication is that label noise and its treatment should be considered across representation-frequency regimes. A correction that helps common instances may leave less frequent instances underserved, motivating different treatments for those regimes rather than assuming one remedy benefits them equally.
summary.tldr: Memorizing noisy labels and applying common remedies affect examples differently depending on their representation frequency.

title: Understanding Instance-Level Label Noise: Disparate Impacts and Treatments

abstract: Deep equilibrium networks (DEQs) are a promising way to construct models which trade off memory for compute. However, theoretical understanding of these models is still lacking compared to traditional networks, in part because of the repeated application of a single set of weights. We show that DEQs are sensitive to the higher order statistics of the matrix families from which they are initialized. In particular, initializing with orthogonal or symmetric matrices allows for greater stability in training. This gives us a practical prescription for initializations which allow for training with a broader range of initial weight scales.

paragraphs: Deep equilibrium networks offer a way to exchange additional computation for reduced memory use. A defining feature is the repeated application of the same weights. This reuse makes their behavior different from that of traditional networks and motivates a closer look at how the initial weights influence whether training remains stable.

The paper shows that initialization matters beyond the overall scale of the weights. Deep equilibrium networks are sensitive to higher-order statistical properties of the families of matrices used to initialize them. Consequently, choosing an initialization involves more than selecting a magnitude: the structure of the matrices also affects training behavior. The authors identify orthogonal and symmetric matrices as choices that allow greater stability.

This finding yields a practical prescription for selecting initializations that support training across a broader range of initial weight scales. Its significance is that matrix structure provides another way to improve the usable training regime of these models. The stated result concerns increased stability and a wider range of workable scales; it does not assert that either matrix family guarantees successful training in every case.
summary.tldr: Orthogonal or symmetric initial weight matrices can make deep equilibrium networks more stable across a broader range of initialization scales.

title: Deep equilibrium networks are sensitive to initialization statistics

abstract: We develop a new approach, named Greedy when Sure and Conservative when Uncertain (GSCU), to competing online against unknown and nonstationary opponents. GSCU improves in four aspects: 1) introduces a novel way of learning opponent policy embeddings offline; 2) trains offline a single best response (conditional additionally on our opponent policy embedding) instead of a finite set of separate best responses against any opponent; 3) computes online a posterior of the current opponent policy embedding, without making the discrete and ineffective decision which type the current opponent belongs to; and 4) selects online between a real-time greedy policy and a fixed conservative policy via an adversarial bandit algorithm, gaining a theoretically better regret than adhering to either. Experimental studies on popular benchmarks demonstrate GSCU’s superiority over the state-of-the-art methods. The code is available online at \url{https://github.com/YeTianJHU/GSCU}.

paragraphs: Competing against an unfamiliar opponent is harder when that opponent’s behavior can change over time. Greedy when Sure and Conservative when Uncertain, or GSCU, addresses this online decision problem by combining a learned representation of opponent policies with a mechanism for choosing between aggressive and conservative responses.

Offline, the method learns embeddings of opponent policies and trains one best-response policy conditioned on those embeddings. This replaces a finite collection of separately trained responses. During interaction, it maintains a posterior distribution over the current opponent’s embedding, preserving uncertainty rather than assigning the opponent to one discrete type.

An adversarial bandit algorithm then selects between a greedy policy computed in real time and a fixed conservative policy. The paper establishes a better theoretical regret guarantee for this selection mechanism than for adhering to either option alone. Experiments on popular benchmarks report improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines uncertainty about opponent behavior with an explicit strategy for balancing exploitation and caution during play.
summary.tldr: GSCU tracks uncertainty over opponent policies and uses a bandit algorithm to choose between greedy and conservative play.

title: Greedy when Sure and Conservative when Uncertain about the Opponents

abstract: Pruning methods can considerably reduce the size of artificial neural networks without harming their performance and in some cases they can even uncover sub-networks that, when trained in isolation, match or surpass the test accuracy of their dense counterparts. Here, we characterize the inductive bias that pruning imprints in such "winning lottery tickets": focusing on visual tasks, we analyze the architecture resulting from iterative magnitude pruning of a simple fully connected network. We show that the surviving node connectivity is local in input space, and organized in patterns reminiscent of the ones found in convolutional networks. We investigate the role played by data and tasks in shaping the architecture of the pruned sub-network. We find that pruning performances, and the ability to sift out the noise and make local features emerge, improve by increasing the size of the training set, and the semantic value of the data. We also study different pruning procedures, and find that iterative magnitude pruning is particularly effective in distilling meaningful connectivity out of features present in the original task. Our results suggest the possibility to automatically discover new and efficient architectural inductive biases in other datasets and tasks.

This paper asks what architectural preferences pruning creates, focusing on visual tasks and a simple fully connected network. The authors examine the connectivity that survives iterative magnitude pruning to understand the structure of these successful subnetworks.

They find that surviving connections become local in input space, with patterns resembling those used in convolutional networks. They also investigate how the data and task shape this emerging architecture. Larger training sets and data with greater semantic value improve pruning performance and its ability to remove noise while exposing local features.

The results suggest that pruning can do more than compress a network: it can reveal useful architectural structure tied to the learning problem. Discovering efficient architectural preferences in other datasets and tasks remains a possibility suggested by these findings.
summary.tldr: Iterative magnitude pruning reveals local, convolution-like connectivity in fully connected networks trained on visual tasks.

title: Neural Network Pruning Denoises the Features and Makes Local Connectivity Emerge in Visual Tasks

abstract: In view of its power in extracting feature representation, contrastive self-supervised learning has been successfully integrated into the practice of (deep) reinforcement learning (RL), leading to efficient policy learning on various applications. Despite its tremendous empirical successes, the understanding of contrastive learning for RL remains elusive. To narrow such a gap, we study contrastive-learning empowered RL for a class of Markov decision processes (MDPs) and Markov games (MGs) with low-rank transitions. For both models, we propose to extract the correct feature representations of the low-rank model by minimizing a contrastive loss. Moreover, under the online setting, we propose novel upper confidence bound (UCB)-type algorithms that incorporate such a contrastive loss with online RL algorithms for MDPs or MGs. We further theoretically prove that our algorithm recovers the true representations and simultaneously achieves sample efficiency in learning the optimal policy and Nash equilibrium in MDPs and MGs. We also provide empirical studies to demonstrate the efficacy of the UCB-based contrastive learning method for RL. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first provably efficient online RL algorithm that incorporates contrastive learning for representation learning.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning has helped reinforcement learning systems learn useful features, but its empirical success leaves a theoretical question: when can those features support efficient decision-making? This paper studies that question for Markov decision processes and Markov games whose transition models have low-rank structure. That structural setting is central to the guarantees.

The proposed approach learns the feature representations of these transition models by minimizing a contrastive loss. It then incorporates that learning objective into online reinforcement learning algorithms based on upper confidence bounds. This connects representation learning with the process of gathering experience and improving decisions, rather than treating the learned features as an unrelated preliminary step.

For the model classes studied, the authors prove recovery of the true representations alongside sample-efficient learning. The decision target is an optimal policy for a Markov decision process and a Nash equilibrium for a Markov game. Empirical studies also support the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is a theoretical connection between contrastive feature learning and online learning efficiency under the stated low-rank transition structure.
summary.tldr: For decision processes and games with low-rank transitions, Contrastive UCB combines contrastive representation learning with provably sample-efficient online reinforcement learning.

title: Contrastive UCB: Provably Efficient Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning in Online Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) is widely used to analyze overparametrized neural networks due to the famous result by Jacot et al. (2018): in the infinite-width limit, the NTK is deterministic and constant during training. However, this result cannot explain the behavior of deep networks, since it generally does not hold if depth and width tend to infinity simultaneously. In this paper, we study the NTK of fully-connected ReLU networks with depth comparable to width. We prove that the NTK properties depend significantly on the depth-to-width ratio and the distribution of parameters at initialization. In fact, our results indicate the importance of the three phases in the hyperparameter space identified in Poole et al. (2016): ordered, chaotic and the edge of chaos (EOC). We derive exact expressions for the NTK dispersion in the infinite-depth-and-width limit in all three phases and conclude that the NTK variability grows exponentially with depth at the EOC and in the chaotic phase but not in the ordered phase. We also show that the NTK of deep networks may stay constant during training only in the ordered phase and discuss how the structure of the NTK matrix changes during training.

The paper examines why that picture can fail for deep networks when depth grows alongside width, studying fully connected ReLU networks whose depth is comparable to their width.

The authors prove that kernel properties depend strongly on the depth-to-width ratio and the parameter distribution at initialization. Their analysis distinguishes ordered, chaotic, and edge-of-chaos regions of the hyperparameter space. They derive exact expressions for kernel dispersion in the joint infinite-depth-and-width limit, making variability across initializations an explicit part of the theory.

The results show exponential growth of kernel variability with depth in the chaotic and edge-of-chaos phases, but not in the ordered phase. They also show that deep-network kernels may remain constant during training only in the ordered phase; this does not assert that every ordered-phase kernel remains constant. The findings clarify why depth and initialization matter when applying an infinite-width kernel description to deep networks.
summary.tldr: When depth grows with width, neural tangent kernel variability and training behavior depend strongly on network proportions and initialization.

title: Neural Tangent Kernel Beyond the Infinite-Width Limit: Effects of Depth and Initialization

abstract: Characteristic functions (from cooperative game theory) are able to evaluate partial inputs and form the basis for attribution methods like Shapley values. These attribution methods allow us to measure how important each input component is for the function output—one of the goals of explainable AI (XAI). Given a standard classifier function, it is unclear how partial input should be realised. Instead, most XAI-methods for black-box classifiers like neural networks consider counterfactual inputs that generally lie off-manifold, which makes them hard to evaluate and easy to manipulate. We propose a setup to directly train characteristic functions in the form of neural networks to play simple two-player games. We apply this to the game of Connect Four by randomly hiding colour information from our agents during training. This has three advantages for comparing XAI-methods: It alleviates the ambiguity about how to realise partial input, makes off-manifold evaluation unnecessary and allows us to compare the methods by letting them play against each other.

paragraphs: Attribution methods such as Shapley values assess how input components contribute to an output by evaluating partial inputs. For an ordinary classifier, however, it can be unclear what a partial input should mean. Common counterfactual constructions may fall outside the data distribution, making their evaluation difficult and susceptible to manipulation.

The paper proposes training neural networks directly as characteristic functions, which are designed to evaluate partial inputs. It does this through simple two-player games and applies the setup to Connect Four. During training, agents randomly lose access to color information, making partial observation an explicit part of the task they learn.

This construction reduces ambiguity about how missing information is represented and removes the need for off-distribution evaluations in the proposed comparison setup. It also allows explanation methods to be compared through game play against one another. The contribution is an evaluation setting where the model’s handling of partial information is trained directly, providing a concrete basis for studying attribution methods.
summary.tldr: Training Connect Four agents with hidden color information creates characteristic functions that support direct, game-based comparisons of attribution methods.

title: Training Characteristic Functions with Reinforcement Learning: XAI-methods play Connect Four

abstract: Recent studies in lossy compression show that distortion and perceptual quality are at odds with each other, which put forward the tradeoff between distortion and perception (D-P). Intuitively, to attain different perceptual quality, different decoders have to be trained. In this paper, we present a nontrivial finding that only two decoders are sufficient for optimally achieving arbitrary (an infinite number of different) D-P tradeoff. We prove that arbitrary points of the D-P tradeoff bound can be achieved by a simple linear interpolation between the outputs of a minimum MSE decoder and a specifically constructed perfect perceptual decoder. Meanwhile, the perceptual quality (in terms of the squared Wasserstein-2 distance metric) can be quantitatively controlled by the interpolation factor. Furthermore, to construct a perfect perceptual decoder, we propose two theoretically optimal training frameworks. The new frameworks are different from the distortion-plus-adversarial loss based heuristic framework widely used in existing methods, which are not only theoretically optimal but also can yield state-of-the-art performance in practical perceptual decoding. Finally, we validate our theoretical finding and demonstrate the superiority of our frameworks via experiments. Code is available at: https://github.com/ZeyuYan/Controllable-Perceptual-Compression
originalAbstract: Recent studies in lossy compression show that distortion and perceptual quality are at odds with each other, which put forward the tradeoff between distortion and perception (D-P). Intuitively, to attain different perceptual quality, different decoders have to be trained. In this paper, we present a nontrivial finding that only two decoders are sufficient for optimally achieving arbitrary (an infinite number of different) D-P tradeoff. We prove that arbitrary points of the D-P tradeoff bound can be achieved by a simple linear interpolation between the outputs of a minimum MSE decoder and a specifically constructed perfect perceptual decoder. Meanwhile, the perceptual quality (in terms of the squared Wasserstein-2 distance metric) can be quantitatively controlled by the interpolation factor. Furthermore, to construct a perfect perceptual decoder, we propose two theoretically optimal training frameworks. The new frameworks are different from the distortion-plus-adversarial loss based heuristic framework widely used in existing methods, which are not only theoretically optimal but also can yield state-of-the-art performance in practical perceptual decoding. Finally, we validate our theoretical finding and demonstrate the superiority of our frameworks via experiments. Code is available at: https://github.com/ZeyuYan/Controllable-Perceptual-Compression

paragraphs: Lossy compression faces a tradeoff between reconstruction distortion and perceptual quality. A natural response is to train different decoders for different positions on that tradeoff. This paper proves that two appropriately chosen decoders suffice to attain arbitrary points on the distortion–perception bound through interpolation.

One decoder minimizes mean squared error. The other is a specifically constructed decoder with perfect perceptual quality. Taking a linear interpolation of their outputs reaches the desired tradeoff points, and the interpolation factor quantitatively controls perceptual quality measured by squared Wasserstein-2 distance. The construction and metric are central to the claim; it is not a statement about interpolating any two decoders.

The authors also propose two theoretically optimal training frameworks for constructing the perceptual decoder. These differ from the widely used heuristic combination of distortion and adversarial losses. Experiments validate the interpolation result and demonstrate the frameworks’ superiority, including state-of-the-art practical perceptual decoding. The contribution links a controllable theoretical tradeoff to procedures for training the decoder needed to realize it.
summary.tldr: Interpolating between a minimum-MSE decoder and a specifically constructed perceptual decoder can optimally control the distortion–perception tradeoff.

title: Optimally Controllable Perceptual Lossy Compression

abstract: Training agents to control a dynamic environment is a fundamental task in AI. In many environments, the dynamics can be summarized by a small set of events that capture the semantic behavior of the system. Typically, these events form chains or cascades. We often wish to change the system behavior using a single intervention that propagates through the cascade. For instance, one may trigger a biochemical cascade to switch the state of a cell or, in logistics, reroute a truck to meet an unexpected, urgent delivery. We introduce a new supervised learning setup called Cascade. An agent observes a system with known dynamics evolving from some initial state. The agent is given a structured semantic instruction and needs to make an intervention that triggers a cascade of events, such that the system reaches an alternative (counterfactual) behavior. We provide a test-bed for this problem, consisting of physical objects. We combine semantic tree search with an event-driven forward model and devise an algorithm that learns to efficiently search in exponentially large semantic trees. We demonstrate that our approach learns to follow instructions to intervene in new complex scenes. When provided with an observed cascade of events, it can also reason about alternative outcomes.

paragraphs: Some dynamic systems can be understood through a chain of meaningful events. A single intervention may change one event and thereby alter the rest of the chain. This paper introduces Cascade, a supervised learning setup in which an agent must choose such an intervention to make a system follow a structured semantic instruction.

The agent observes a system evolving from an initial state, and the system dynamics are known. The task is to cause an alternative behavior through a cascade of events. The authors provide a test environment involving physical objects and combine semantic tree search with an event-driven forward model. Their algorithm learns how to search efficiently through semantic trees whose size grows exponentially.

The reported demonstrations show that the approach learns to follow intervention instructions in new, complex scenes. Given an observed sequence of events, it can also reason about alternative outcomes. The contribution brings intervention selection and counterfactual reasoning into one setup, with event structure guiding the search. Its stated setting relies on known dynamics, which is central to understanding what the learned agent is asked to solve.
summary.tldr: Cascade trains agents to choose a single intervention that changes an event chain, using learned semantic search and known system dynamics.

title: Learning to Initiate and Reason in Event-Driven Cascading Processes

abstract: This paper presents Ske2Grid, a new representation learning framework for improved skeleton-based action recognition. In Ske2Grid, we define a regular convolution operation upon a novel grid representation of human skeleton, which is a compact image-like grid patch constructed and learned through three novel designs. Specifically, we propose a graph-node index transform (GIT) to construct a regular grid patch through assigning the nodes in the skeleton graph one by one to the desired grid cells. To ensure that GIT is a bijection and enrich the expressiveness of the grid representation, an up-sampling transform (UPT) is learned to interpolate the skeleton graph nodes for filling the grid patch to the full. To resolve the problem when the one-step UPT is aggressive and further exploit the representation capability of the grid patch with increasing spatial size, a progressive learning strategy (PLS) is proposed which decouples the UPT into multiple steps and aligns them to multiple paired GITs through a compact cascaded design learned progressively. We construct networks upon prevailing graph convolution networks and conduct experiments on six mainstream skeleton-based action recognition datasets. Experiments show that our Ske2Grid significantly outperforms existing GCN-based solutions under different benchmark settings, without bells and whistles. Code and models are available at https://github.com/OSVAI/Ske2Grid.

paragraphs: Skeleton-based action recognition represents human movement through joints and their relationships. Ske2Grid learns to arrange this information into a compact, image-like grid so that regular convolution can operate on it. The paper's contribution is a coordinated set of transformations for constructing and progressively learning that grid representation.

A graph-node index transform assigns skeleton nodes to grid cells. A learned upsampling transform interpolates additional nodes to fill the grid, supporting a one-to-one assignment and a more expressive representation. Because a large expansion in a single step can be too aggressive, the method breaks upsampling into several stages paired with corresponding index transforms.

These stages form a compact cascade trained progressively as the grid grows. The authors build networks on established graph convolution architectures and evaluate them on six mainstream skeleton-based action recognition datasets. They report significant improvements over existing graph convolution solutions across benchmark settings. The findings support learning how skeleton information is arranged for convolution as a useful component of action-recognition modeling.
summary.tldr: Ske2Grid progressively maps skeleton graphs into learned image-like grids, improving action recognition in the reported benchmarks.

title: Ske2Grid: Skeleton-to-Grid Representation Learning for Action Recognition

abstract: We investigate the use of natural language to drive the generalization of policies in multi-agent settings. Unlike single-agent settings, the generalization of policies should also consider the influence of other agents. Besides, with the increasing number of entities in multi-agent settings, more agent-entity interactions are needed for language grounding, and the enormous search space could impede the learning process. Moreover, given a simple general instruction, e.g., beating all enemies, agents are required to decompose it into multiple subgoals and figure out the right one to focus on. Inspired by previous work, we try to address these issues at the entity level and propose a novel framework for language grounding in multi-agent reinforcement learning, entity divider (EnDi). EnDi enables agents to independently learn subgoal division at the entity level and act in the environment based on the associated entities. The subgoal division is regularized by agent modeling to avoid subgoal conflicts and promote coordinated strategies. Empirically, EnDi demonstrates the strong generalization ability to unseen games with new dynamics and expresses the superiority over existing methods. The code is available at https://github.com/PKU-RL/EnDi.

paragraphs: A general instruction such as defeating all enemies leaves a multi-agent system with several decisions: which entities matter, how to divide the instruction into subgoals, and which subgoal each agent should pursue. As the number of entities grows, grounding language in possible interactions becomes harder. Each agent must also account for the behavior of its teammates.

The proposed Entity Divider framework, EnDi, organizes this learning around entities. Agents independently learn how to divide instructions into entity-level subgoals, then act based on their associated entities. Agent modeling regularizes this division to discourage conflicting subgoals and encourage coordinated strategies. This connects instruction interpretation to both the objects involved and the other agents’ behavior.

Experiments report strong generalization to unseen games with new dynamics and better performance than existing methods. These findings support entity-level subgoal division as a useful structure for language-guided multi-agent learning. The stated evidence concerns generalization in the evaluated games, where successful instruction following requires agents to coordinate their choices as well as understand the language.
summary.tldr: EnDi grounds instructions in entity-level subgoals and uses agent modeling to encourage coordination and generalization to unseen games.

title: Entity Divider with Language Grounding in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we introduce neural network accelerated implicit filtering (NNAIF), a novel family of methods for solving noisy derivative free (i.e. black box, zeroth order) optimization problems. NNAIF intelligently combines the established literature on implicit filtering (IF) optimization methods with a neural network (NN) surrogate model of the objective function, resulting in accelerated derivative free methods for unconstrained optimization problems. The NN surrogate model consists of a fixed number of parameters, which can be as few as $\approx 1.3 \times 10^{4}$, that are updated as NNAIF progresses. We show that NNAIF directly inherits the convergence properties of IF optimization methods, and thus NNAIF is guaranteed to converge towards a critical point of the objective function under appropriate assumptions. Numerical experiments with $31$ noisy problems from the CUTEst optimization benchmark set demonstrate the benefits and costs associated with NNAIF. These benefits include NNAIF’s ability to minimize structured functions of several thousand variables much more rapidly than well-known alternatives, such as Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) and finite difference based variants of gradient descent (GD) and BFGS, as well as its namesake IF.

paragraphs: Optimizing a noisy black-box function is difficult when derivatives are unavailable. Neural Network Accelerated Implicit Filtering, or NNAIF, combines an established derivative-free optimization method with a neural network that approximates the objective. The goal is to accelerate unconstrained optimization while retaining the convergence properties of implicit filtering.

The neural surrogate has a fixed number of parameters, potentially as few as roughly 13,000, and its parameters are updated as optimization proceeds. The authors show that the combined method inherits implicit filtering’s convergence properties. Under appropriate assumptions, it therefore converges toward a critical point of the objective; this is a conditional guarantee about a critical point, rather than a claim of finding a global optimum.

Numerical experiments use 31 noisy CUTEst benchmark problems to examine both benefits and costs. The reported benefits include much faster minimization of structured functions with several thousand variables than CMA-ES, finite-difference versions of gradient descent and BFGS, and implicit filtering itself. The results demonstrate how a learned surrogate can accelerate an established search procedure while preserving its theoretical foundation.
summary.tldr: NNAIF adds an evolving neural surrogate to implicit filtering, accelerating reported noisy optimization problems while inheriting conditional convergence guarantees.

title: Neural Network Accelerated Implicit Filtering: Integrating Neural Network Surrogates With Provably Convergent Derivative Free Optimization Methods

abstract: We study the problem of generating diverse candidates in the context of Multi-Objective Optimization. In many applications of machine learning such as drug discovery and material design, the goal is to generate candidates which simultaneously optimize a set of potentially conflicting objectives. Moreover, these objectives are often imperfect evaluations of some underlying property of interest, making it important to generate diverse candidates to have multiple options for expensive downstream evaluations. We propose Multi-Objective GFlowNets (MOGFNs), a novel method for generating diverse Pareto optimal solutions, based on GFlowNets. We introduce two variants of MOGFNs: MOGFN-PC, which models a family of independent sub-problems defined by a scalarization function, with reward-conditional GFlowNets, and MOGFN-AL, which solves a sequence of sub-problems defined by an acquisition function in an active learning loop. Our experiments on wide variety of synthetic and benchmark tasks demonstrate advantages of the proposed methods in terms of the Pareto performance and importantly, improved candidate diversity, which is the main contribution of this work.

paragraphs: Design problems often involve competing objectives, so there may be several worthwhile tradeoffs instead of one best candidate. Moreover, objective scores can be imperfect stand-ins for the properties that ultimately matter. This paper therefore targets both strong tradeoffs and diverse candidates, giving expensive downstream evaluations multiple distinct options to investigate.

Multi-Objective GFlowNets use GFlowNets to generate diverse Pareto-optimal solutions: candidates whose objectives cannot be improved without sacrificing something elsewhere. The paper introduces two variants. MOGFN-PC uses reward-conditioned GFlowNets to represent a family of subproblems defined by scalarization, which combines multiple objectives into a single score. MOGFN-AL instead follows a sequence of subproblems determined by an acquisition function within an active-learning loop.

Experiments across synthetic and benchmark tasks show advantages in Pareto performance and, especially, candidate diversity. The authors identify the diversity improvement as the main contribution. This matters because strong objective scores alone may leave a downstream evaluator with very similar options, whereas diverse candidates provide a broader set of possibilities when those scores only imperfectly reflect the desired properties.
summary.tldr: Multi-Objective GFlowNets generate diverse candidates across competing objectives, with reported gains in tradeoff quality and especially diversity.

title: Multi-Objective GFlowNets

abstract: Inductive knowledge graph completion has been considered as the task of predicting missing triplets between new entities that are not observed during training. While most inductive knowledge graph completion methods assume that all entities can be new, they do not allow new relations to appear at inference time. This restriction prohibits the existing methods from appropriately handling real-world knowledge graphs where new entities accompany new relations. In this paper, we propose an INductive knowledge GRAph eMbedding method, InGram, that can generate embeddings of new relations as well as new entities at inference time. Given a knowledge graph, we define a relation graph as a weighted graph consisting of relations and the affinity weights between them. Based on the relation graph and the original knowledge graph, InGram learns how to aggregate neighboring embeddings to generate relation and entity embeddings using an attention mechanism. Experimental results show that InGram outperforms 14 different state-of-the-art methods on varied inductive learning scenarios.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph completion predicts missing relationships between entities. Inductive methods address entities absent from training, but many still assume that every relation type is already known. This becomes restrictive when a new graph introduces unfamiliar entities alongside unfamiliar relations. InGram is designed to generate representations for both at inference time.

The method constructs a second graph whose nodes are the relations in the original knowledge graph. Weighted connections in this relation graph describe affinities between relation types. InGram then uses both graphs, learning through attention how to aggregate neighboring embeddings into representations of entities and relations. This gives relation structure an explicit role in constructing representations for new graph elements.

Experiments compare InGram with 14 state-of-the-art methods across varied inductive learning scenarios, and the authors report that it outperforms them. The methodological contribution is the use of a relation graph to extend inductive embedding beyond new entities alone. The empirical findings support that design in settings where the kinds of relationships encountered during inference can also differ from those seen during training.
summary.tldr: InGram uses attention over knowledge and relation graphs to embed previously unseen entities and relation types at inference time.

title: InGram: Inductive Knowledge Graph Embedding via Relation Graphs

abstract: There has been growing interest in employing neural network (NN) to directly solve constrained optimization problems with low run-time complexity. However, it is non-trivial to ensure NN solutions strictly satisfying problem constraints due to inherent NN prediction errors. Existing feasibility-ensuring methods either are computationally expensive or lack performance guarantee. In this paper, we propose homeomorphic projection as a low-complexity scheme to guarantee NN solution feasibility for optimization over a general set homeomorphic to a unit ball, covering all compact convex sets and certain classes of nonconvex sets. The idea is to (i) learn a minimum distortion homeomorphic mapping between the constraint set and a unit ball using an invertible NN (INN), and then (ii) perform a simple bisection operation concerning the unit ball so that the INN-mapped final solution is feasible with respect to the constraint set with minor distortion-induced optimality loss. We prove the feasibility guarantee and bound the optimality loss under mild conditions. Simulation results, including those for non-convex AC-OPF problems in power grid operation, show that homeomorphic projection outperforms existing methods in solution feasibility and run-time complexity, while achieving similar optimality loss.

paragraphs: Neural networks can quickly predict solutions to constrained optimization problems, but prediction errors can violate the constraints. This paper proposes a low-complexity correction method with a feasibility guarantee. Its scope is constraint sets homeomorphic to a unit ball, covering all compact convex sets and certain nonconvex classes described by the authors.

The method learns an invertible mapping between the constraint set and a unit ball, seeking to keep geometric distortion small. It then performs a simple bisection operation in relation to the ball and uses the invertible network to map the result into a feasible solution. The ball supplies a simpler geometry for enforcing feasibility.

Under mild conditions, the authors prove feasibility and bound the optimality loss caused by distortion. Simulations include nonconvex alternating-current optimal power flow problems in power grids. They show better feasibility and runtime complexity than existing methods, with similar optimality loss. The result ties the speed of neural solution prediction to a correction procedure whose guarantees depend on the stated geometric setting and conditions.
summary.tldr: An invertible mapping to a unit ball enables efficient correction of neural optimization outputs with conditional feasibility and optimality-loss guarantees.

title: Low Complexity Homeomorphic Projection to Ensure Neural-Network Solution Feasibility for Optimization over (Non-)Convex Set

abstract: The noise transition matrix plays a central role in the problem of learning with noisy labels. Among many other reasons, a large number of existing solutions rely on the knowledge of it. Identifying and estimating the transition matrix without ground truth labels is a critical and challenging task. When label noise transition depends on each instance, the problem of identifying the instance-dependent noise transition matrix becomes substantially more challenging. Despite recently proposed solutions for learning from instance-dependent noisy labels, the literature lacks a unified understanding of when such a problem remains identifiable. The goal of this paper is to characterize the identifiability of the label noise transition matrix. Building on Kruskal’s identifiability results, we are able to show the necessity of multiple noisy labels in identifying the noise transition matrix at the instance level. We further instantiate the results to explain the successes of the state-of-the-art solutions and how additional assumptions alleviated the requirement of multiple noisy labels. Our result reveals that disentangled features improve identification. This discovery led us to an approach that improves the estimation of the transition matrix using properly disentangled features. Code is available at https://github.com/UCSC-REAL/Identifiability.

paragraphs: A label-noise transition matrix describes how true labels can become corrupted. Many approaches to learning with noisy labels depend on knowing this matrix, yet recovering it without ground-truth labels is difficult. The problem becomes more challenging when the corruption process differs from one data instance to another.

This paper studies identifiability: whether the available information can determine the transition matrix. Building on Kruskal’s identifiability results, the authors establish the necessity of multiple noisy labels for instance-level identification in the analyzed setting. They also explain how additional assumptions in existing approaches alleviate that requirement. The role of those assumptions matters because identification depends on what information and structure are available.

The analysis further shows that disentangled features improve identification. This motivates a method that uses appropriately disentangled features to improve transition-matrix estimation. The contribution connects a theoretical question about when recovery is possible with a practical approach to making that recovery better, while clarifying why existing methods can succeed under additional assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when label-noise transitions are identifiable and uses disentangled features to improve their estimation.

title: Identifiability of Label Noise Transition Matrix

abstract: We propose a new dataset distillation algorithm using reparameterization and convexification of implicit gradients (RCIG), that substantially improves the state-of-the-art. To this end, we first formulate dataset distillation as a bi-level optimization problem. Then, we show how implicit gradients can be effectively used to compute meta-gradient updates. We further equip the algorithm with a convexified approximation that corresponds to learning on top of a frozen finite-width neural tangent kernel. Finally, we improve bias in implicit gradients by parameterizing the neural network to enable analytical computation of final-layer parameters given the body parameters. RCIG establishes the new state-of-the-art on a diverse series of dataset distillation tasks. Notably, with one image per class, on resized ImageNet, RCIG sees on average a 108% improvement over the previous state-of-the-art distillation algorithm. Similarly, we observed a 66% gain over SOTA on Tiny-ImageNet and 37% on CIFAR-100.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation seeks a compact training dataset that remains useful for learning. This paper introduces RCIG, an algorithm that treats distillation as a bilevel optimization problem. Its central concern is how to compute the updates that improve the distilled data through their effect on the model trained with them.

RCIG uses implicit gradients to compute these meta-level updates. It adds a convexified approximation corresponding to learning on a frozen, finite-width neural tangent kernel. A further reparameterization allows the network's final-layer parameters to be calculated analytically once its body parameters are given, addressing bias in the implicit gradients.

The authors report new state-of-the-art results across diverse distillation tasks. With one image per class on resized ImageNet, they report an average improvement of 108% over the previous leading distillation algorithm. They also report gains of 66% on Tiny-ImageNet and 37% on CIFAR-100. These findings show substantial reported benefits from changing the optimization machinery used to construct distilled datasets, especially in the highlighted highly compressed setting.
summary.tldr: RCIG improves dataset distillation through convexified implicit gradients and a reparameterization that makes final-layer optimization analytical.

title: Dataset Distillation with Convexified Implicit Gradients

abstract: We propose the first federated correlation test framework compatible with secure aggregation, namely FED-$\chi^2$. In our protocol, the statistical computations are recast as frequency moment estimation problems, where the clients collaboratively generate a shared projection matrix and then use stable projection to encode the local information in a compact vector. As such encodings can be linearly aggregated, secure aggregation can be applied to conceal the individual updates. We formally establish the security guarantee of FED-$\chi^2$ by proving that only the minimum necessary information (i.e., the correlation statistics) is revealed to the server. We show that our protocol can be naturally extended to estimate other statistics that can be recast as frequency moment estimations. By accommodating Shannon’e Entropy in FED-$\chi^2$, we further propose the first secure federated entropy estimation protocol, FED-$H$. The evaluation results demonstrate that FED-$\chi^2$ and FED-$H$ achieve good performance with small client-side computation overhead in several real-world case studies.

paragraphs: Computing statistics across distributed clients requires a way to combine their information while protecting individual contributions. This paper introduces FED-χ², a federated correlation-testing framework compatible with secure aggregation. The design makes the statistical calculation fit an aggregation procedure that conceals each client’s update.

The authors reformulate the computation as frequency-moment estimation. Clients jointly generate a shared projection matrix and use stable projections to encode local information into compact vectors. Those vectors can be added together, which is the key property enabling secure aggregation. The paper proves a security guarantee that the server learns only the minimum required information, namely the correlation statistics.

The same construction can extend to other statistics expressible through frequency-moment estimation. Applying it to Shannon entropy yields FED-H, a secure federated entropy-estimation protocol. Evaluations in several real-world case studies report good performance with small client-side computational overhead. The contribution combines a formally analyzed information guarantee with compact, aggregatable representations, allowing useful statistical calculations without exposing individual client updates.
summary.tldr: FED-χ² and FED-H use compact, securely aggregatable projections for federated correlation testing and entropy estimation.

title: Secure Federated Correlation Test and Entropy Estimation

abstract: Many important real-world Reinforcement Learning (RL) problems involve partial observability and require policies with memory. Unfortunately, standard deep RL algorithms for partially observable settings typically condition on the full history of interactions and are notoriously difficult to train. We propose a novel deep, partially observable RL algorithm based on modelling belief states — a technique typically used when solving tabular POMDPs, but that has traditionally been difficult to apply to more complex environments. Our approach simplifies policy learning by leveraging state information at training time, that may not be available at deployment time. We do so in two ways: first, we decouple belief state modelling (via unsupervised learning) from policy optimization (via RL); and second, we propose a representation learning approach to capture a compact set of reward-relevant features of the state. Experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on partially observable domains requiring information seeking and long-term memory.

paragraphs: An agent often has to act without observing the full state of its environment. Its current observation may be insufficient, making memory and information gathering important. Standard deep reinforcement learning approaches that condition decisions on the entire interaction history can be difficult to train. This paper instead builds policy learning around learned belief-state representations.

The method uses state information during training that may be unavailable when the policy is deployed. It separates learning the belief representation, through unsupervised learning, from optimizing the policy through reinforcement learning. It also learns a compact representation of state features relevant to reward. This separation gives policy learning a more focused input than an undifferentiated interaction history.

Experiments demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness in partially observable domains requiring information seeking and long-term memory. The contribution brings a belief-modeling strategy associated with tabular partially observable problems into more complex deep learning settings. Its practical setup depends on access to additional state information during training, while allowing deployment without that same information.
summary.tldr: Learning compact belief representations separately from policies helps reinforcement learning agents handle partial observability and long-term memory.

title: Learning Belief Representations for Partially Observable Deep RL

abstract: Health conditions among patients in intensive care units (ICUs) are monitored via electronic health records (EHRs), composed of numerical time series and lengthy clinical note sequences, both taken at $\textit{irregular}$ time intervals. Dealing with such irregularity in every modality, and integrating irregularity into multimodal representations to improve medical predictions, is a challenging problem. Our method first addresses irregularity in each single modality by (1) modeling irregular time series by dynamically incorporating hand-crafted imputation embeddings into learned interpolation embeddings via a gating mechanism, and (2) casting a series of clinical note representations as multivariate irregular time series and tackling irregularity via a time attention mechanism. We further integrate irregularity in multimodal fusion with an interleaved attention mechanism across temporal steps. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to thoroughly model irregularity in multimodalities for improving medical predictions. Our proposed methods for two medical prediction tasks consistently outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines in each single modality and multimodal fusion scenarios. Specifically, we observe relative improvements of 6.5%, 3.6%, and 4.3% in F1 for time series, clinical notes, and multimodal fusion, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods and the importance of considering irregularity in multimodal EHRs.

paragraphs: Intensive-care electronic health records contain numerical measurements and clinical notes collected at uneven intervals. Their timing complicates both learning from each source and combining them. This paper builds irregular timing into the representations of both modalities and into the mechanism that fuses them for medical prediction.

For numerical time series, a gate dynamically combines handcrafted imputation embeddings with learned interpolation embeddings. For clinical notes, the method treats sequences of note representations as multivariate irregular time series and applies time attention. An interleaved attention mechanism then integrates the modalities across temporal steps, carrying timing considerations into their interaction.
