title: Towards Efficient and Expressive Offline RL via Flow-Anchored Noise-conditioned Q-Learning

abstract: Implicit in-context learning (ICL) has newly emerged as a promising paradigm that simulates ICL behaviors in the representation space of large language models (LLMs), aiming to attain few-shot performance at zero-shot cost. However, existing approaches largely rely on injecting shift vectors into residual flows, which are typically constructed from labeled demonstrations or task-specific alignment. Such designs fall short of utilizing the structural mechanisms underlying ICL and suffer from limited generalizability. To address this, we propose In-Context Routing (ICR), a novel implicit ICL method that internalizes generalizable ICL patterns at the attention logits level. It extracts reusable structural directions that emerge during ICL and employs a learnable input-conditioned router to modulate attention logits accordingly, enabling an efficient train-once-and-reuse framework. We evaluate ICR on 12 real-world datasets spanning diverse domains and multiple LLMs. The results show that ICR consistently outperforms existing implicit ICL methods that require task-specific retrieval or training, while demonstrating robust generalization to out-of-domain tasks where they struggle. These findings position ICR to push the boundary of the practical value of ICL.

paragraphs: Implicit in-context learning seeks to reproduce the benefits of examples in a prompt through changes inside a model’s representations, aiming for few-shot performance at zero-shot cost. Existing methods often inject shift vectors derived from labeled demonstrations or task-specific alignment. This paper argues that such approaches underuse the structural mechanisms behind in-context learning and generalize poorly.

In-Context Routing instead operates on attention logits, the scores that govern how attention is distributed. It extracts reusable structural directions that arise during in-context learning. A learned router, conditioned on the current input, uses those directions to modulate attention scores. The resulting framework is designed to be trained once and reused across tasks.

Evaluation spans 12 real-world datasets from diverse domains and multiple language models. ICR consistently outperforms existing implicit methods that need task-specific retrieval or training, and shows robust generalization on out-of-domain tasks where those methods struggle. These findings support attention-level structure as a reusable basis for internalizing in-context learning behavior.
summary.tldr: In-Context Routing learns reusable, input-dependent attention adjustments that improve implicit in-context learning across tasks and domains.

title: Train Once, Reuse Everywhere: Generalizable Implicit In-Context Learning by Routing Attention

abstract: We present WhisperSplat, the first lossless steganography method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models that hides a full-resolution 2D image in a single view without any degradation of the model’s rendering quality elsewhere. Prior work embeds data by retraining or modifying model weights, altering novel-view synthesis fidelity and limiting capacity. Instead, we learn a small, view-specific noise key applied to each Gaussian’s spherical-harmonic (SH) features while keeping all other views remain indistinguishable from the original renders. We further propose a Gradual Pixel Perturbation (GPP) strategy with a cosine-decay schedule, bootstrapping fast divergence from the clean render before transitioning to a combined reconstruction and SSIM loss. Unlike prior works that are highly dependent on accurate and large pretrained decoders, our method is able to recover the hidden image through rendering with noise key, and an optional lightweight refiner to enhance recovery image quality. Across nine standard 3DGS data scenes, WhisperSplat demonstrates superior hidden image recovery quality without sacrifice in clean 3DGS model performance, when compared to prior work such as GS-Hider and KeySS.

paragraphs: WhisperSplat hides a full-resolution two-dimensional image in a single view of a 3D Gaussian Splatting model while preserving rendering quality elsewhere. Earlier approaches embed data by retraining or changing model weights, which can affect novel views and restrict capacity. This method instead learns a small noise key specific to the selected view.

The key is applied to each Gaussian’s spherical-harmonic features, allowing the hidden image to be recovered through rendering with the key. Other views remain indistinguishable from the original renders. Training uses Gradual Pixel Perturbation with a cosine-decay schedule, first encouraging rapid departure from the clean image and then shifting to a combined reconstruction and structural-similarity objective.

Across nine standard scenes, WhisperSplat reports better hidden-image recovery than methods including GS-Hider and KeySS while preserving clean model performance. The lossless claim concerns preserving the original rendering quality; recovery quality is separately evaluated and can benefit from refinement.
summary.tldr: WhisperSplat uses a view-specific noise key to hide an image in a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene while preserving clean rendering quality.

title: WhisperSplat: Lossless Steganography in 3D Gaussian Splatting

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demand substantial computational and memory resources, posing challenges for efficient deployment. Two complementary approaches have emerged to address these issues: token-adaptive layer execution, which reduces floating-point operations (FLOPs) by selectively bypassing layers, and quantization, which lowers memory footprint by reducing weight precision. However, naively integrating these techniques leads to additional accuracy degradation due to reduced redundancy in token-adaptive models. We propose QTALE (Quantization-Robust Token-Adaptive Layer Execution for LLMs), a novel framework that enables seamless integration of token-adaptive execution with quantization while preserving accuracy. Conventional token-adaptive methods reduce redundancy in two ways: (1) by limiting the diversity of training paths explored during fine-tuning, and (2) by lowering the number of parameters actively involved in inference. To overcome these limitations, QTALE introduces two key components: (1) a training strategy that ensures diverse execution paths are actively explored during fine-tuning, and (2) a post-training mechanism that allows flexible adjustment of the execution ratio at inference to reintroduce redundancy when needed. Experimental results show that QTALE enables seamless integration of token-adaptive layer execution with quantization, showing no noticeable accuracy difference, with the gap to quantization-only models kept below 0.5% on CommonsenseQA benchmarks. By combining token-adaptive execution for FLOPs reduction and quantization for memory savings, QTALE provides an effective solution for efficient LLM deployment.

paragraphs: Skipping selected layers for each token reduces language-model computation, while quantizing weights reduces memory use. Combining these methods directly can cause extra accuracy loss. This paper attributes the difficulty to reduced redundancy: token-adaptive training explores fewer execution paths, and inference activates fewer parameters that might otherwise help absorb quantization effects.

The method therefore treats the amount of active computation as something that can be adjusted alongside reduced weight precision.

Experiments show that QTALE combines these efficiency techniques with no noticeable accuracy difference in the reported comparison, keeping the gap from quantization-only models below 0.5% on CommonsenseQA benchmarks. The result supports jointly managing training-path diversity and inference execution to obtain computation and memory savings while limiting the additional accuracy cost of combining them.
summary.tldr: QTALE combines adaptive layer skipping with quantization by preserving execution-path diversity and allowing inference-time adjustments to active computation.

title: QTALE: Quantization-Robust Token-Adaptive Layer Execution for LLMs

abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a policy by verifying sampled completions and reinforcing higher-scoring outputs, but practical verifiers (e.g., incomplete unit tests or noisy judges) are prone to false positives and false negatives. We ask when such noise merely slows learning and when it reverses it. Modeling GRPO-style RLVR as a bandit over recurring reasoning modes, we derive mean-field replicator-style (natural-selection) flow on the probability simplex. The dynamics decouples into within-correct-mode competition and a one-dimensional evolution for the mass on incorrect modes, whose drift is determined solely by Youden’s index $J=\mathrm{TPR}-\mathrm{FPR}$. This yields a sharp phase transition: when $J>0$, the incorrect mass is driven toward extinction (learning); when $J=0$, the process is neutral; and when $J<0$, incorrect modes amplify until they dominate (anti-learning and collapse). In the learning regime $J>0$, noise primarily rescales convergence time (“rate, not fate”). Experiments on verifiable programming tasks under synthetic noise reproduce the predicted $J=0$ boundary. Beyond noise, the framework offers a general lens for analyzing RLVR stability, convergence, and algorithmic interventions.

The result gives a sharp condition within the analyzed model for distinguishing slower learning from systematic reinforcement of errors.
summary.tldr: In the paper's model, verifier noise slows learning when true positives exceed false positives and reverses learning when the inequality flips.

title: Rate or Fate? RLV$^\varepsilon$R: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Noisy Rewards

abstract: Diffusion models are effective for waypoint prediction in visual navigation, but standard sampling and test time guidance can produce unreliable or inefficient trajectories when updates drift off the training manifold. We propose Fisher Preserving Guidance with Outer Product Span Projection, a training-free inference method that avoids large Fisher drift associated with off-distribution actions while optimizing a task objective. Our method computes the Fisher-preserving update via a low-rank Jacobian factorization, requiring only a single backward pass per step and enabling real-time use. We further introduce Truncated Fisher Denoising Sensitivity as an uncertainty signal and use it for robust multi-sample action blending. Experiments on toy and realistic navigation benchmarks, including Maze2D with TSDF-based guidance, PushT with official Diffusion Policy weights, and visual navigation in simulation and on real robots, demonstrate consistent improvements in performance over strong diffusion-policy baselines without additional training.

Such drift can produce inefficient or unreliable trajectories. This paper proposes an inference-time method that pursues the task objective while avoiding large changes measured through Fisher geometry.

A low-rank Jacobian factorization makes the computation require only one backward pass per step, enabling real-time use. Because the intervention operates during inference, it can guide an existing diffusion model without additional training. The method therefore addresses both the direction of guidance and its computational cost.

The authors also introduce Truncated Fisher Denoising Sensitivity as an uncertainty signal for blending multiple sampled actions robustly. Experiments cover Maze2D, PushT with existing Diffusion Policy weights, simulated visual navigation, and real robots. Consistent improvements over strong diffusion-policy baselines support combining constrained guidance with uncertainty-aware action blending in the evaluated control settings.
summary.tldr: Fisher-preserving guidance improves evaluated diffusion-control tasks by constraining inference updates and blending actions using an uncertainty signal.

title: Fisher-Preserving Guidance: Training-Free Manifold Constraints for Safe Diffusion Control

abstract: We propose and study distributionally robust Markov games (DR-MGs) with the average-reward criterion as a crucial framework for multi-agent decision-making under model mismatches and over extended horizons. Under a standard irreducible assumption, we first derive a correspondence between the optimal policies and the solutions of the robust Bellman equation, based on which we further show the existence of a stationary Nash Equilibrium (NE) of the game. We further study DR-MGs under a more general weakly communicating setting. We construct a set-valued map based on the constant-gain optimal robust Bellman operator and show that its value is a subset of the best-response policies. We further prove that this map admits a fixed point, which implies the existence of NE. We then design two algorithms, Robust Nash-Iteration and robust TD Descent, with provably convergent guarantees. Finally, we show that the NE under average-reward can be approximated by the ones for the discounted DR-MGs as the discount factor approaches one. Our studies provide a comprehensive theoretical and algorithmic foundation for decision-making in complex, uncertain, and long-running multi-player environments.

paragraphs: The paper studies multi-agent decision-making when the environment’s dynamics may differ from the assumed model. Its framework combines distributional robustness with an average-reward objective, focusing on performance over extended operation. A central question is whether the players can reach a Nash equilibrium, where their policies are mutual best responses.

Under a standard irreducibility assumption, the authors connect optimal policies to solutions of a robust Bellman equation and establish the existence of a stationary equilibrium. They then consider the more general weakly communicating setting. This links the long-run formulation to discounted problems and provides both existence results and algorithms for the uncertain multi-player setting.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes equilibrium existence and convergent algorithms for robust multi-agent games with long-run average rewards.

title: Distributionally Robust Markov Games with Average Reward

abstract: Deep learning methods based on backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) have emerged as competitive alternatives to physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs). By leveraging probabilistic representations, BSDE approaches can avoid the curse of dimensionality and often admit second-order-free training objectives that do not require explicit Hessian evaluations. It has recently been established that the commonly used Euler–Maruyama (EM) time discretization induces an intrinsic bias in BSDE training losses. While high-order schemes such as Heun can fully eliminate this bias, such schemes re-introduce second-order spatial derivatives and incur substantial computational overhead. In this work, we provide a principled analysis of EM-induced loss bias and propose an unbiased, second-order-free training framework that preserves the computational advantages of BSDE methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/seojaemin22/Un-EM-BSDE.

paragraphs: Backward stochastic differential equations provide probabilistic representations that can make high-dimensional partial differential equations more tractable for deep learning. These approaches can avoid the curse of dimensionality and often train without explicit Hessian evaluations. However, the commonly used Euler–Maruyama discretization introduces an intrinsic bias into the training loss.

Higher-order schemes such as Heun can remove that bias, but they bring second-order spatial derivatives back into the calculation. This creates a computational tradeoff: eliminating the loss bias can sacrifice an important efficiency advantage of the original training formulation. The paper analyzes the source of the Euler–Maruyama-induced bias to address that tradeoff directly.

The authors propose a training framework that is both unbiased and free of second-order derivative evaluations. Its contribution is to preserve the computational advantages of the BSDE approach while removing the identified loss bias. The claim concerns the training objective and its derivative requirements, connecting the statistical correctness of that objective with the computational structure needed for high-dimensional equation solving.
summary.tldr: A BSDE training framework removes discretization-induced loss bias while avoiding costly second-order spatial derivative evaluations.

title: Unbiased and Second-Order-Free Training for High-Dimensional PDEs

abstract: Pretrained score-based diffusion models provide strong unconditional priors, yet enforcing measurement or physics consistency in inverse problems is often handled by heuristic guidance, intermittent projections, or task-specific conditional training, with limited guarantees of feasibility at the end of inference. We propose terminal-conditioned inversion for score-based SDE priors. Given a frozen Score-SDE prior and a task-defined terminal feasibility specification, we construct an associated backward stochastic differential equation whose adapted solution defines a principled inverse map from the terminal requirement to a prior state at a chosen noise level. Under standard regularity conditions, we establish existence and uniqueness of the adapted solution and obtain terminal consistency by construction. We further develop a practical neural BSDE solver that composes arbitrary pretrained diffusion priors with domain constraints without modifying the score-defined coefficients, producing an anchored prior state that enables neighborhood sampling for uncertainty characterization. Experiments on toy datasets validate stable terminal-conditioned inversion and distributionally consistent neighborhood sampling. As a real-world case study, we apply the framework to sparse-view CT reconstruction and achieve improved reconstruction quality over representative training-free baselines while satisfying strict measurement feasibility under the prescribed terminal specification.

paragraphs: A pretrained diffusion model can supply a strong prior for reconstructing data, but its output must also agree with measurements or physical requirements. Common ways of enforcing agreement offer limited guarantees about the final result. This paper instead begins with a specified terminal requirement and constructs an inverse mapping back to a state at a chosen noise level.

The mapping is defined through a backward stochastic differential equation associated with a frozen score-based diffusion prior. Under standard regularity conditions, the authors establish existence and uniqueness of its adapted solution, with terminal consistency built into the construction. A neural solver combines pretrained priors with domain constraints while leaving the score-defined coefficients unchanged.

The resulting anchored state also supports nearby sampling to characterize uncertainty. Toy experiments validate stable inversion and distributionally consistent neighborhood samples. In sparse-view CT reconstruction, the framework improves reconstruction quality over representative training-free baselines while satisfying the prescribed measurement feasibility requirement. The guarantee is therefore tied to the stated terminal specification and mathematical conditions.
summary.tldr: A backward stochastic equation connects frozen diffusion priors to specified physical constraints, with conditional theoretical guarantees and improved sparse-view CT results.

title: Backward SDEs-based Diffusion for Physics-Constrained Generation

abstract: Diffusion models have significantly advanced the field of talking head generation (THG). However, slow inference speeds and prevalent non-autoregressive paradigms severely constrain the application of diffusion-based THG models. In this study, we propose REST, a pioneering diffusion-based, real-time, end-to-end streaming audio-driven talking head generation framework. To support real-time end-to-end generation, a compact video latent space is first learned through a spatiotemporal variational autoencoder with a high compression ratio. Additionally, to enable semi-autoregressive streaming within the compact video latent space, we introduce an ID-Context Cache mechanism, which integrates ID-Sink and Context-Cache principles into key-value caching for maintaining identity consistency and temporal coherence during long-term streaming generation. Furthermore, an Asynchronous Streaming Distillation (ASD) strategy is proposed to mitigate error accumulation and enhance temporal consistency in streaming generation, leveraging a non-streaming teacher with an asynchronous noise schedule to supervise the streaming student. REST bridges the gap between autoregressive and diffusion-based approaches, achieving a breakthrough in efficiency for applications requiring real-time THG. Experimental results demonstrate that REST outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both generation speed and overall performance.

title: REST: Diffusion-based Real-time End-to-end Streaming Talking Head Generation via ID-Context Caching and Asynchronous Streaming Distillation

abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) is important in building real-world learning systems. In CLIP-based CIL, the model performs classification by comparing similarity between visual and textual embeddings obtained from template prompts, e.g., “a photo of a [CLASS]”. This seemingly monolithic matching process can be decomposed into two conceptually distinct stages: attribute extraction and attribute aggregation. For example, a model may recognize cat using attributes such as fur texture and whiskers. When learning a new class like car, the model must extract additional attributes like wheels and adjust how they are aggregated in the shared representation space. However, since only data from the current task is available, incremental updates can bias both attribute extraction and aggregation toward new classes, leading to catastrophic forgetting. Therefore, we propose AREA for attribute extraction and aggregation in CLIP-based CIL. To stabilize extraction, we anchor class-level visual and textual attributes on the hyperspherical embedding space via principal geodesic analysis. To stabilize aggregation, we learn lightweight task-specific experts with scoring and residual refinement, regularized by a variational information bottleneck objective. During inference, we perform routing over task attribute manifolds via optimal transport for more concise prediction. Experiments show that AREA consistently outperforms SOTA methods. Code is available at https://github.com/LAMDA-CL/ICML2026-AREA.

paragraphs: AREA studies how a CLIP-based classifier can learn new classes without forgetting earlier ones. It separates image–text matching into recognizing attributes and combining those attributes into a class representation. Learning a car, for example, requires identifying wheels and integrating them into the shared representation. When only current-task data is available, both processes can shift toward new classes.

To stabilize attribute extraction, AREA anchors class-level visual and textual attributes in the model’s spherical embedding space using principal geodesic analysis. To stabilize their combination, it learns small task-specific experts that score and refine representations. An information-bottleneck objective regularizes these experts, making the organization of attributes an explicit part of incremental learning.

At prediction time, optimal transport routes inputs across the attribute structures associated with different tasks. The design addresses forgetting at several stages rather than treating image–text similarity as one indivisible operation. Experiments report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, supporting this separation of attribute extraction, aggregation, and inference routing for the evaluated class-incremental settings.
summary.tldr: AREA reduces forgetting in CLIP-based incremental learning by stabilizing how attributes are extracted, combined, and routed.

title: AREA: Attribute Extraction and Aggregation for CLIP-Based Class-Incremental Learning

abstract: Instruction-based image editing (IIE) is a vital tool for iterative content creation, enabling multi-round interactions that refine visual details while preserving cross-round consistency. However, this workflow is constrained by the compute-bound nature of Diffusion Transformers (DiTs): because DiTs process tokens uniformly, they waste substantial computation on regions untouched by the instruction. We investigate the Round–Step–Layer hierarchy of DiT-based editing and identify a phenomenon we term Delayed Latent Emergence (DLE). Although pronounced latent changes emerge only in the late denoising stages, deep-layer activations within transformer blocks at the very first sampling step already diverge markedly in edited regions. Building on this insight, we propose CacheEdit, a training-free framework centered on an Adaptive Activation Cache (Acache) that exploits early-step sensitivity to detect invariant tokens and reuse their cached activations across subsequent sampling steps, thereby bypassing redundant computation. Experiments on FLUX.1 Kontext and Qwen-Image-Edit show that CacheEdit achieves up to $2.5\times$ end-to-end acceleration. Moreover, by isolating and reusing static features, CacheEdit mitigates stochastic drift and improves instruction-following and structural consistency over full-recomputation baselines.

paragraphs: Repeated instruction-based image editing often changes only part of an image, but diffusion transformers still spend computation processing all image tokens. CacheEdit investigates how to identify the regions that can reuse earlier computation while an edit develops across sampling steps and transformer layers.

The key observation concerns when changes become detectable. Large changes in the latent representation appear late in denoising, yet deep transformer layers already show substantial differences in edited regions at the first sampling step. CacheEdit uses this early signal to identify tokens that remain invariant. Its adaptive cache then reuses their activations during subsequent steps, bypassing redundant work without additional training.

Reusing static features also reduces random drift, improving instruction following and structural consistency compared with recomputing everything. The stated result connects efficiency with editing quality: preserving stable internal features can help retain unchanged content across an iterative editing workflow.
summary.tldr: CacheEdit uses early activation changes to reuse computation for unchanged image regions, achieving up to 2.5-fold faster editing with improved consistency.

title: CacheEdit: Efficient Multi-round Image Editing via Adaptive Token-wise Reuse.

abstract: Adapting to latent confounded shift remains a core challenge in modern AI. This setting is driven by hidden variables that induce spurious correlations between inputs and outputs during training, leading models to rely on non-causal shortcuts. For example, a model may learn to treat metadata (e.g., data source like "Amazon") as a proxy for positive sentiment, causing failure when the source becomes predominantly negative during deployment. To address this latent confounded shift, we introduce Causal Fine-Tuning (CFT). Using a structural causal model as an inductive bias, we derive sufficient identification conditions that motivate a fine-tuning objective for decomposing representations into high-level stable and low-level shift-sensitive components. Instantiating this framework in BERT, we show that learning such causal/spurious representations and adjusting them accordingly yield a more robust predictor. Experiments on spurious correlation injection attacks in text demonstrate that our method outperforms black-box domain generalization baselines, highlighting the benefits of explicitly modeling causal structure.

paragraphs: A model can perform well during training by relying on a relationship that later changes. The paper studies a specific source of this problem: hidden variables that create misleading associations between inputs and outputs. For example, a text model may associate a particular data source with positive sentiment, then fail when that source contains mostly negative material.

The authors derive sufficient identification conditions that motivate dividing representations into stable, high-level components and lower-level components that are sensitive to shifts. These conditions support the proposed objective; they are not presented as conditions that every successful adaptation method must satisfy.

The framework is implemented in BERT, where learning and adjusting the causal and spurious components produces a more robust predictor. Experiments involving injected spurious correlations in text outperform black-box domain generalization baselines. The findings support explicitly representing causal structure when adapting to this kind of shift, with the reported evidence coming from the studied text attacks.
summary.tldr: Causal Fine-Tuning separates stable and shift-sensitive representations to improve robustness against misleading correlations in text.

title: Causal Fine-Tuning under Latent Confounded Shift

abstract: Context management enables agentic models to solve long-horizon tasks through iterative summarization of previous interaction histories. However, this process typically incurs substantial decoding overhead for the extra summarization tokens, which significantly affect the end-to-end response latency at deployment. In this paper, we introduce CoMem, a novel framework that decouples memory management from the primary agent workflow, enabling these processes to execute in parallel. We propose a $k$-step-off asynchronous pipeline that overlaps the memory model’s summarization with the agent’s inference, effectively masking the latency of context processing. To ensure robustness under this asynchronous setting, we introduce a reward-driven training strategy that aligns the memory model to capture sufficient statistics for the agent’s decision-making. Theoretical analysis confirms that CoMem offers a superior efficiency-effectiveness trade-off compared to coupled architectures. Our extensive experimental results on SWE-Bench-Verified show that CoMem provides 1.4x latency improvements upon vanilla long-context solutions while preserving most of the performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these latency gains scale favorably with increased system throughput, offering a modular path forward for the independent optimization of agent reasoning and memory compression.

paragraphs: Agents handling long tasks often summarize earlier interactions so they can continue reasoning with a manageable context. Producing those summaries takes decoding time and can delay the overall response. CoMem separates memory management from the main agent so summarization and agent inference can proceed in parallel.

Because memory processing and action selection are no longer tightly synchronized, the memory model is trained through rewards to retain sufficient information for the agent's decisions. title: CoMem: Context Management with A Decoupled Long-Context Model

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have opened new paradigms in optimization modeling by enabling the generation of executable solver code from natural language descriptions. Despite this promise, existing approaches typically remain solver-driven: they rely on single-pass forward generation and apply limited post-hoc fixes based on solver error messages, leaving undetected semantic errors that silently produce syntactically correct but logically flawed models. To address this challenge, we propose SAC-Opt, a backward-guided correction framework that grounds optimization modeling in problem semantics rather than solver feedback. At each step, SAC-Opt aligns the original semantic anchors with those reconstructed from the generated code and selectively corrects only the mismatched components, driving convergence toward a semantically faithful model. This anchor-driven correction enables fine-grained refinement of constraint and objective logic, enhancing both fidelity and robustness without requiring additional training or supervision. Empirical results on seven public datasets demonstrate that SAC-Opt improves average modeling accuracy by 7.7%, with gains of up to 21.9% on the ComplexLP dataset. These findings highlight the importance of semantic-anchored correction in LLM-based optimization workflows to ensure faithful translation from problem intent to solver-executable code.

paragraphs: Language models can translate a natural-language optimization problem into executable solver code, but successful execution does not establish that the code expresses the intended problem. A model can contain logically incorrect constraints or objectives without triggering a solver error. SAC-Opt targets these semantic mistakes, which limited post-hoc debugging can leave undetected.

The framework repeatedly compares semantic anchors from the original problem with anchors reconstructed from the generated code. It then corrects only the components whose meanings do not match. The results support iterative checks of meaning as a useful complement to executable-code generation. The central contribution is a targeted correction process that can identify discrepancies even when the solver accepts the program.
summary.tldr: SAC-Opt improves generated optimization models by repeatedly checking their recovered meaning against the original problem and correcting mismatches.

title: SAC-Opt: Semantic Anchors for Iterative Correction in Optimization Modeling

abstract: Multi-modal spatio-temporal forecasting underpins many real-world applications but remains challenging due to the complex and evolving interactions across modalities and time steps. Moreover, the lack of interpretability in existing models limits their reliability in safety-critical scenarios. In this paper, we present CausalX, a unified and causally interpretable plug-and-play model for multi-modal spatio-temporal forecasting. CausalX achieves interpretability by learning a dynamic causal graph across modalities and time, whose edge weights quantify causal attribution strength, and are further refined by a diffusion-based generative process guided by structural priors. To overcome the absence of ground-truth causal structures, CausalX aggregates multi-source constraints from causal analysis techniques and a variational autoencoder, spanning predictive, temporal, interventional, and generative aspects to jointly learn a more comprehensive causal graph. Extensive experiments on real-world forecasting tasks, including pedestrian trajectory prediction and tropical cyclone forecasting, demonstrate that CausalX achieves superior accuracy while producing interpretable causal graphs. CausalX is modular, architecture-agnostic, and generalizable, offering a new perspective on bridging causal inference and spatio-temporal forecasting.

paragraphs: Forecasting events across space and time becomes harder when several kinds of input interact and those relationships change. CausalX addresses both prediction and interpretation by learning a dynamic graph connecting modalities and time steps. Its edge weights represent the strength of causal attribution within the model, providing a structured account of influences on a forecast.

A central challenge is that the true causal graph is unavailable. CausalX combines constraints from causal analysis methods and a variational autoencoder, drawing on predictive, temporal, interventional, and generative information. A diffusion-based generation process, guided by structural priors, further refines the graph. These components supply several complementary sources of structure for learning the relationships.

Experiments include pedestrian trajectory prediction and tropical cyclone forecasting. The authors report superior forecasting accuracy together with interpretable causal graphs. CausalX is presented as a modular, architecture-agnostic component, allowing the graph-based approach to support different forecasting models. Its stated contribution is a way to improve predictions while exposing the learned relationships across inputs and time that help explain them.
summary.tldr: CausalX combines dynamically learned causal graphs with multiple structural constraints to improve and interpret multimodal forecasting.

title: CausalX: A Unified and Causally-Interpretable Plug-and-Play Model for Multi-modal Spatio-Temporal Forecasting

abstract: Spurious correlations that lead models to correct predictions for the wrong reasons pose a critical challenge for robust real-world generalization. Existing research attributes this issue to group imbalance and addresses it by maximizing group-balanced or worst-group accuracy, which heavily relies on expensive bias annotations. A compromise approach involves predicting bias information using extensively pretrained foundation models, which requires large-scale data and is limited to physically interpretable biases. To address these challenges, we offer a novel perspective by reframing the spurious correlations as imbalances/mismatches in class-conditional distributions caused by general biases, whether interpretable or not, and propose a simple yet effective robust learning method that mitigates the need for bias annotations or predictions. With the goal of maximizing the conditional entropy (uncertainty) of the label given spurious factors, our method leverages a sample reweighting strategy to achieve class-conditional distribution balancing, which automatically highlights minority groups and classes, effectively mitigating spurious correlations and producing a debiased data distribution for classification. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that our approach consistently delivers strong overall performance, and is competitive with methods that rely on bias supervision.

paragraphs: A classifier can make correct predictions by relying on incidental patterns that stop working in a different setting. Many approaches counter these spurious correlations by balancing predefined groups, but identifying those groups requires bias annotations or predictions. This paper instead frames the problem as a mismatch between class-conditional distributions caused by biases that need not have an interpretable meaning.

The proposed method reweights training examples to balance those distributions. Its objective is to increase uncertainty about the label when only spurious factors are available. In plain terms, the method seeks a weighted dataset in which misleading factors provide less useful information about which class an example belongs to.

The reweighting automatically emphasizes minority groups and classes while mitigating the need to annotate or predict biases. Experiments and analysis show consistently strong overall performance and results competitive with methods that use bias supervision. The contribution is a distribution-balancing route to robustness that can address general biases without first requiring a human-readable account of each one.
summary.tldr: The paper improves robust classification by reweighting examples to balance class-conditional distributions without requiring explicit bias labels or predictions.

title: Class-Conditional Distribution Balancing for Group Robust Classification

abstract: Generative diffusion models can provide powerful prior probability models for inverse problems in imaging, but existing implementations suffer from two key limitations: $(i)$ the prior density is represented implicitly, and $(ii)$ they rely on likelihood approximations that introduce sampling biases. We address these challenges by introducing a new energy-based model trained for denoising with a covariance-based regularization term that enforces consistency across different measurement conditions. The trained model can compute normalized posterior densities for diverse linear inverse problems, without additional retraining or fine tuning. In addition to preserving the sampling capabilities of diffusion models, this enables previously unavailable capabilities: energy-guided adaptive sampling that adjusts schedules on-the-fly, unbiased Metropolis-Hastings correction steps, and blind estimation of the degradation operator via Bayes rule. We validate the method on multiple datasets (ImageNet, CelebA, AFHQ) and tasks (inpainting, deblurring), demonstrating competitive or superior performance to established baselines.

paragraphs: Imaging inverse problems reconstruct an image from incomplete or degraded measurements. Diffusion models provide useful prior knowledge for this task, but the paper identifies two obstacles: their prior density is implicit, and approximate likelihoods can bias sampling. The proposed energy-based model aims to retain generative sampling while making posterior probabilities explicitly computable.

The model is trained for denoising with a covariance-based regularizer that enforces consistency across measurement conditions. After training, it can compute normalized posterior densities for different linear inverse problems without further training or fine-tuning. This connects one learned model to multiple reconstruction settings through a consistent probabilistic representation.

Explicit posterior densities enable energy-guided adjustment of sampling schedules, unbiased Metropolis–Hastings correction steps, and Bayesian estimation of an unknown degradation operator. Evaluations on ImageNet, CelebA, and AFHQ include inpainting and deblurring, with competitive or superior performance relative to established baselines. The contribution therefore concerns both reconstruction quality and the additional inference operations made possible by accessible posterior densities.
summary.tldr: A denoising energy model computes normalized posteriors across linear imaging problems, enabling adaptive sampling, sampling corrections, and degradation estimation without retraining.

abstract: Multinomial distributions are often used to model text documents. However, they do not capture well the phenomenon that words in a document tend to appear in bursts: if a word appears once, it is more likely to appear again. In this paper, we propose the Dirichlet compound multinomial model (DCM) as an alternative to the multinomial. The DCM model has one additional degree of freedom, which allows it to capture burstiness. We show experimentally that the DCM is substantially better than the multinomial at modeling text data, measured by perplexity. We also show using three standard document collections that the DCM leads to better classification than the multinomial model. DCM performance is comparable to that obtained with multiple heuristic changes to the multinomial model.

paragraphs: Words often appear in bursts within a document: once a word occurs, further occurrences become more likely. The paper argues that the multinomial distributions commonly used for text do not capture this behavior well. It proposes the Dirichlet compound multinomial, or DCM, as an alternative document model.

The DCM has one additional degree of freedom that enables it to represent burstiness. This gives the model a way to account for repetition as part of its probability distribution. The change directly addresses a stated property of text, making the modeling choice depend on how word occurrences behave within documents.

Experiments show substantially better text modeling than the multinomial when measured by perplexity. On three standard document collections, the DCM also improves classification over the multinomial model. Its performance is comparable to a multinomial model augmented with several heuristic modifications. Together, these findings show benefits both for assigning probabilities to text and for classifying documents, with the additional modeling flexibility providing an alternative to those heuristic adjustments.
summary.tldr: A Dirichlet compound multinomial captures repeated-word bursts and improves text modeling and document classification in the reported experiments.

title: Modeling word burstiness using the Dirichlet distribution

abstract: We present a new machine learning framework called “self-taught learning” for using unlabeled data in supervised classification tasks. We do not assume that the unlabeled data follows the same class labels or generative distribution as the labeled data. Thus, we would like to use a large number of unlabeled images (or audio samples, or text documents) randomly downloaded from the Internet to improve performance on a given image (or audio, or text) classification task. Such unlabeled data is significantly easier to obtain than in typical semi-supervised or transfer learning settings, making selftaught learning widely applicable to many practical learning problems. We describe an approach to self-taught learning that uses sparse coding to construct higher-level features using the unlabeled data. These features form a succinct input representation and significantly improve classification performance. When using an SVM for classification, we further show how a Fisher kernel can be learned for this representation.

paragraphs: Self-taught learning uses unlabeled data to help a supervised classification task without assuming that the unlabeled examples share the labeled data's classes or generative distribution. This broadens the possible source material: the motivating examples include images, audio, and text collected from the Internet, where abundant unlabeled data may be easier to obtain than task-specific examples.

The proposed approach uses sparse coding to learn higher-level features from that unlabeled material. These features then provide a compact representation for the classification task. The transferred knowledge is therefore a representation learned from the additional data, allowing the supervised learner to benefit without requiring labels for those examples.

The authors report that the resulting features significantly improve classification performance. They also show how to learn a Fisher kernel for the representation when classification uses an SVM. The contribution combines a broader setting for learning from unlabeled data with a concrete feature-learning method. Removing the shared-distribution assumption expands where the framework can be considered; it does not assert that every unrelated collection will improve every classifier.
summary.tldr: Self-taught learning uses sparse coding on unlabeled data to improve classification without assuming matching classes or data distributions.

title: Self-taught learning: transfer learning from unlabeled data

abstract: We propose a new method to quantify the solution stability of a large class of combinatorial optimization problems arising in machine learning. As practical example we apply the method to correlation clustering, clustering aggregation, modularity clustering, and relative performance significance clustering. Our method is extensively motivated by the idea of linear programming relaxations. We prove that when a relaxation is used to solve the original clustering problem, then the solution stability calculated by our method is conservative, that is, it never overestimates the solution stability of the true, unrelaxed problem. We also demonstrate how our method can be used to compute the entire path of optimal solutions as the optimization problem is increasingly perturbed. Experimentally, our method is shown to perform well on a number of benchmark problems.

paragraphs: An optimization procedure returns a solution, but understanding how that solution responds to changes in the problem is a separate question. This paper introduces a method for quantifying solution stability across a large class of combinatorial optimization problems in machine learning. Its development is strongly motivated by linear programming relaxations.

The authors apply the method to correlation clustering, clustering aggregation, modularity clustering, and relative performance significance clustering. They prove that when a relaxation is used to solve the original clustering problem, their calculated stability is conservative. Specifically, it never overestimates the stability of the original, unrelaxed problem, giving the estimate a clear direction of reliability.

The method can also compute the entire sequence of optimal solutions as the optimization problem is increasingly perturbed. This describes how solutions change beyond a single stability assessment. Experiments show good performance on several benchmark problems. Together, these contributions provide both a conservative stability measure and a way to follow changes in the optimizer under growing perturbations.
summary.tldr: A relaxation-based method conservatively measures clustering solution stability and can trace optimal solutions as perturbations increase.

title: Solution stability in linear programming relaxations: graph partitioning and unsupervised learning

abstract: In Passive POMDPs actions do not affect the world state, but still incur costs. When the agent is bounded by information-processing constraints, it can only keep an approximation of the belief. We present a variational principle for the problem of maintaining the information which is most useful for minimizing the cost, and introduce an efficient and simple algorithm for finding an optimum.
originalAbstract: In Passive POMDPs actions do not affect the world state, but still incur costs. When the agent is bounded by information-processing constraints, it can only keep an approximation of the belief. We present a variational principle for the problem of maintaining the information which is most useful for minimizing the cost, and introduce an efficient and simple algorithm for finding an optimum.

paragraphs: The paper studies decision-making in passive partially observable Markov decision processes. In this setting, the agent cannot change how the world's state evolves through its actions, but its choices still incur costs. The planning problem therefore concerns choosing well under uncertainty about a world whose evolution the agent does not control.

An information-processing limit prevents the agent from keeping a complete belief about the hidden state. It must maintain an approximation instead. The central question becomes which information deserves to be retained when the purpose of that information is to support lower-cost decisions. This connects the representation of uncertainty directly to the agent's decision objective.

The authors present a variational principle for retaining the information most useful for minimizing cost, together with a simple, efficient algorithm for finding an optimum. The contribution gives a principled way to approach belief approximation under processing constraints. Its scope is the passive setting: actions have costs, but they do not alter the underlying world state.
summary.tldr: A variational approach helps information-limited agents retain the belief information most useful for minimizing costs in passive POMDPs.

title: Bounded Planning in Passive POMDPs

abstract: LSTD is one of the most popular reinforcement learning algorithms for value function approximation. Whenever the number of samples is larger than the number of features, LSTD must be paired with some form of regularization. In particular, L1-regularization methods tends to perform feature selection by promoting sparsity and thus they are particularly suited in high–dimensional problems. Nonetheless, since LSTD is not a simple regression algorithm but it solves a fixed–point problem, the integration with L1-regularization is not straightforward and it might come with some drawbacks (see e.g., the P-matrix assumption for LASSO-TD). In this paper we introduce a novel algorithm obtained by integrating LSTD with the Dantzig Selector. In particular, we investigate the performance of the algorithm and its relationship with existing regularized approaches, showing how it overcomes some of the drawbacks of existing solutions.

Whenever the number of samples is larger than the number of features, LSTD must be paired with some form of regularization. In particular, L1-regularization methods tends to perform feature selection by promoting sparsity and thus they are particularly suited in high–dimensional problems. Nonetheless, since LSTD is not a simple regression algorithm but it solves a fixed–point problem, the integration with L1-regularization is not straightforward and it might come with some drawbacks (see e.g., the P-matrix assumption for LASSO-TD). In this paper we introduce a novel algorithm obtained by integrating LSTD with the Dantzig Selector. In particular, we investigate the performance of the algorithm and its relationship with existing regularized approaches, showing how it overcomes some of the drawbacks of existing solutions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to regularize least-squares temporal difference learning, or LSTD, when approximating value functions in reinforcement learning. A central concern is choosing useful features from a potentially large collection. Regularization based on the L1 penalty encourages sparse solutions, allowing many feature weights to become zero and making it attractive for this purpose.

Applying this idea to LSTD is more complicated than applying it to ordinary regression. LSTD solves a fixed-point problem, so a regularization method must fit that structure. Existing combinations can introduce additional requirements or drawbacks; the abstract identifies the P-matrix assumption used by LASSO-TD as one example.

The authors introduce an alternative that combines LSTD with the Dantzig Selector. They investigate its performance and connections to other regularized approaches, showing that it avoids some drawbacks of existing solutions. The contribution is a different route to sparse value-function approximation that accounts for the structure of temporal difference learning, rather than treating its integration with regularization as straightforward.
summary.tldr: Combining LSTD with the Dantzig Selector offers a route to sparse value-function approximation that overcomes some drawbacks of existing regularized methods.

title: A Dantzig Selector Approach to Temporal Difference Learning
